chem_edx.1.0.summary: Our model of the atom has changed as new evidence was discovered. Dalton pictured atoms as tiny solid spheres that could not be divided; Thomson's discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model; Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment showed that atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with mostly empty space around it; Bohr placed electrons in fixed shells; and Chadwick discovered the neutron inside the nucleus. This story shows how scientific models are tested against evidence and replaced when they cannot explain new results.

core.p: Nobody can see inside an atom directly, so scientists build **models** that explain the observations they have. When an experiment produces a result that the existing model cannot explain, the model has to be **modified or replaced**. The development of the atomic model is the classic example of this.
bullets: A **scientific model** is a simplified description used to explain observations and make predictions.
A model is accepted while it explains all the evidence; it is changed when **new evidence** contradicts it.
New evidence often comes from **new technology** or new experiments (e.g. cathode ray tubes, radioactive sources).
Each new model kept the parts of the old one that still worked and changed the parts that did not.
Edexcel asks you to describe **how Dalton's model changed because of the discovery of subatomic particles**.

callouts.p: Dalton solid sphere, then Thomson plum pudding, then Rutherford nuclear model, then Bohr electron shells, then Chadwick adds the neutron.

core.p: In the early 1800s **John Dalton** proposed that all matter is made of atoms. In his model atoms were **tiny solid spheres that could not be divided** into anything smaller.
bullets: All matter is made of tiny particles called **atoms**.
Atoms are **solid spheres** and **cannot be broken down** into smaller particles.
Atoms of the **same element are identical** (same mass and properties).
Atoms of **different elements are different** (different masses).
Atoms combine in fixed whole-number ratios to form compounds.
Dalton's model explained the fixed ratios in compounds, but had **no internal structure**: no charges and no particles inside the atom.

callouts.p: The idea that atoms cannot be divided was disproved by the discovery of subatomic particles. The idea that all atoms of an element are identical was disproved by isotopes.

core.p: In 1897 **J.J. Thomson** experimented with cathode rays and showed that they were streams of tiny **negatively charged particles** much smaller and lighter than any atom. These were **electrons**, the first subatomic particle discovered.
bullets: The particles were the same whatever metal was used, so they must be **part of all atoms**.
This proved that atoms **can be divided**: they contain smaller particles, so Dalton's model had to change.
Atoms are **neutral overall**, so if they contain negative electrons they must also contain **positive charge** to balance it.
The electron is very light: about **1/1836** (roughly 1/2000) of the mass of a hydrogen atom.

callouts.t: Why the model had to change
callouts.p: Discovering the electron showed atoms have internal structure. Since atoms are neutral, there had to be positive charge too, which led to the plum pudding model.

core.p: Thomson suggested that the atom is a **ball of positive charge** with **negative electrons embedded in it**, like plums in a pudding (or currants in a bun).
bullets: The **positive charge is spread throughout** the whole atom.
Negative **electrons are scattered** through the positive 'pudding'.
The total negative charge of the electrons **balances** the positive charge, so the atom is neutral.
The mass is spread evenly through the atom: there is **no nucleus** and **no empty space**.
This model was accepted until the alpha particle scattering experiment produced results it could not explain.

callouts.p: A model in which the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

core.p: In about 1909, **Geiger and Marsden**, working under **Ernest Rutherford**, fired **alpha particles** (small, fast, positively charged particles) at a very thin sheet of **gold foil** and recorded where they went using a detector screen.
bullets: Alpha particles are **positive** and relatively heavy, and travel very fast.
Gold foil was used because it can be hammered extremely thin (only a few hundred atoms thick).
The experiment was done in a vacuum so the alpha particles were not stopped by air.
A detector (a zinc sulfide screen that gives tiny flashes) was moved around the foil to count particles at different angles.
If the plum pudding model were correct, the spread-out positive charge would be too weak to deflect the fast alpha particles much, so they should **all pass straight through** with tiny deflections.

core.p: The results were a huge surprise. Most alpha particles went straight through, but a few were deflected through large angles and a very small number **bounced back** towards the source. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back and hit you.
bullets: Each observation leads directly to a conclusion about the atom.
The very small number bouncing back is the key evidence that destroyed the plum pudding model.

head: Observation
Conclusion about the atom
rows: Most alpha particles passed straight through
Most of the atom is empty space
Some were deflected (scattered) through small or large angles
The centre of the atom carries a positive charge that repels alpha particles
A very small number bounced straight back
The mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus
Very few particles were strongly deflected
The nucleus is very small compared with the whole atom

callouts.p: Exam questions usually give 2 marks per result: 1 for the observation and 1 for what it shows. Always pair them.

core.p: In 1911 Rutherford used these results to propose the **nuclear model**: a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** at the centre, containing almost all the mass, with electrons **around** it and the rest of the atom being **empty space**.
bullets: The **nucleus is positively charged** and contains nearly all the **mass** of the atom.
The nucleus is **tiny**: the radius of an atom is roughly **100 000 times** the radius of its nucleus.
**Electrons** move around the nucleus at a relatively large distance.
Most of the atom is **empty space**.
Rutherford later showed that the positive charge in the nucleus is carried by particles he called **protons**.

callouts.p: Plum pudding: positive charge and mass spread out, no empty space. Nuclear: positive charge and mass concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, mostly empty space.

core.h: Comparing the plum pudding and nuclear models
core.p: A common exam question asks you to compare the two models. Make direct comparisons point by point.
bullets: Both models contain **negative electrons** and are **neutral overall**.
Use comparative words such as 'whereas' or 'but' to make the comparison clear.

core.p: Rutherford's model had a problem: electrons moving around a nucleus were expected to lose energy and spiral into it, so atoms would collapse. In 1913 **Niels Bohr** suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus only at **specific distances**, in fixed **shells** (energy levels).
bullets: Electrons occupy **shells** at fixed distances from the nucleus.
Each shell has a fixed **energy**; electrons in a shell do not lose energy, so the atom is stable.
Bohr's calculations agreed with **experimental observations** (the light given out by heated atoms).
Electrons can move between shells by absorbing or emitting energy.
This is the model you use when drawing electronic configurations such as 2.8.1.

core.p: Scientists noticed that the mass of most nuclei was greater than the mass of their protons alone. In 1932 **James Chadwick** provided evidence for a **neutral** particle in the nucleus with about the same mass as a proton: the **neutron**.
bullets: Neutrons have **no charge** and a relative mass of **1**, the same as a proton.
They explained the 'missing mass' of nuclei.
The neutron also explained the existence of **isotopes**: atoms of the same element with different masses, which contradicted Dalton's idea that all atoms of an element are identical.
This completed the model used at GCSE: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells around it.

callouts.p: Electron (1897), then nucleus (1911), then proton (around 1919), then neutron (1932).

core.h: How Dalton's model changed: the full picture
core.p: Edexcel's spec point asks how Dalton's model changed because of subatomic particles. Link each discovery to the change it caused.
bullets: **Electron** discovered: atoms are not indivisible; they contain smaller charged particles.
**Nucleus** discovered: atoms are not solid; they are mostly empty space with a dense centre.
**Proton** identified: the positive charge of the nucleus is carried by protons, and the number of protons defines the element.
**Neutron** discovered: atoms of one element can have different masses (isotopes), so they are not all identical.
Dalton's ideas that matter is made of atoms and that atoms combine in fixed ratios **survived** all these changes.

callouts.p: Structure a 6-mark answer in time order: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford (with evidence), Bohr, Chadwick. For each give the model and the evidence that caused the change.

core.h: The modern view and how science works
core.p: The model of the atom is still developing, which shows that scientific knowledge is **tentative**: it is the best explanation of current evidence, not final truth.
bullets: Ideas were checked by **other scientists** repeating experiments (peer review), which made them more widely accepted.
Models are judged by how well they **explain observations** and **predict** new results.
Older models are still useful for some purposes: Dalton's spheres are fine for showing particles in states of matter.
Even Bohr's shell model is a simplification, but it explains chemical bonding and the periodic table well at GCSE.

analogy.t: Working out what is inside a wrapped present
analogy.p: Imagine you cannot open a box, so you throw tiny ball bearings at it and watch how they come out. If nearly all pass straight through but a few bounce back hard, you conclude the box is mostly empty with something small and very heavy in the middle. That is what Rutherford did with alpha particles and gold atoms. Each new test changes your idea of what is inside, just as each discovery changed the atomic model. The analogy breaks down because a real nucleus repels alpha particles by electrical (positive-positive) repulsion without the particles ever touching it, whereas ball bearings bounce only by physical collisions.

terms.d: A simplified representation used to explain observations and make predictions; it is changed when new evidence does not fit.
Atoms are tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided; atoms of the same element are identical.
A particle smaller than an atom: proton, neutron or electron.
Negatively charged subatomic particle with very small mass, found in shells around the nucleus; discovered by Thomson.
Thomson's model of the atom as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
A small, fast-moving, positively charged particle given out by some radioactive substances.
Experiment by Geiger and Marsden (under Rutherford) firing alpha particles at thin gold foil, which led to the nuclear model.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing almost all its mass (protons and neutrons).
Rutherford's model: a tiny positive nucleus containing most of the mass, surrounded by electrons and mostly empty space.
Changed direction; alpha particles were deflected by repulsion from the positive nucleus.
A fixed energy level at a set distance from the nucleus where electrons are found (Bohr).
Positively charged particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1.
Uncharged particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1; discovered by Chadwick in 1932.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The region of the atom outside the nucleus where there is almost no mass; it makes up most of the atom's volume.

mistakes.w: Most alpha particles passed through because the gold foil was thin.
mistakes.r: Most passed straight through because most of the atom is empty space.

mistakes.w: Some alpha particles bounced back because they hit electrons.
mistakes.r: They were repelled by the small, dense, positively charged nucleus; electrons are far too light to deflect them.

mistakes.w: The alpha particles were attracted to the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Alpha particles and the nucleus are both positive, so the alpha particles are repelled.

mistakes.w: Rutherford discovered the electron.
mistakes.r: Thomson discovered the electron; Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) discovered the nucleus.

mistakes.w: In the plum pudding model the electrons orbit the positive charge.
mistakes.r: In the plum pudding model electrons are embedded in (spread through) a ball of positive charge.

mistakes.w: The nuclear model says the nucleus contains protons, neutrons and electrons.
mistakes.r: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons are outside the nucleus in shells.

mistakes.w: Dalton's model was completely wrong.
mistakes.r: Dalton's ideas that matter is made of atoms that combine in fixed ratios were kept; the ideas of indivisible, identical, solid atoms were changed.

mistakes.w: Bohr discovered the neutron.
mistakes.r: Bohr proposed electron shells (1913); Chadwick discovered the neutron (1932).

exam.q: Name the subatomic particle discovered by J.J. Thomson.
model: Electron.
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark.

exam.q: Describe Dalton's model of the atom.
model: Atoms are tiny solid spheres.
Atoms cannot be divided / broken down (atoms of the same element are identical).
exam.tip: Use the words 'solid' and 'cannot be divided'.

exam.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
model: A ball / sphere of positive charge.
With (negative) electrons embedded / scattered in it.
exam.tip: Both the positive charge and the electrons must be described.

exam.q: Explain why the discovery of the electron meant that Dalton's model had to be changed.
model: Electrons are particles smaller than atoms, so atoms can be divided / have internal structure.
Atoms are neutral so there must also be positive charge in the atom.
exam.tip: Link the discovery to the specific part of Dalton's model it disproved.

exam.q: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this show about the atom?
model: Most of the atom is empty space.
exam.tip: Do not mention the foil being thin.

exam.q: Explain why a few alpha particles were deflected back towards the source.
model: They approached a (very small) nucleus head on / very closely.
The nucleus is positively charged so it repelled the positive alpha particles.
The nucleus contains most of the mass / is dense, so it could turn back the alpha particles.
exam.tip: Repulsion between positive charges is the key physics; say 'repelled', not 'hit'.

exam.q: Give two differences between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model of the atom.
model: Plum pudding: positive charge spread throughout, whereas nuclear: positive charge concentrated in the nucleus.
Plum pudding has no empty space / no nucleus, whereas nuclear model is mostly empty space with a nucleus (mass concentrated in the centre).
exam.tip: Each difference must state both sides of the comparison.

exam.q: State the contribution of Niels Bohr to the model of the atom.
model: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed shells / at specific distances (energy levels).
exam.tip: Bohr = shells.

exam.q: Explain how the discovery of the neutron changed ideas about atoms of the same element.
model: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons (isotopes).
So atoms of the same element can have different masses / are not all identical, as Dalton said.
exam.tip: Connect neutrons to isotopes and back to Dalton.

exam.q: Describe how the model of the atom has changed from Dalton's model to the model used today. Refer to the evidence that caused each change.
model: Dalton: atoms are solid spheres that cannot be divided.
Thomson discovered the electron, showing atoms contain smaller particles.
This led to the plum pudding model: ball of positive charge with electrons embedded.
Alpha scattering: most went through (empty space); a few bounced back (small dense positive nucleus).
Rutherford proposed the nuclear model with electrons around a positive nucleus.
Bohr placed electrons in fixed shells; Chadwick discovered neutrons in the nucleus.
exam.tip: Level-marked: a clear time sequence with evidence linked to each change reaches the top level.

worked.q: A student is given these results from the scattering experiment: (1) most alpha particles passed through undeflected, (2) some were deflected through small angles, (3) about 1 in many thousands bounced back. Use each result to build a model of the atom.
steps: Result 1: undeflected particles met nothing that could push them, so most of the atom is empty space.
Result 2: deflection means a force acted. Alpha particles are positive, so the force is repulsion from positive charge in the atom.
Result 3: to turn a fast, heavy alpha particle completely around, the positive charge must be concentrated with a large mass in one place.
Because so few bounced back, that concentrated region must be tiny compared with the whole atom.
Electrons are needed outside this region to make the atom neutral overall.
worked.ans: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass, surrounded by electrons, with most of the atom being empty space: Rutherford's nuclear model.

worked.q: Explain why the plum pudding model predicts that all alpha particles should pass straight through the gold foil.
steps: In the plum pudding model the positive charge is spread thinly throughout the atom.
The mass is also spread out, so there is no single dense region.
Alpha particles are fast and relatively heavy, so the weak, spread-out charge produces only a tiny force on them.
Electrons are far too light to change the path of an alpha particle significantly.
worked.ans: Spread-out positive charge and mass cannot exert a large enough force to deflect fast alpha particles much, so the model predicts they all pass through with at most tiny deflections. The observed back-scattering therefore disproved it.

chem_edx.1.1.summary: An atom has a tiny, positively charged nucleus, made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons arranged in shells. The nucleus is extremely small compared with the whole atom but contains almost all of its mass, because protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1 while an electron's is only 1/1836. Atoms are neutral because they contain equal numbers of protons (+1) and electrons (-1), and every atom of a given element has the same number of protons, a number unique to that element.

core.h: The basic structure of an atom
core.p: Every atom has two regions: a tiny central **nucleus** and the surrounding space where the **electrons** are found. The nucleus is **positively charged** and the electrons are **negatively charged**.
bullets: The **nucleus** is at the centre and contains **protons** and **neutrons**.
**Electrons** move around the nucleus in **shells** (energy levels).
The nucleus is **positive** because protons are positive and neutrons are neutral.
Most of the volume of the atom is the space occupied by the electrons; almost all the **mass** is in the nucleus.
Protons and neutrons together are sometimes called **nucleons**.

callouts.p: An atom is a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons; the nuclear radius is much smaller than that of the atom and almost all of the mass is in the nucleus.

fig.cap: A lithium atom: a nucleus of 3 protons and 4 neutrons, surrounded by 3 electrons in two shells (2 in the first shell, 1 in the second). Not to scale: the real nucleus is far smaller.

core.p: You must recall the **relative charge** and **relative mass** of each subatomic particle. 'Relative' means compared with a standard: a proton is given a mass of 1 and a charge of +1, and the others are measured against it.
bullets: Protons and neutrons have the **same relative mass (1)**.
The electron's mass is so small (**1/1836**) that it is often described as **negligible** or almost zero.
Proton and electron charges are **equal in size but opposite in sign**.
The **neutron has no charge** (it is neutral), which is where its name comes from.

callouts.p: Proton: +1, mass 1. Neutron: 0, mass 1. Electron: -1, mass 1/1836. This is one of the most frequently tested facts in Topic 1.

fig.cap: Relative charge and relative mass of the three subatomic particles. The electron has the same size of charge as the proton but a tiny fraction of its mass.

core.p: The nucleus contains **protons and neutrons** held tightly together. Because both have a relative mass of 1 and they are packed into a tiny volume, the nucleus is extremely **dense**.
bullets: Protons give the nucleus its **positive charge**; the charge of the nucleus equals the number of protons.
Neutrons add **mass** but no charge.
Hydrogen-1 is the only common atom with **no neutrons**: its nucleus is a single proton.
Electrons are **never** in the nucleus.
The number of neutrons does not change which element an atom is.

callouts.p: A common error is to say the nucleus contains electrons. The nucleus contains only protons and neutrons.

core.h: Size: the nucleus is tiny compared with the atom
core.p: Atoms are extremely small, with a radius of about **0.1 nm (1 x 10^-10 m)**. The nucleus is tens of thousands of times smaller still: its radius is roughly **1/100 000** of the radius of the atom. So almost all of an atom is empty space where the electrons move.
bullets: If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea at the centre spot.
The radius of a nucleus is of the order of **1 x 10^-15 m**.
Electrons are spread out over the whole volume of the atom, so they determine the atom's **size**.
Because the nucleus is so small but holds almost all the mass, it is extraordinarily dense.
This structure explains why most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil.

callouts.p: The nuclear radius is much smaller than the atomic radius, AND almost all the mass is in the nucleus. Both are needed in a full description.

fig.cap: Atom versus nucleus scale (not drawn to scale: a true-scale nucleus would be invisible at this size). The atom's radius is about 100 000 times the nucleus's radius.

core.h: Mass: almost all of it is in the nucleus
core.p: Each proton and neutron has a relative mass of 1, while an electron has only 1/1836. So even in a large atom, the electrons contribute a tiny fraction of the total mass.
bullets: In a carbon-12 atom: 6 protons + 6 neutrons give a mass of 12; 6 electrons add only 6/1836, about 0.003.
So more than **99.9%** of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
This is why the **mass number** of an atom counts only protons and neutrons.
When an atom gains or loses electrons to form an ion, its mass hardly changes.

core.h: Why atoms are neutral: equal protons and electrons
core.p: An atom has **no overall charge**. A proton has a charge of +1 and an electron has a charge of -1, which are **equal in size and opposite in sign**. Neutrons have no charge. So for the charges to cancel, an atom must contain **equal numbers of protons and electrons**.
bullets: Total positive charge = number of protons x (+1).
Total negative charge = number of electrons x (-1).
Neutral atom: number of protons = number of electrons, so the charges add up to zero.
Example: a sodium atom has 11 protons (+11) and 11 electrons (-11), so overall charge = 0.
Neutrons do not affect the charge, so the number of neutrons can be anything without changing neutrality.
If the numbers are unequal, the particle is an **ion**, not an atom (covered later in the topic).

callouts.p: Say: protons and electrons have equal but opposite charges (+1 and -1); atoms have equal numbers of each, so the charges cancel; neutrons have no charge.

core.h: Same element, same number of protons
core.p: What makes an atom belong to a particular element is the **number of protons** in its nucleus. All atoms of the same element have the same number of protons, and this number is **unique** to that element: no two elements share it.
bullets: Every carbon atom has **6 protons**; every oxygen atom has **8 protons**.
If an atom had 7 protons it would not be carbon or oxygen: it would be nitrogen.
The number of protons is called the **atomic number** (details in 1.7-1.10).
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of **neutrons** but are still the same element.
Because neutral atoms have protons = electrons, all neutral atoms of an element also have the same number of electrons, giving them the same chemical properties.

callouts.p: Atoms of a given element have the same number of protons in the nucleus, and this number is unique to that element.

core.p: Electrons are arranged in **shells** (energy levels) at different distances from the nucleus. Shells closer to the nucleus have lower energy and fill first.
bullets: Electrons are attracted to the nucleus because they are **negative** and the nucleus is **positive**.
Inner shells are filled before outer shells.
For the first 20 elements: the first shell holds up to **2**, the second up to **8**, the third up to **8** before the fourth starts.
The arrangement of electrons determines how an atom **reacts**; the nucleus is not involved in chemical reactions.
Detailed electronic configurations are covered in 1.19-1.20.

core.h: Why the electrons matter for chemistry
core.p: Chemical reactions involve only the **electrons**, especially those in the outer shell. The nucleus stays unchanged. This links atomic structure to everything else in chemistry.
bullets: In ionic bonding, electrons are **transferred**; in covalent bonding, electrons are **shared**.
The number of protons fixes the number of electrons in the neutral atom, which fixes its chemical behaviour.
Changing the nucleus (number of protons) would make a different element; this happens only in nuclear reactions, never in chemical ones.

callouts.p: In chemical reactions, atoms are not created or destroyed and nuclei do not change: only electrons are rearranged.

core.h: Relative values and why we use them
core.p: The actual mass of a proton is about 1.67 x 10^-27 kg and its charge is about 1.6 x 10^-19 C. These numbers are awkward, so chemists use **relative** values: everything is compared with the proton.
bullets: Relative mass compares each particle's mass with that of a proton (taken as 1).
Relative charge compares each particle's charge with that of a proton (taken as +1).
Relative values have **no units**.
Edexcel expects the electron mass as **1/1836**; 'negligible' or 'almost 0' is often also accepted.

core.p: This model is supported by the evidence from the development of the atomic model (spec point 1.1). Knowing why we believe it helps with explanation questions.
bullets: Alpha particles mostly passing through gold foil supports a **mostly empty** atom.
Alpha particles bouncing back supports a **tiny, dense, positive nucleus**.
The discovery of the **neutron** explains why nuclear masses are larger than the mass of the protons alone.
Bohr's work supports electrons in **fixed shells**.

analogy.t: A pea in a football stadium
analogy.p: Picture a football stadium with a pea on the centre spot. The pea is the nucleus: tiny, but heavier than everything else in the stadium put together. A few midges buzzing around the outer stands are the electrons: they mark out how big the atom is but weigh almost nothing. Everything between is empty space. The analogy breaks down because the electrons are not tiny objects following set paths like midges; they exist in shells (energy levels), and they are held in place by electrostatic attraction to the positive nucleus, which a pea does not have.

terms.d: The smallest particle of an element; a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, containing protons and neutrons and almost all of the mass.
Subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
Subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative charge 0 and relative mass 1.
Subatomic particle in shells around the nucleus with relative charge -1 and relative mass 1/1836.
A particle smaller than an atom: proton, neutron or electron.
The charge of a particle compared with the charge of a proton (+1).
The mass of a particle compared with the mass of a proton (1).
So small it can be ignored; used to describe the mass of an electron.
An energy level at a fixed distance from the nucleus where electrons are found.
Having no overall charge; an atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
The radius of the nucleus, about 1/100 000 of the radius of the atom.
The radius of an atom, about 1 x 10^-10 m (0.1 nm).
A substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons in the nucleus.
The particles in the nucleus: protons and neutrons.

mistakes.w: The nucleus contains protons, neutrons and electrons.
mistakes.r: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons only; electrons are in shells around it.

mistakes.w: The neutron has a charge of -1.
mistakes.r: The neutron has a relative charge of 0 (no charge).

mistakes.w: The electron has a relative mass of 0.
mistakes.r: Relative mass of the electron is 1/1836 (negligible), not exactly zero.

mistakes.w: The electron has a relative mass of -1.
mistakes.r: Mass cannot be negative: the electron's relative charge is -1 and its relative mass is 1/1836.

mistakes.w: Atoms are neutral because they have equal numbers of protons and neutrons.
mistakes.r: Atoms are neutral because they have equal numbers of protons and electrons, whose charges are equal and opposite.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is large compared with the atom.
mistakes.r: The nucleus is tiny: the nuclear radius is much smaller (about 1/100 000) than the atomic radius.

mistakes.w: Most of the mass is in the electrons because they take up most of the space.
mistakes.r: Almost all the mass is in the nucleus; electrons occupy most of the volume but have negligible mass.

mistakes.w: Atoms of the same element have the same number of neutrons.
mistakes.r: Atoms of the same element have the same number of protons; neutron numbers can differ.

exam.q: State the relative charge of a neutron.
model: 0 (no charge / neutral).
exam.tip: Write 0, not 'nothing' or a blank.

exam.q: State the relative mass of an electron.
model: 1/1836 (accept negligible / almost zero).
exam.tip: 1/1836 is safest; never write a negative mass.

exam.q: Complete the table of relative charges and relative masses for the proton, neutron and electron.
model: Proton: charge +1, mass 1.
Neutron: charge 0, mass 1.
Electron: charge -1, mass 1/1836.
exam.tip: Usually 1 mark per correct row; include the + sign for the proton.

exam.q: Name the two types of particle found in the nucleus of an atom.
model: Protons and neutrons.
exam.tip: Both are needed for the mark.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom.
model: A (positively charged) nucleus containing protons and neutrons.
Surrounded by (negatively charged) electrons in shells.
The nucleus is very small compared with the atom / contains almost all the mass.
exam.tip: Mention charge, location of each particle, and size or mass.

exam.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
model: Protons and electrons have equal and opposite charges (+1 and -1).
An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel.
exam.tip: Neutrons are not part of the reason; do not say protons cancel neutrons.

exam.q: Explain why almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
model: Protons and neutrons (in the nucleus) each have relative mass 1.
Electrons have a much smaller / negligible mass (1/1836).
exam.tip: Compare the masses using the numbers.

exam.q: An atom has 15 protons. State how many electrons it has and explain your answer.
model: Atoms are neutral so the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
exam.tip: Always give the reason when asked to explain.

exam.q: An atom of element X has 9 protons and 10 neutrons. Another atom has 9 protons and 9 neutrons. Explain whether these atoms are the same element.
model: Yes, they are the same element.
Both have 9 protons; the number of protons is the same for all atoms of an element (unique to that element).
exam.tip: Neutron number does not change the element.

exam.q: The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m and the radius of its nucleus is about 1 x 10^-15 m. Calculate how many times larger the atom's radius is than the nucleus's radius.
exam.tip: Subtract the powers: -10 - (-15) = 5.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom, giving the relative charge, relative mass and position of each subatomic particle, and explain why atoms are neutral.
model: Nucleus at the centre containing protons and neutrons.
Protons: relative charge +1, relative mass 1.
Neutrons: relative charge 0, relative mass 1.
Electrons in shells around the nucleus: charge -1, mass 1/1836.
Nucleus is tiny compared with the atom but contains almost all the mass.
Equal numbers of protons and electrons, with equal and opposite charges, so atoms are neutral.
exam.tip: Level-marked: cover structure, all three particles with values, size/mass and neutrality.

worked.q: A magnesium atom has 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 12 electrons. Calculate (a) its overall charge and (b) the percentage of its mass that comes from electrons.
steps: (a) Charge from protons = 12 x (+1) = +12.
Charge from electrons = 12 x (-1) = -12.
Neutrons contribute 0. Overall charge = +12 - 12 + 0 = 0.
(b) Mass of nucleus = 12 + 12 = 24.
Mass of electrons = 12 x 1/1836 = 0.00654.
Total mass = 24.00654.
Percentage from electrons = 0.00654 / 24.00654 x 100 = 0.027%.
worked.ans: (a) Overall charge = 0 (neutral). (b) About 0.03% of the mass comes from electrons, so over 99.9% is in the nucleus.

worked.q: A model atom is built with a nucleus of radius 1 mm. If the real atom's radius is 100 000 times its nucleus's radius, how big would the model atom be?
steps: Atom radius = 100 000 x nucleus radius.
Diameter = 2 x 100 m = 200 m.
worked.ans: The model atom would have a radius of 100 m (diameter 200 m), larger than a football pitch, around a 1 mm nucleus: this shows how much of an atom is empty space.

chem_edx.1.10.summary: A **covalent bond** forms when **two atoms share a pair of electrons**; the shared pair is attracted to the nuclei of both atoms, which holds the atoms together. Covalent bonding between non-metal atoms produces **molecules**, which are tiny: atoms and small molecules have a typical size of about **10^-10 m** (0.1 nm). **Dot-and-cross diagrams** show how atoms share electrons so that each atom gets a full outer shell, and you must be able to draw them for hydrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, methane, oxygen and carbon dioxide.

core.p: Edexcel 1.28-1.31 covers four ideas: how a covalent bond forms, that covalent bonding makes molecules, the size of atoms and small molecules, and dot-and-cross diagrams for six named molecules.
bullets: 1.28: a covalent bond is formed when a **pair of electrons is shared** between two atoms.
1.29: covalent bonding results in the formation of **molecules**.
1.30: typical size (order of magnitude) of atoms and small molecules: **about 10^-10 m**.
1.31: dot-and-cross diagrams for **H2, HCl, H2O, CH4, O2 and CO2**.
Covalent bonding happens between **non-metal atoms**.

callouts.p: A covalent bond is formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

core.p: Non-metal atoms need to **gain** electrons to get a full outer shell. When two non-metals meet, neither can easily give electrons away, so instead they **share** outer electrons. Each shared electron counts towards the outer shell of both atoms.
bullets: Hydrogen needs 1 more electron for a full shell of 2.
Carbon (2.4) needs 4 more; nitrogen (2.5) needs 3; oxygen (2.6) needs 2; chlorine (2.8.7) needs 1.
The number of covalent bonds an atom usually makes equals the number of electrons it needs: H 1, Cl 1, O 2, N 3, C 4.
Sharing lets every atom reach a stable, full outer shell (like a noble gas).
Compare ionic bonding: metal + non-metal, electrons are **transferred**, not shared.

core.h: Why a shared pair holds atoms together
core.p: The grade 9 explanation is about **electrostatic attraction**. The shared pair of electrons (negative) sits between the two nuclei (positive) and is **attracted to both nuclei**. This attraction pulls the two atoms together.
bullets: Each nucleus is attracted to the shared electrons between them.
This strong attraction is the covalent bond.
Covalent bonds are **strong** - a lot of energy is needed to break them.
A covalent bond is between **two specific atoms** (it is directional), unlike ionic attraction in all directions.
Each atom usually provides **one electron** to each shared pair.

callouts.p: Strong electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms.

core.p: When a small, fixed number of atoms are joined by covalent bonds, the result is a **molecule**. The formula gives the exact number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
bullets: H2: 2 hydrogen atoms joined by 1 covalent bond.
H2O: 1 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms, 2 covalent bonds.
CO2: 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms.
Molecules can be elements (H2, O2, Cl2) or compounds (HCl, CH4).
The bonds **inside** a molecule are strong covalent bonds; the forces **between** molecules are weak intermolecular forces (this links to 1.34).
Some covalent substances form giant structures instead (diamond, graphite - 1.35).

callouts.p: A group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.
When a simple molecular substance melts, the weak forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds do not break.

core.h: Size of atoms and small molecules
core.p: Atoms and small molecules are extraordinarily small. Edexcel wants the **order of magnitude**: about **1 x 10^-10 m**, which is 0.1 nanometres (1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m).
bullets: Typical atomic radius: about **1 x 10^-10 m** (0.1 nm).
Small molecules such as H2O or CO2 are also of the order of **10^-10 m** (a few tenths of a nanometre).
The nucleus is about **1 x 10^-14 m** across - roughly 10 000 times smaller than the atom.
Order of magnitude = the nearest power of ten.
About 10 million atoms side by side would span just 1 mm.

callouts.p: Atoms and small molecules have a typical size of about 10^-10 m.

core.p: Dot-and-cross diagrams show **outer shell electrons only**. Electrons from one atom are drawn as dots and from the other as crosses, so you can see where each electron came from.
bullets: Draw a circle for the outer shell of each atom; **overlap** circles where atoms share.
Put each **shared pair** (one dot, one cross) in the overlap.
Put remaining outer electrons (**lone pairs**) on the rest of each atom's circle, in pairs.
Check: every atom has a full outer shell (H has 2, others have 8).
Check: total electrons drawn = sum of outer electrons of all atoms.
Single bond = 1 shared pair; **double bond = 2 shared pairs**.
Inner shells can be left out unless asked.

callouts.p: For water: O has 6 outer electrons + 2 from H = 8 electrons drawn in total. If your count is wrong, the diagram is wrong.

core.h: Hydrogen, H2, and hydrogen chloride, HCl
core.p: Both contain a **single covalent bond** - one shared pair of electrons.
bullets: **H2**: each H atom has 1 electron; they share them so each H has 2 (a full first shell).
Displayed formula: H-H.
**HCl**: H shares its 1 electron with one of chlorine's 7 outer electrons.
Chlorine then has 8 outer electrons (6 as three lone pairs + the shared pair); H has 2.
Displayed formula: H-Cl.

core.p: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more, so it forms **two single covalent bonds**, one with each hydrogen atom.
bullets: Two shared pairs (one O-H bond each).
Oxygen keeps **two lone pairs** (4 non-bonding electrons).
Oxygen ends with 8 outer electrons; each H has 2.
Displayed formula: H-O-H.
Total outer electrons drawn: 6 + 1 + 1 = 8.

core.p: **Methane**: carbon has 4 outer electrons and needs 4 more, so it forms **four single covalent bonds**, one to each H. **Oxygen gas**: each O needs 2 more, so the two atoms share **two pairs** - a **double bond**.
bullets: CH4: four shared pairs, **no lone pairs** on carbon; C has 8 outer electrons, each H has 2.
Displayed formula of CH4: C in the centre with four C-H bonds.
O2: two shared pairs (4 electrons) in the overlap = **double bond**, O=O.
Each O in O2 also has **two lone pairs**, so each has 6 + 2 = 8 outer electrons.
Total outer electrons in O2: 6 + 6 = 12 drawn.

core.p: Carbon needs 4 more electrons and each oxygen needs 2. Carbon forms a **double bond** with each oxygen atom: **O=C=O**.
bullets: Two double bonds = **four shared pairs** (8 shared electrons in total).
Carbon has no lone pairs; it has 8 outer electrons, all in bonds.
Each oxygen has **two lone pairs** plus two shared pairs = 8 electrons.
Total outer electrons drawn: 4 + 6 + 6 = 16.
The molecule is linear (straight) - O=C=O.

callouts.p: Make the overlapping regions wide enough to fit 4 electrons clearly. Examiners must be able to see two dots and two crosses in each overlap.

core.p: Use this table to check any dot-and-cross diagram you draw. The number of shared pairs and lone pairs is what examiners mark.
bullets: Single bond = 1 shared pair (2 electrons).
Double bond = 2 shared pairs (4 electrons).
Lone pairs are outer-shell pairs not used in bonding.
Hydrogen never has lone pairs and always makes exactly 1 bond.

head: Molecule
Bonds
Shared pairs
Lone pairs (central / each O or Cl)

core.h: Other ways to represent covalent molecules
core.p: Dot-and-cross diagrams are one model. Each representation shows some features well but has limitations (link to 1.41).
bullets: **Displayed formula** (e.g. H-O-H): shows which atoms are bonded, but not the electrons or the 3D shape.
**Dot-and-cross**: shows which atom each electron came from, but not the shape or relative sizes; electrons are actually identical.
**Ball-and-stick**: shows 3D shape (e.g. methane is tetrahedral) but not electrons.
**Space-filling**: shows the overall shape and relative sizes of atoms, but bonds are hidden.
Molecular formula (CH4) shows only the number of each atom.

callouts.t: Dots and crosses are the same
callouts.p: Electrons from different atoms are identical; dots and crosses are just bookkeeping to show where they came from.

core.h: Covalent vs ionic: the big contrast
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to compare the two types of bonding. Always state what happens to the electrons and what holds the particles together.
bullets: **Ionic**: metal + non-metal; electrons **transferred**; ions held by electrostatic attraction; giant lattice.
**Covalent**: non-metal + non-metal; electrons **shared**; nuclei attracted to shared pair; usually molecules.
Both kinds of bond are strong.
Covalent molecules have no overall charge and contain no ions.
Simple molecular substances have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

analogy.t: A tug-of-war rope held by two teams
analogy.p: Picture two people each holding the same rope (the shared pair of electrons). Both pull on it, and because both are holding the same rope, they stay locked together - just as two nuclei are both attracted to the shared electrons between them. A double bond is like holding two ropes, which is even harder to pull apart. Where it breaks down: in the real bond the 'people' (nuclei) are pulled towards the electrons rather than pulling away, and electrons are not a solid rope but tiny charged particles that move around.

terms.d: A bond formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
Two electrons, usually one from each atom, located between two bonded atoms.
A pair of outer-shell electrons on an atom that is not involved in bonding.
One shared pair of electrons between two atoms, e.g. H-H.
Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms, e.g. O=O.
A group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.
A substance made of small molecules with strong covalent bonds within them and weak forces between them.
A diagram showing the outer-shell electrons of atoms in a molecule or ion, using dots and crosses to show which atom each electron came from.
The highest occupied energy level of an atom; its electrons are involved in bonding.
Attraction between opposite charges; in a covalent bond, between the shared electrons and both nuclei.
The size of a quantity to the nearest power of ten.
The typical size of an atom, about 1 x 10^-10 m.
1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m; an atom is about 0.1 nm.
A diagram showing all the atoms in a molecule and every covalent bond as a line.
A molecule made of two atoms, e.g. H2, O2, HCl.

mistakes.w: A covalent bond is when electrons are shared
mistakes.r: A covalent bond is a shared PAIR of electrons between two atoms.

mistakes.w: Covalent bonds form between a metal and a non-metal
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms.

mistakes.w: O2 drawn with a single shared pair
mistakes.r: O2 has a double bond: two shared pairs, plus two lone pairs on each oxygen.

mistakes.w: Water drawn with no lone pairs on oxygen
mistakes.r: Oxygen in water has two lone pairs and two shared pairs, giving 8 outer electrons.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen with 8 electrons in its outer shell
mistakes.r: Hydrogen's outer (first) shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

mistakes.w: Atoms are about 10^-14 m across
mistakes.r: Atoms are about 10^-10 m; 10^-14 m is the size of the nucleus.

mistakes.w: When water boils, the covalent bonds break
mistakes.r: The weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; O-H bonds are not broken.

mistakes.w: Covalent bonds are weak
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong; it is the forces between simple molecules that are weak.

mistakes.w: CO2 drawn with single bonds C-O
mistakes.r: CO2 has two double bonds, O=C=O, so carbon has 8 outer electrons.

exam.q: Describe how a covalent bond is formed.
model: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms
exam.tip: Say 'pair' - just 'sharing electrons' may not score.

exam.q: State the typical size of an atom.
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: What type of particle is formed when atoms join by covalent bonding?
model: molecule
exam.tip: Not ions.

exam.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl. Show outer electrons only.
model: one shared pair (one dot and one cross) between H and Cl
three lone pairs on Cl (6 further electrons)
exam.tip: Total outer electrons = 1 + 7 = 8.

exam.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of water, H2O. Show outer electrons only.
model: two shared pairs, one between O and each H
two lone pairs on O
exam.tip: Total outer electrons = 6 + 1 + 1 = 8.

exam.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for methane, CH4.
model: four shared pairs between C and each H
no other electrons on carbon / each pair one dot one cross
exam.tip: Carbon has no lone pairs in methane.

exam.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for an oxygen molecule, O2, and state the type of bond.
model: two shared pairs between the O atoms
two lone pairs on each O atom
double (covalent) bond
exam.tip: Count: 12 outer electrons in total.

exam.q: Explain why a covalent bond holds two atoms together.
model: the shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nuclei of both atoms
(strong) electrostatic attraction between negative electrons and positive nuclei
exam.tip: Mention both nuclei.

exam.q: A water molecule is about 2.8 x 10^-10 m across. A hair is about 1 x 10^-4 m wide. Estimate how many water molecules would fit across the width of the hair.
model: = 3.6 x 10^5 (approximately 4 x 10^5)
exam.tip: Divide the bigger length by the smaller one.

exam.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for carbon dioxide and use it to explain how each atom achieves a full outer shell.
model: two shared pairs between C and each O (two double bonds)
two lone pairs on each O
carbon has 8 outer electrons (4 own + 4 shared from O)
each oxygen has 8 outer electrons (6 own + 2 from C)
exam.tip: Check the total: 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 electrons.

exam.q: Compare how the bonding forms in sodium chloride and in hydrogen chloride. Refer to electrons, the particles formed and the forces involved.
model: NaCl: metal and non-metal; sodium transfers one electron to chlorine
forms Na+ and Cl- ions with full outer shells
held by strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice
HCl: two non-metals; a pair of electrons is shared between H and Cl
forms a molecule (no ions) where H has 2 and Cl has 8 outer electrons
held by strong electrostatic attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei
exam.tip: Write it as a side-by-side comparison: transfer vs share, ions vs molecules, attraction in each.

worked.q: Deduce how many shared pairs and lone pairs are in a molecule of ammonia, NH3, and describe its dot-and-cross diagram.
steps: N is 2.5: 5 outer electrons, needs 3 more.
Each H has 1 electron and needs 1 more.
N forms 3 single covalent bonds, one with each H: 3 shared pairs.
N's remaining outer electrons: 5 - 3 = 2, so 1 lone pair.
Check: N has 6 shared + 2 lone = 8; each H has 2. Total drawn = 5 + 3 = 8.
worked.ans: 3 shared pairs and 1 lone pair on nitrogen.

worked.q: An oxygen atom has a radius of about 6 x 10^-11 m. Give its order of magnitude and state how many times larger it is than a nucleus of about 1 x 10^-14 m.
steps: 6 x 10^-11 m is closest to 1 x 10^-10 m, so order of magnitude 10^-10 m.
worked.ans: Order of magnitude 10^-10 m; the atom is about 10 000 times larger than the nucleus.

worked.q: Explain, using electrons, why carbon dioxide contains double bonds but methane contains single bonds.
steps: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and needs 4 more in both molecules.
In CH4, each H can share only 1 electron, so carbon needs 4 H atoms, each joined by 1 shared pair (single bond).
In CO2, each O needs 2 more electrons, so it shares 2 pairs with carbon.
Two O atoms x 2 shared pairs = 4 shared pairs, giving carbon 8 outer electrons.
So CO2 has two double bonds: O=C=O.
worked.ans: Hydrogen can form only one bond, so methane has four single bonds; oxygen needs two electrons, so each O shares two pairs with carbon, giving two double bonds in CO2.

chem_edx.1.11.summary: Every element and compound can be classified by its **bonding and structure** as **ionic**, **simple molecular (covalent)**, **giant covalent** or **metallic**. The type of particle (ions, molecules, atoms or positive ions with delocalised electrons) and the forces holding them together decide the physical properties: **relative melting and boiling points**, **solubility in water** and **whether it conducts electricity as a solid, when molten and in solution**. At grade 9 you must be able to work backwards from a table of data to the structure, and explain each property in terms of what must be overcome and whether charged particles are free to move.

core.p: Edexcel expects you to sort substances into four groups. The key question is always: **what particles are there, and what holds them together?**
bullets: **Ionic**: a giant lattice of oppositely charged **ions** held by strong **electrostatic forces of attraction**, e.g. sodium chloride, magnesium oxide.

**Simple molecular (covalent)**: small **molecules** with strong **covalent bonds** inside each molecule but only **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules, e.g. water, carbon dioxide, methane, chlorine.
**Giant covalent**: a huge network of **atoms** all joined by strong covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide.
**Metallic**: a giant lattice of **positive metal ions** surrounded by a sea of **delocalised electrons**, e.g. copper, iron, magnesium.
Elements can be simple molecular (O2, Cl2), giant covalent (C, Si) or metallic (Cu); only compounds can be ionic.

head: Type
Particles
Force holding them
Example
rows: Weak intermolecular forces (strong covalent bonds inside)
Strong electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons

callouts.p: Properties depend on what has to be **overcome** when a substance melts, and whether there are **charged particles that are free to move**.

core.h: Predicting the type from the elements
core.p: Before looking at any data you can often predict the structure from which elements are present.
bullets: **Metal + non-metal** compound: usually **ionic** (electrons transferred), e.g. NaCl, CaO, K2S.
**Non-metals only**: **covalent**; usually **simple molecular** (H2O, NH3, CO2) but a few are **giant covalent** (diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide).
**Metal element or alloy**: **metallic**.
Noble gases exist as single atoms and behave like simple molecular substances (weak forces between atoms, very low boiling points).
Learn the giant covalent examples: **diamond, graphite, graphene and silicon dioxide (silica, sand)**; almost every other non-metal compound at GCSE is simple molecular.

callouts.p: If an exam question names a covalent substance and it is not carbon or silicon dioxide, assume it is **simple molecular**.

core.h: Melting and boiling points: what must be overcome
core.p: Melting and boiling need energy to overcome the forces holding particles in place. **Strong forces = lots of energy = high melting point.**
bullets: **Ionic**: high melting points because many **strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions** in the lattice must be overcome.
**Giant covalent**: very high melting points because many **strong covalent bonds** must be **broken**.
**Metallic**: generally high melting points because the **strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons** must be overcome.
**Simple molecular**: low melting and boiling points because only the **weak intermolecular forces** need to be overcome; the covalent bonds are **not** broken.
Simple molecular substances are often **gases or liquids at room temperature**; the other three types are almost always **solids**.

callouts.p: Never say covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts or boils. Only the **intermolecular forces** are overcome.

core.p: To conduct electricity, a substance must contain **charged particles** (ions or electrons) that are **free to move**. Both parts are needed in your answer.
bullets: **Metals**: conduct as solids and liquids because **delocalised electrons** are free to move through the structure.
**Ionic**: do **not** conduct as solids because the **ions are fixed** in the lattice; **do** conduct when **molten** or **dissolved in water** because the **ions are free to move**.
**Simple molecular**: do **not** conduct in any state because molecules have **no overall charge** and there are no free electrons or ions.
**Giant covalent**: do **not** conduct (all outer electrons are used in bonds), **except graphite**, which has **delocalised electrons**.
Electrons carry the charge in metals and graphite; **ions** carry the charge in molten or aqueous ionic compounds.

core.p: The spec asks about **relative solubility in water**. These are general patterns, not absolute rules.
bullets: **Ionic**: many are **soluble** in water (e.g. sodium chloride), though some are insoluble (e.g. calcium carbonate, silver chloride).
**Simple molecular**: most are **insoluble** in water (e.g. methane, iodine, wax), but some dissolve (e.g. sugar, ethanol, ammonia).
**Giant covalent**: **insoluble** in water (diamond, graphite, sand).
**Metallic**: **insoluble** in water (some very reactive metals react with water instead of dissolving).
A substance that dissolves to give a solution that conducts is almost certainly **ionic**.

callouts.t: Using solubility in a data question
callouts.p: Solubility alone rarely decides the structure; combine it with melting point and conductivity.

core.p: Learn this table: it is the key to almost every classification question.
bullets: Read across a row to describe a structure.
Read down a column to compare one property across all four types.
Exceptions you must know: **graphite conducts**; **mercury** is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.

core.p: A favourite question gives a table of substances A to D with melting points and conductivity and asks you to identify each structure. Use a fixed order of checks.
bullets: Step 1: **Conducts as a solid?** Yes = **metallic** (or graphite).
Step 2: If not, **low melting point** (below about 200 °C, or a gas/liquid at room temperature)? Yes = **simple molecular**.
Step 3: High melting point and **conducts when molten or dissolved but not when solid**? = **ionic**.
Step 4: Very high melting point and **never conducts** (and insoluble) = **giant covalent**.
Always quote the data in your answer, e.g. 'D melts at 1610 °C and does not conduct when molten, so it is giant covalent.'

callouts.p: Marks are often given for linking each conclusion to a specific piece of data, not just for the name.

core.h: Why ionic compounds behave as they do
core.p: In an ionic lattice every ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge, attracting it **in all directions**.
bullets: **High melting point**: lots of energy needed to overcome the **strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions**.
Ions with **larger charges** (e.g. Mg2+ and O2-) attract more strongly, so **magnesium oxide** has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
**Solid**: ions held in fixed positions, so no conduction.
**Molten or aqueous**: lattice broken down, **ions free to move** and carry charge, so it conducts.

core.h: Why simple molecular substances behave as they do
core.p: Each molecule is a tight unit held together by strong covalent bonds, but molecules are only weakly attracted to each other.
bullets: **Low melting and boiling points**: little energy needed to overcome the **weak intermolecular forces**.
**Larger molecules** have stronger intermolecular forces, so melting and boiling points **increase with molecular size** (e.g. down group 7: F2 gas, Br2 liquid, I2 solid).
**Do not conduct**: molecules are **neutral** and there are no delocalised electrons or ions.
Polymers are long molecules, so they have higher melting points than small molecules but are still covalent molecules.

core.h: Why giant covalent and metallic substances behave as they do
core.p: Both are giant structures held by strong forces throughout, so both have high melting points, but they differ in conductivity.
bullets: **Giant covalent**: every atom joined to others by **strong covalent bonds**; melting means **breaking** a huge number of bonds, so melting points are very high.
No free electrons or ions in diamond or silicon dioxide, so they **do not conduct**.
**Graphite**: each carbon forms 3 bonds, leaving **one delocalised electron per atom**, so it conducts.
**Metallic**: **delocalised electrons** move through the lattice, so metals conduct as solid and liquid; strong attraction between ions and electrons gives high melting points.
Layers of metal ions can slide, so metals are **malleable**; giant covalent solids such as diamond are hard and brittle.

callouts.p: Graphite is giant covalent but **conducts**. If a non-metal solid conducts and has a very high melting point, think graphite.

core.p: Grade 9 answers compare and explain, rather than just state.
bullets: Compare **type of force** (intermolecular vs covalent vs electrostatic) and **amount of energy** needed.
Use the words **overcome** (for forces/attractions) and **break** (for bonds) correctly.
For conductivity, always say **what** carries the charge (**ions** or **delocalised electrons**) and that they are **free to move**.
Recognise that the models are simplifications: e.g. not all ionic compounds dissolve, and the 'sea of electrons' is a model, not a picture.

analogy.p: Think of particles as people. **Ionic**: a dance floor where everyone holds hands with partners of the opposite team on all sides; it is hard to pull apart, and nobody can wander unless the floor is melted or flooded. **Simple molecular**: couples hugging tightly (covalent bonds) but only lightly brushing other couples (intermolecular forces), so the crowd scatters easily. **Giant covalent**: a gym full of people all locked arm-in-arm in one huge net. **Metallic**: a crowd of people standing in rows while footballs (electrons) zoom freely between them. Where it breaks down: real particles have no choice or personality, forces act in all directions at once, and electrons are not little balls.

terms.d: A giant lattice of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A substance made of small molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces, with strong covalent bonds within each molecule.
The weak forces of attraction between molecules.
A large network of atoms all joined to each other by strong covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide.
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons around them.
Electrons that are not attached to a particular atom and are free to move through a structure.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of particles.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles.
Melted; in the liquid state because it has been heated above its melting point.
A solution in which water is the solvent, shown by (aq).
A substance that allows charge to flow through it because it contains charged particles that are free to move.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.

mistakes.w: Simple molecular substances have low melting points because their covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong; the **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules are overcome, not the covalent bonds.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds conduct when molten because electrons move.
mistakes.r: **Ions** are free to move and carry the charge in molten or aqueous ionic compounds.

mistakes.w: Sodium chloride conducts as a solid.
mistakes.r: Solid ionic compounds **do not conduct** because the ions are **fixed in position** in the lattice.

mistakes.w: Diamond has a high melting point because it has strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Diamond is giant covalent: many **strong covalent bonds** must be **broken**; there are no molecules, so no intermolecular forces.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds have high melting points because they have strong ionic bonds between molecules.
mistakes.r: There are no molecules in an ionic lattice; strong **electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions** must be overcome.

mistakes.w: All covalent substances have low melting points.
mistakes.r: Only **simple molecular** ones do; **giant covalent** substances (diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide) have very high melting points.

mistakes.w: Metals conduct because they have free ions.
mistakes.r: Metals conduct because of **delocalised electrons** that are free to move through the structure.

mistakes.w: It conducts because it has electrons.
mistakes.r: Must say charged particles are **free to move**; every substance has electrons.

exam.q: State the type of structure in sodium chloride.
model: Giant ionic lattice (ionic).
exam.tip: Giant ionic lattice is the safest full phrase.

exam.q: Methane, CH4, boils at -162 °C. State the type of structure in methane and explain its low boiling point.
model: Simple molecular (covalent).
Weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Little energy needed to overcome them.
exam.tip: Say forces between molecules, not bonds.

exam.q: Explain why solid potassium chloride does not conduct electricity but its solution does.
model: In the solid, ions are in fixed positions / cannot move.
In solution, ions are free to move.
Ions carry the charge.
exam.tip: The word ions must appear; electrons lose the mark.

exam.q: Silicon dioxide melts at 1710 °C. Explain why its melting point is high.
model: Giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, needing a lot of energy.
exam.tip: Use break for covalent bonds.

exam.q: Explain why copper conducts electricity.
model: Contains delocalised electrons.
Which are free to move through the structure (carry charge).
exam.tip: Two marks: delocalised electrons + free to move.

exam.q: Substance X melts at 2852 °C, does not conduct as a solid but conducts when molten. Identify the type of structure in X and justify your answer.
model: Ionic.
High melting point shows strong forces between particles.
Conducts only when molten, so contains ions that become free to move.
exam.tip: Use both pieces of evidence.

exam.q: Give two reasons why a substance that is a gas at room temperature and does not conduct is likely to be simple molecular.
model: Low boiling point shows weak forces between particles (weak intermolecular forces).
Does not conduct, so no ions or delocalised electrons free to move.
exam.tip: Link each property to its structural cause.

exam.q: Magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. Suggest why.
model: Mg2+ and O2- ions have larger charges than Na+ and Cl-.
Stronger electrostatic forces between ions so more energy needed to overcome them.
exam.tip: Compare charge sizes explicitly.

exam.q: The table shows data for four substances. A: mp 1083 °C, conducts solid yes, molten yes. B: mp 801 °C, solid no, molten yes. C: mp -7 °C, solid no, liquid no. D: mp 1610 °C, solid no, molten no, insoluble. Classify each substance as ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent or metallic and justify your choices.
model: A is metallic.
A conducts as a solid, so has delocalised electrons free to move; high melting point.
B is ionic.
B conducts only when molten, so ions are free to move only when the lattice is broken; high melting point from strong electrostatic forces.
C is simple molecular: low melting point, weak intermolecular forces; does not conduct, no charged particles.
D is giant covalent: very high melting point, many strong covalent bonds broken; never conducts, no free charged particles.
exam.tip: One identification plus one justification per substance gives a well-structured 6-mark answer.

exam.q: Compare the structure and properties of sodium chloride and carbon dioxide.
model: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions.
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, so high melting point (solid at room temperature).
Conducts when molten or dissolved because ions are free to move, not when solid.
Carbon dioxide is simple molecular: small molecules with strong covalent bonds inside.
Weak intermolecular forces, so low boiling point (gas at room temperature).
Does not conduct because molecules have no overall charge / no free electrons.
exam.tip: Make paired comparisons: structure, forces, melting point, conductivity for each.

worked.q: Substance P has a melting point of 44 °C, is insoluble in water and does not conduct electricity when solid or liquid. Classify P.
steps: Check conduction as a solid: no, so not metallic.
Check melting point: 44 °C is low, so only weak forces are overcome on melting.
Does not conduct when liquid, so no ions or delocalised electrons are present.
Low melting point plus no conduction in any state matches simple molecular.
worked.ans: P is **simple molecular**: low melting point because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome, and it does not conduct because its molecules are neutral.

worked.q: Substance Q melts at 3550 °C, is insoluble and conducts electricity as a solid. It contains only one non-metal element. Classify Q.
steps: Conducts as a solid: usually means metallic, but Q is a non-metal element.
Very high melting point: many strong bonds must be broken, so a giant structure.
A non-metal giant covalent structure that conducts must contain delocalised electrons.
The only common example is graphite (carbon).
worked.ans: Q is **giant covalent (graphite)**: strong covalent bonds give a very high melting point and delocalised electrons allow it to conduct.

svg.cap: The four types of structure. Ionic: a lattice of alternating positive and negative ions. Simple molecular: separate small molecules. Giant covalent: atoms linked by covalent bonds in a continuous network. Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
