chem_edx.1.12.summary: **Ionic compounds** are giant lattices of oppositely charged ions held by **strong electrostatic forces of attraction**, so they have **high melting and boiling points**; they **do not conduct as solids** (ions fixed) but **do conduct when molten or in aqueous solution** (ions free to move). **Simple molecular substances** have strong covalent bonds inside each molecule but only **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules, so they have **low melting and boiling points** and are **poor conductors** because their molecules carry no overall charge. Grade 9 answers always name the force being overcome and say which charged particles are, or are not, free to move.

core.p: Spec points 1.33 and 1.34 ask you to **explain** properties, not just list them. The explanation always comes from the structure.
bullets: 1.33 Ionic compounds: **high melting and boiling points** in terms of **forces between ions**.
1.33 Ionic compounds: whether they conduct as **solids**, when **molten** and in **aqueous solution**.
1.34 Simple molecular covalent substances: **low melting and boiling points** in terms of **forces between molecules (intermolecular forces)**.
1.34 Simple molecular covalent substances: **poor conduction of electricity**.
Command word 'explain' means you must give the **because**: structure, force, energy, particles moving.

core.p: An ionic compound such as sodium chloride is a **giant ionic lattice**: a regular three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions.
bullets: Each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl- ions, and each Cl- ion by six Na+ ions.
Oppositely charged ions attract each other by **strong electrostatic forces of attraction**.
These forces act **in all directions** throughout the lattice.
There are **no molecules** in an ionic compound, so there are no intermolecular forces.
The formula (e.g. NaCl) shows the **ratio** of ions, not a molecule.

callouts.p: The **strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions**.

core.h: Why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points
core.p: To melt an ionic solid the ions must be given enough energy to break out of their fixed positions.
bullets: There are **many strong electrostatic forces** between oppositely charged ions in the giant lattice.
A **large amount of (heat) energy** is needed to **overcome** these forces.
So ionic compounds have **high melting and boiling points**, e.g. NaCl melts at 801 °C.
They are therefore **solids at room temperature**.
Ions with **higher charges** attract more strongly: MgO (Mg2+, O2-) melts at about 2850 °C, far higher than NaCl (Na+, Cl-).

callouts.p: 'Lots of energy is needed to overcome the **strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions**.'

core.h: Conductivity of ionic compounds: the three states
core.p: An electric current is a **flow of charged particles**. In ionic compounds the charge carriers are **ions**.
bullets: **Solid**: the ions are held in **fixed positions** in the lattice and **cannot move**, so it **does not conduct**.
**Molten**: heating breaks down the lattice; the ions are **free to move**, so it **conducts**.
**Aqueous solution**: dissolving separates the ions; they are **free to move** through the water, so it **conducts**.
When conducting, the ions move to the electrodes and the compound is decomposed: this is **electrolysis** (Topic 3).
The ions carry the charge, **not electrons**.

callouts.p: Writing 'electrons are free to move' for a molten ionic compound scores zero. It is the **ions** that move.

core.p: Many ionic compounds dissolve in water; when they do, the ions spread out among the water molecules.
bullets: Many ionic compounds are **soluble** in water, e.g. sodium chloride, copper sulfate.
Some are **insoluble**, e.g. calcium carbonate, barium sulfate, silver chloride.
An insoluble ionic compound can still conduct **when molten**.
A conducting aqueous solution is strong evidence of ions.

core.h: Structure of a simple molecular substance
core.p: Simple molecular substances are made of **small, separate molecules**, such as H2O, CO2, CH4, O2, Cl2 and NH3.
bullets: Inside each molecule, atoms are joined by **strong covalent bonds** (shared pairs of electrons).
Between molecules there are only **weak intermolecular forces**.
So there are two very different strengths of attraction in the same substance.
Molecules are **neutral**: they have **no overall electric charge**.

callouts.p: The **weak forces of attraction between molecules**.

core.h: Why simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points
core.p: When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the molecules separate from each other but the molecules themselves stay intact.
bullets: Only the **weak intermolecular forces** have to be **overcome**.
Only a **small amount of energy** is needed.
So simple molecular substances have **low melting and boiling points**, e.g. methane boils at -162 °C, water at 100 °C.
Many are **gases or liquids at room temperature**.
The **covalent bonds are not broken** on melting or boiling: steam is still H2O molecules.

callouts.p: Do not say 'covalent bonds are weak' or 'covalent bonds break when it boils'. Covalent bonds are **strong**; it is the **intermolecular forces** that are weak.

core.p: Intermolecular forces get stronger as molecules get larger, so bigger molecules need more energy to separate.
bullets: **Larger molecules** have **stronger intermolecular forces**, so higher melting and boiling points.
Halogens: F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid, I2 is a solid at room temperature.
Alkanes: methane (gas) to longer chains such as those in petrol (liquid) and wax (solid).
Even so, simple molecular substances have much lower melting points than ionic or giant covalent ones.

core.h: Why simple molecular substances are poor conductors
core.p: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. Simple molecular substances have neither ions nor delocalised electrons.
bullets: Molecules have **no overall charge**, so moving molecules do not carry charge.
All the electrons are held in **covalent bonds** or within atoms; there are **no delocalised electrons**.
There are **no ions**.
So they **do not conduct** as solids, liquids or gases.
Most do not dissolve in water; some dissolve and react to form ions (e.g. HCl gas gives hydrochloric acid, which conducts) but that is a reaction, not the molecules conducting.

callouts.p: The spec says **poor conduction of electricity**: no charged particles free to move.

core.p: Many questions ask you to compare the two. Use a matching point for each property.
bullets: Always compare the **type of force** overcome and the **amount of energy** needed.
Always compare **which charged particles** exist and whether they can move.
Use data in the question to back up each statement.

core.p: A grade 9 answer is a chain of linked reasoning.
bullets: Structure: 'giant ionic lattice' or 'simple molecules'.
Force: 'strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions' or 'weak intermolecular forces'.
Energy: 'a lot of energy' or 'little energy' needed to **overcome** the forces.
Conductivity: name the **charged particles** and say whether they are **free to move**.
Avoid vague words like 'strong bonds' without saying which bonds or forces.

callouts.p: Link each step with 'so' or 'because' to show the chain of reasoning examiners reward.

analogy.p: An ionic lattice is like a huge wall built of north and south magnets packed alternately: each magnet is gripped on every side, so you need a lot of effort to pull the wall apart. Melt or flood the wall and the magnets can drift, carrying their 'charge' with them, which is like conduction. A simple molecular substance is like a drawer of socks stitched into pairs: each pair is sewn together firmly (covalent bond), but pairs only cling to each other slightly by static (intermolecular forces), so tipping the drawer scatters the pairs easily without unpicking any stitches. Where it breaks down: magnets have poles rather than single charges, and intermolecular forces are not static cling, though both are attractions.

terms.d: A compound made of oppositely charged ions arranged in a giant lattice.
A regular three-dimensional arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions.
The force between oppositely charged particles; very strong between ions in a lattice.
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
The temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid.
In the liquid state after melting; shown by (l).
A solution in which the solvent is water; shown by (aq).
The ability of a substance to allow charge to flow, which needs charged particles free to move.
A substance made of small molecules with strong covalent bonds within them and weak intermolecular forces between them.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms; a strong bond.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules.
Two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds; overall neutral.
The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in solution, by passing an electric current through it.

mistakes.w: Simple molecular substances have low boiling points because the covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong; **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules are overcome.

mistakes.w: When water boils, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen break.
mistakes.r: Only **intermolecular forces** are overcome; the H2O molecules stay intact.

mistakes.w: Molten sodium chloride conducts because the electrons are free to move.
mistakes.r: **Ions** are free to move and carry the charge.

mistakes.w: Solid sodium chloride doesn't conduct because there are no ions.
mistakes.r: There **are** ions, but they are **fixed in position** in the lattice and cannot move.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds have high melting points because of strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Ionic compounds contain no molecules; strong **electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions** must be overcome.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the bonds are strong.
mistakes.r: Need the full idea: **many strong electrostatic forces** between **oppositely charged ions**, needing **a lot of energy** to overcome.

mistakes.w: Simple molecular substances don't conduct because they have no electrons.
mistakes.r: They have electrons, but **no delocalised electrons or ions**: no charged particles **free to move**; molecules are neutral.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds conduct when dissolved because the molecules move.
mistakes.r: There are no molecules; the dissolved **ions** move.

exam.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
model: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
exam.tip: Name the ions as oppositely charged and use 'overcome'.

exam.q: State why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity.
model: Ions are in fixed positions / not free to move.
exam.tip: Do not say there are no ions.

exam.q: Explain why sodium chloride solution conducts electricity.
model: Contains ions.
Which are free to move (and carry charge).
exam.tip: Ions + free to move = 2 marks.

exam.q: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature. Explain why, in terms of structure and bonding.
model: Simple molecular / made of small Cl2 molecules.
Weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Little energy needed to overcome them, so low boiling point.
exam.tip: Name the forces as between molecules.

exam.q: Explain why methane does not conduct electricity.
model: Molecules have no overall charge.
No ions or delocalised electrons free to move.
exam.tip: Say no charged particles free to move.

exam.q: Iodine is a solid at room temperature but chlorine is a gas. Both are simple molecular. Suggest why iodine has the higher melting point.
model: Iodine molecules are larger.
Stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy needed to overcome them.
exam.tip: Compare size and force strength.

exam.q: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2850 °C; sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Explain the difference.
model: Mg2+ and O2- ions have higher charges than Na+ and Cl-.
Stronger electrostatic forces of attraction between ions in MgO.
More energy needed to overcome them.
exam.tip: Higher charge, stronger attraction, more energy.

exam.q: Give one property of a simple molecular substance.
model: Low melting/boiling point OR does not conduct electricity.
exam.tip: One correct property is enough.

exam.q: Potassium bromide is an ionic compound. Describe and explain whether it conducts electricity as a solid, when molten and when dissolved in water.
model: Does not conduct as a solid.
Because ions are in fixed positions in the lattice.
Conducts when molten and when dissolved in water.
Because the ions are free to move and carry charge.
exam.tip: Cover all three states.

exam.q: Compare the properties of sodium chloride and water and explain them in terms of structure and bonding.
model: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice; water is simple molecular.
NaCl has strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, so a lot of energy needed: high melting point, solid at room temperature.
Water has weak intermolecular forces between molecules, so little energy needed: low melting/boiling point, liquid at room temperature.
Covalent bonds within water molecules are not broken when it melts or boils.
NaCl conducts when molten or dissolved because ions are free to move, but not as a solid because ions are fixed.
Pure water is a very poor conductor because molecules are neutral and there are no free ions or electrons.
exam.tip: Pair each NaCl point with the matching water point.

worked.q: Use the data to decide which substance is ionic and which is simple molecular. Substance A: melting point 714 °C, conducts when dissolved in water. Substance B: melting point -95 °C, does not conduct as a liquid.
steps: A has a high melting point, so strong forces must be overcome: suggests strong electrostatic forces between ions.
A conducts when dissolved, so it contains ions that become free to move.
B has a low melting point, so only weak forces are overcome: weak intermolecular forces.
B does not conduct as a liquid, so it has no ions or delocalised electrons: neutral molecules.
worked.ans: A is **ionic** and B is **simple molecular**.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why ammonia, NH3, has a boiling point of -33 °C and does not conduct electricity. (4 marks)
steps: Ammonia is a **simple molecular** substance made of small NH3 molecules.
There are **weak intermolecular forces** between the molecules (the N-H covalent bonds are strong but are not broken).
Only a **small amount of energy** is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point is low.
NH3 molecules have **no overall charge** and there are **no ions or delocalised electrons free to move**, so it does not conduct.
worked.ans: Low boiling point from weak intermolecular forces; poor conductor because there are no charged particles free to move.

chem_edx.1.13.summary: **Graphite and diamond** are two different forms of the element **carbon** and both are **giant covalent substances**: huge networks of carbon atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, so both have **very high melting points**. In **diamond** each carbon is covalently bonded to **four** others in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral lattice, making it **very hard** and used in **cutting tools**; it has no delocalised electrons so it does not conduct. In **graphite** each carbon is bonded to **three** others in **layers of hexagons** with **weak forces between the layers**, so the layers slide (**lubricant**), and each atom has **one delocalised electron**, so graphite **conducts electricity** and is used for **electrodes**.

core.p: Spec points 1.35 to 1.37 cover two forms of carbon and how their structures explain their uses.
bullets: 1.35 **Recall** that graphite and diamond are **different forms of carbon** and are examples of **giant covalent substances**.
1.36 **Describe** the structures of graphite and diamond.
1.37 **Explain**, in terms of structure and bonding, why **graphite** is used to make **electrodes** and as a **lubricant**, whereas **diamond** is used in **cutting tools**.
Every 'explain' answer must link **structure, then property, then use**.

core.p: A giant covalent substance is a huge network of atoms in which **every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds**. There are no separate molecules.
bullets: Because there are no small molecules, there are **no intermolecular forces to overcome** when melting.
To melt the substance, **many strong covalent bonds must be broken**, which needs a **lot of energy**.
So giant covalent substances have **very high melting and boiling points** and are solids at room temperature.
They are **insoluble in water**.
Examples: **diamond, graphite**, graphene and **silicon dioxide (silica)**.

callouts.p: A structure in which a very large number of atoms are joined by **strong covalent bonds** in a continuous network.

core.h: Different forms of the same element
core.p: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms. They differ only in **how the atoms are bonded and arranged**, which is why their properties are so different.
bullets: Both are pure **carbon**: burning either completely in oxygen gives only carbon dioxide.
Both are **giant covalent**, so both have **very high melting points** (both above 3500 °C).
Diamond: each C forms **4** covalent bonds. Graphite: each C forms **3** covalent bonds.
The difference in bonding explains the difference in hardness and conductivity.
Graphene and fullerenes are further forms of carbon (spec 1.38).

callouts.p: Different arrangements of the **same atoms** give **completely different properties**.

core.p: Diamond is a rigid, three-dimensional giant covalent lattice.
bullets: Each carbon atom forms **four strong covalent bonds** to four other carbon atoms.
The four bonds point to the corners of a **tetrahedron**.
This builds a **rigid three-dimensional giant lattice** with strong bonds in every direction.
All four outer electrons of each carbon are used in bonding, so there are **no delocalised electrons**.
There are no ions.

core.p: Each property of diamond comes straight from its structure.
bullets: **Very hard**: a rigid 3D network of many strong covalent bonds; to scratch or deform it, bonds must be broken.
**Very high melting point**: many strong covalent bonds must be broken, needing a lot of energy.
**Does not conduct electricity**: no delocalised electrons or ions, so no charged particles are free to move.
**Insoluble in water**.
Diamond is the hardest natural substance.

core.h: Why diamond is used in cutting tools
core.p: Saw blades, drill bits and glass cutters are tipped with diamond.
bullets: Each carbon atom is bonded to **four** others by **strong covalent bonds**.
This makes a **rigid giant 3D lattice**, so diamond is **very hard**.
Being very hard means it can **cut or grind** other materials without wearing away.
Its **very high melting point** means it is not damaged by the heat produced when cutting.

callouts.p: 'Each carbon forms **four strong covalent bonds** in a **rigid giant lattice**, so diamond is **very hard**, so it is used in cutting tools.'

core.p: Graphite is made of flat **layers** of carbon atoms stacked on top of each other.
bullets: Each carbon atom forms **three strong covalent bonds** to three other carbon atoms.
The atoms are arranged in **hexagonal rings** forming flat **layers**.
There are **weak forces between the layers** (the layers are not covalently bonded to each other).
Each carbon has **one outer electron not used in bonding**, which becomes **delocalised**.
The delocalised electrons can move along the layers.

callouts.p: The covalent bonds **within** each layer are strong. Only the forces **between** the layers are weak.

core.p: Graphite shares the high melting point of diamond but is soft and conducts.
bullets: **Very high melting point**: many strong covalent bonds within the layers must be broken.
**Soft and slippery**: weak forces between the layers mean the **layers can slide over each other** easily.
**Conducts electricity** (and heat): the **delocalised electrons** are **free to move** through the structure.
**Insoluble in water**.
Graphite is the only non-metal element you need to know that conducts electricity.

core.h: Why graphite is used as a lubricant
core.p: A lubricant reduces friction between moving parts.
bullets: Graphite has **layers** of carbon atoms with **weak forces between the layers**.
The layers can **slide over each other** easily, so graphite is **soft and slippery**.
This reduces friction between surfaces.
Its **high melting point** means it can be used as a lubricant in hot conditions where oil might break down.
The same sliding of layers is why pencil 'lead' (graphite) leaves marks on paper.

core.h: Why graphite is used to make electrodes
core.p: Electrodes in electrolysis must conduct electricity and survive the conditions in the cell.
bullets: Each carbon forms only **three** covalent bonds, leaving **one delocalised electron per atom**.
The **delocalised electrons are free to move** through the structure and carry charge, so graphite **conducts electricity**.
Graphite has a **very high melting point** (many strong covalent bonds), so it does not melt in molten electrolytes, e.g. in the extraction of aluminium.
Graphite electrodes are also fairly **unreactive** and cheap.
Electrodes made of graphite are often described as **inert electrodes** in electrolysis.

callouts.p: Two marks usually come from **delocalised electrons free to move** (conducts) and **high melting point**.

core.p: A comparison table is the best way to revise and to answer 6-mark comparison questions.
bullets: Pair each structural point with the property it causes.
Both: carbon only, giant covalent, very high melting point, insoluble.
Different: number of bonds per atom, layers vs 3D lattice, delocalised electrons, hardness, conductivity, uses.

core.p: Most marks are lost by vague language or by mixing up the forces.
bullets: Say '**strong covalent bonds**', not just 'strong bonds'.
For graphite, say '**weak forces between layers**', not 'weak bonds'.
For conduction, say '**delocalised electrons**' that are '**free to move**'.
Never mention intermolecular forces for diamond; it has no molecules.
For a use, finish with the link: 'so it is used for...'.

callouts.p: Write three linked steps every time: structure feature, the property it causes, the use that property allows.

analogy.t: Scaffolding and a stack of paper
analogy.p: Diamond is like a building's steel scaffolding where every pole is clamped to four others in every direction: rigid, impossible to squash, but with no wires running through it, so no current. Graphite is like a stack of sheets of chain-link fence lying on top of each other: each sheet is strongly linked within itself, but the sheets only rest loosely on one another so they slide apart easily, and a loose ball bearing (the delocalised electron) can roll along each sheet, carrying charge. Where it breaks down: the forces between graphite layers are attractions, not just gravity, and electrons are not little balls rolling on a surface.

terms.d: A substance made of a very large network of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A form of carbon in which each atom forms four covalent bonds in a rigid 3D giant lattice.
A form of carbon in which each atom forms three covalent bonds in layers of hexagons with weak forces between layers.
An electron not tied to one atom or bond, free to move through the structure.
The shape formed when four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, as around each carbon in diamond.
A ring of six atoms; graphite layers are made of these.
A flat sheet of covalently bonded carbon atoms in graphite.
A substance that reduces friction between moving surfaces.
A conductor through which electricity enters or leaves an electrolyte in electrolysis.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
Resistance of a material to being scratched or deformed.
Ability to conduct electricity, requiring charged particles that are free to move.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of particles.

mistakes.w: Diamond is hard because it has strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Diamond has no molecules; it is hard because each carbon forms **four strong covalent bonds** in a **rigid giant lattice**.

mistakes.w: Graphite is soft because its covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds within layers are strong; the **forces between the layers are weak**, so layers slide.

mistakes.w: Graphite conducts because it has free ions.
mistakes.r: Graphite conducts because it has **delocalised electrons** that are free to move.

mistakes.w: Graphite has a low melting point because it is soft.
mistakes.r: Graphite has a **very high melting point** because many **strong covalent bonds** must be broken.

mistakes.w: In graphite each carbon is bonded to four other carbons.
mistakes.r: Each carbon in graphite forms **three** covalent bonds; it is **diamond** that forms four.

mistakes.w: Diamond conducts electricity because carbon has electrons.
mistakes.r: Diamond **does not conduct**: all outer electrons are used in bonds, so there are **no delocalised electrons**.

mistakes.w: Graphite is used for electrodes because it is soft.
mistakes.r: Graphite is used for electrodes because it **conducts electricity** (delocalised electrons) and has a **high melting point**.

mistakes.w: Graphite and diamond are compounds of carbon.
mistakes.r: They are **different forms of the element carbon**; they contain only carbon atoms.

exam.q: Name the element that diamond and graphite are both made from.
model: Carbon.
exam.tip: Simple recall.

exam.q: State the type of structure shared by diamond and graphite.
model: Giant covalent.
exam.tip: Use the exact words giant covalent.

exam.q: Describe the structure of diamond.
model: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms.
Giant (3D) lattice / network.
Strong covalent bonds (tetrahedral arrangement).
exam.tip: Number of bonds is always a marking point.

exam.q: Describe the structure of graphite.
model: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others.
Arranged in layers of hexagonal rings.
Weak forces between layers / one delocalised electron per atom.
exam.tip: Three bonds, layers, weak forces between layers.

exam.q: Explain why diamond is used in cutting tools.
model: Each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid giant lattice.
So diamond is very hard.
exam.tip: Link structure to hardness.

exam.q: Explain why graphite can be used as a lubricant.
model: Weak forces between layers.
So layers can slide over each other (slippery).
exam.tip: Say between layers.

exam.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.
model: Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron (only three bonds formed).
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.
exam.tip: Delocalised + free to move.

exam.q: Explain why graphite has a high melting point even though it is soft.
model: Giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken to melt it, needing lots of energy.
Softness is due to weak forces between layers, which are not what holds atoms in the layers.
exam.tip: Distinguish bonds within layers from forces between layers.

exam.q: Graphite is used for the electrodes in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide. Explain two properties of graphite that make it suitable.
model: It conducts electricity.
Because it has delocalised electrons free to move.
It has a very high melting point.
Because many strong covalent bonds must be broken, so it does not melt in the hot molten electrolyte.
exam.tip: Property plus reason, twice.

exam.q: Compare the structures and properties of diamond and graphite, and explain how these lead to their different uses.
model: Both are giant covalent forms of carbon with very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid 3D lattice.
So diamond is very hard and is used in cutting tools.
Graphite: each carbon bonded to three others in layers of hexagons with weak forces between layers.
Layers slide over each other, so graphite is soft and slippery and used as a lubricant.
Graphite has one delocalised electron per atom free to move, so it conducts and is used for electrodes; diamond has no delocalised electrons so does not conduct.
exam.tip: Cover a similarity, then structure-property-use for each form.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why diamond is used in drill bits but graphite is not. (4 marks)
steps: In diamond each carbon atom forms **four strong covalent bonds** to other carbon atoms.
This gives a **rigid three-dimensional giant lattice**, so diamond is **very hard** and will cut through rock without wearing.
In graphite each carbon forms only **three** bonds and atoms are in **layers** with **weak forces between them**.
The layers **slide over each other**, so graphite is soft and would be worn away, making it useless for drilling.
worked.ans: Diamond is very hard because of its rigid 3D network of four strong covalent bonds per atom; graphite is soft because its layers slide.

worked.q: A student finds that a black, slippery solid made only of carbon conducts electricity and does not melt in a Bunsen flame. Use structure and bonding to explain each observation.
steps: Slippery: the solid is **graphite**, made of **layers** with **weak forces between layers**, so the layers slide over each other.
Conducts electricity: each carbon forms three bonds, leaving **one delocalised electron per atom**; these electrons are **free to move** and carry charge.
Does not melt in a Bunsen flame: it is **giant covalent**, so a huge number of **strong covalent bonds** must be broken, needing far more energy than the flame provides (melting point above 3500 °C).
worked.ans: The solid is **graphite**: weak forces between layers (slippery), delocalised electrons (conducts), many strong covalent bonds (very high melting point).

chem_edx.1.14.summary: Fullerenes and graphene are forms (allotropes) of pure carbon whose properties are explained entirely by their structure and bonding. **Graphene** is a single layer of graphite: a giant covalent sheet, one atom thick, of hexagonal carbon rings with delocalised electrons, so it is extremely strong, very light and conducts electricity. **Fullerenes** such as buckminsterfullerene, C60, are hollow molecules (spheres or tubes) made of rings of carbon atoms; C60 is a simple molecular substance with weak intermolecular forces, while carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with huge tensile strength and good electrical conductivity. In the exam you must always link a property to the structure: type of bonding, how many bonds each carbon makes, whether electrons are delocalised, and whether forces between molecules are weak.

core.p: Carbon can form several different structures made only of carbon atoms. These are called **allotropes**. Diamond and graphite (spec 1.35-1.37) are giant covalent structures. Graphene and the fullerenes are newer discoveries that show how changing the arrangement of the same atoms completely changes the properties.
bullets: All allotropes of carbon contain only carbon atoms joined by **covalent bonds**.
**Diamond**: each carbon bonded to 4 others, giant 3D lattice, no free electrons.
**Graphite**: each carbon bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers, delocalised electrons, weak forces between layers.
**Graphene**: a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
**Fullerenes**: hollow molecules of carbon atoms arranged in rings, usually hexagons with some pentagons (or heptagons).
Fullerenes include **buckminsterfullerene (C60)** and **carbon nanotubes**.
The key exam skill: explain each property using structure and bonding, not just state it.

head: Allotrope
Bonds per C
Structure type
Delocalised electrons?
rows: Yes, but only within each molecule

callouts.p: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

core.p: Graphene is a **single layer of graphite**. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to **three** other carbon atoms, forming a flat sheet of **hexagonal rings** that is only **one atom thick**. Because each carbon has four outer electrons but uses only three in bonds, the fourth electron is **delocalised** and free to move across the sheet.
bullets: Giant covalent structure in two dimensions (a sheet, not a 3D lattice).
Thickness: one atom, so it is the thinnest material known.
Every carbon atom forms 3 strong covalent bonds within the sheet.
One delocalised electron per carbon atom.
There are no layers stacked on top, so there are no weak forces between layers inside graphene itself.

callouts.p: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick, in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings, with one delocalised electron per atom.

core.p: Every property of graphene comes from the strong covalent bonds in the sheet and the delocalised electrons. Always use a **because** chain: structure leads to bonding leads to property.
bullets: **Very strong** (about 100 times stronger than steel of the same thickness) because of the many **strong covalent bonds** between carbon atoms in the sheet.
**Very high melting point** because a lot of energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds.
**Conducts electricity** (excellent conductor) because it has **delocalised electrons** that can move through the whole sheet and carry charge.
**Very light / low density** because it is only one atom thick.
**Transparent** because it is so thin.
**Flexible** because a single sheet can bend without breaking its bonds.
Uses: electronics (fast, flexible circuits and touchscreens), composites to strengthen materials, sensors.

head: Property
Explanation
rows: Many strong covalent bonds within the sheet
Lots of energy to break many strong covalent bonds
Delocalised electrons free to move across the sheet

callouts.p: For a 2-mark property question give the property AND the structural reason, e.g. conducts electricity (1) because delocalised electrons can move through the structure (1).

core.p: **Fullerenes** are molecules of carbon atoms with **hollow shapes**. Their structure is based on **hexagonal rings** of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings of **five (pentagons)** or **seven** carbon atoms. The pentagons are what allow a flat hexagon pattern to curve into a closed ball or a tube.
bullets: Made only of carbon atoms.
Hollow: closed cages (spheres) or tubes (cylinders).
Each carbon atom bonded to 3 other carbon atoms by covalent bonds.
Hexagons alone give a flat sheet; adding pentagons makes the sheet curve.
First fullerene discovered: buckminsterfullerene, C60, in 1985.
Fullerenes have a fixed number of atoms per molecule (for spheres), so they are molecules, not giant lattices.

callouts.p: A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape, based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, sometimes with rings of five or seven carbon atoms.

core.p: **Buckminsterfullerene** has the molecular formula **C60**. Its 60 carbon atoms form a hollow **sphere** made of **20 hexagons and 12 pentagons**, like a football. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others. C60 is a **simple molecular** substance: the bonds inside each ball are strong, but the forces **between** separate C60 molecules are **weak intermolecular forces**.
bullets: Molecular formula C60; relative formula mass = 60 x 12 = 720.
Hollow spherical cage of carbon atoms.
Rings: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
Strong covalent bonds within each molecule.
Weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
It is a molecule, NOT a giant covalent structure.

callouts.p: C60 is simple molecular. When it melts or sublimes, the covalent bonds inside the ball do NOT break; only the weak intermolecular forces between balls are overcome.

core.p: Because C60 is simple molecular, its properties are very different from graphene even though both contain carbon atoms bonded to three others.
bullets: **Low melting / sublimation point** (compared with diamond or graphite) because only **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules need to be overcome, which takes little energy.
**Soft and slippery** because the weak forces between the spherical molecules let them roll and slide past each other, so C60 can be used as a **lubricant**.
**Poor conductor of electricity** in the solid: each molecule has delocalised electrons, but these cannot move from one molecule to the next.
**Dissolves in some organic solvents** (e.g. it forms a coloured solution in methylbenzene) but not in water.
Hollow cage: other atoms or drug molecules can be trapped inside, so fullerenes are researched for **drug delivery** into the body.
Large surface area: fullerenes can be used as **catalysts** or catalyst supports.

callouts.p: C60: weak intermolecular forces lead to a low melting point and slippery feel; strong covalent bonds inside each ball mean each molecule itself is very stable.

core.p: **Carbon nanotubes** are **cylindrical fullerenes**. You can picture one as a sheet of graphene rolled up into a tube. They are only a few nanometres across but can be millions of times longer than they are wide, so they have a **very high length to diameter ratio**.
bullets: Hollow cylinder (tube) of carbon atoms, walls made of hexagonal rings.
Each carbon bonded to 3 others by strong covalent bonds.
Delocalised electrons can move along the tube.
Diameter around 1 nm (1 nm = 0.000000001 m); length can be micrometres to millimetres.
Very high length:diameter ratio.

core.p: Nanotubes combine the strong covalent bonding of graphene with a tube shape, giving them remarkable properties.
bullets: **High tensile strength** (very hard to pull apart) because of the strong covalent bonds along the tube, so they are used to **reinforce materials**, e.g. in tennis rackets, bike frames and sports equipment.
**Conduct electricity** because of delocalised electrons that move along the tube, so they are used in **electronics** and nanoscale wires.
**Conduct heat** well.
Very low density, so they strengthen materials without adding much mass.
Their tiny size means they belong to **nanotechnology** (structures 1 to 100 nm).

core.p: All three have each carbon atom bonded to three others, but the overall shape decides whether the substance behaves as a giant structure or as separate molecules.
bullets: Graphene: flat sheet, giant covalent, very high melting point, excellent conductor.
C60: closed ball, simple molecular, low melting point, poor conductor between molecules, slippery.
Nanotube: rolled-up sheet, very large molecule, very high tensile strength, conducts along its length.
Common feature: strong covalent C-C bonds, hexagonal rings, delocalised electrons.
Key difference: C60 molecules are separate, held together only by weak intermolecular forces.

callouts.p: In a compare question, write a point about each substance in the same sentence, e.g. graphene has a high melting point because strong covalent bonds must break, whereas C60 has a lower one because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

core.p: Graphene and nanotubes conduct because their delocalised electrons can travel through the whole structure. In C60 each molecule has delocalised electrons, but the molecules are separate, so electrons cannot easily pass from one ball to the next across the gaps between molecules.
bullets: To conduct electricity a substance needs **charged particles that are free to move**.
Graphene: delocalised electrons move across the entire sheet, so it conducts.
Nanotube: delocalised electrons move along the length of the tube, so it conducts.
C60 solid: electrons are delocalised only within each molecule, so it is a poor conductor.
Diamond (for contrast): no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct.

callouts.p: Never say graphene conducts because of free ions. Carbon allotropes conduct (when they do) because of delocalised electrons.

core.p: Fullerenes and graphene are examples of **nanoparticles / nanomaterials**, which have structures 1 to 100 nm in size. Their very high surface area to volume ratio and unusual shapes give them new uses, which is why they are a major area of research.
bullets: Drug delivery: medicine molecules carried inside hollow fullerene cages.
Catalysts: large surface area gives more sites for reactions.
Lubricants: spherical C60 molecules roll like tiny ball bearings.
Electronics and solar cells: conducting nanotubes and graphene.
Strengthening composites: nanotubes added to plastics.

core.p: Most marks come from linking structure to property. Examiners reward specific words: covalent bonds, delocalised electrons, weak intermolecular forces, layer one atom thick, hollow.
bullets: Name the bonding: **strong covalent bonds** between carbon atoms.
State how many bonds each carbon makes: **three**.
Mention **delocalised electrons** for conductivity.
For C60 melting point, mention **weak intermolecular forces** (not weak covalent bonds).
For strength, mention **many strong covalent bonds** that need lots of energy to break.
Learn one use for each and link it to a property.

callouts.p: Avoid 'weak bonds' on its own. Say exactly which: weak intermolecular forces between molecules. Covalent bonds in all carbon allotropes are strong.

analogy.p: Graphene is like a single sheet of **chicken wire**: a flat mesh of hexagons where every wire joint (carbon atom) is fixed to three others, so the sheet is very strong for its weight. Roll that chicken wire into a pipe and you have a **nanotube**. Stitch hexagons together with a few pentagons and the mesh curves into a closed **football**: that is C60, and a box of footballs rolls about easily because nothing glues the balls together (weak intermolecular forces), which is why C60 is slippery. Where it breaks down: real chicken wire does not conduct electricity through free electrons, real footballs are far apart compared with C60 molecules which do attract each other weakly, and atoms are not solid joints but nuclei surrounded by electrons.

terms.d: One of two or more different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, e.g. diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes are allotropes of carbon.
A single layer of graphite, one atom thick, with each carbon atom covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape, based on hexagonal rings, sometimes containing rings of five or seven carbon atoms.
The fullerene with formula C60: a hollow spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms arranged in 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
A cylindrical fullerene: a hollow tube of carbon atoms with a very high length to diameter ratio.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
An electron not associated with a single atom or bond, free to move through the structure.
Weak forces of attraction between separate molecules.
A substance made of separate molecules with strong covalent bonds inside them and weak intermolecular forces between them.
A very large network of atoms all joined by covalent bonds, with no separate molecules.
The ability of a material to resist being pulled apart (stretched) without breaking.
How many times longer an object is than it is wide; very high for nanotubes.
A substance that reduces friction between surfaces; C60 works because its molecules slide and roll past each other.
A particle 1 to 100 nm in size, containing a few hundred atoms.
A ring of six carbon atoms; the basic repeating unit of graphite, graphene and fullerenes.

mistakes.w: Graphene has a high melting point because of strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Graphene is giant covalent: many strong covalent bonds must be broken, which needs a lot of energy.

mistakes.w: C60 has a low melting point because its covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds in C60 are strong; it melts easily because only weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome.

mistakes.w: Graphene conducts because it has free ions.
mistakes.r: Graphene conducts because it has delocalised electrons that can move through the sheet.

mistakes.w: Each carbon in graphene is bonded to four other carbons.
mistakes.r: Each carbon in graphene (and fullerenes) is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms; four is diamond.

mistakes.w: C60 is a giant covalent structure.
mistakes.r: C60 is a simple molecular substance made of separate C60 molecules.

mistakes.w: Graphene is many layers of graphite.
mistakes.r: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.

mistakes.w: Fullerenes are made of hexagons only.
mistakes.r: Fullerenes are based on hexagons but also contain rings of five (or seven) carbon atoms, which allow the curve.

mistakes.w: Nanotubes are strong because they are hollow.
mistakes.r: Nanotubes have high tensile strength because of the strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms in the tube.

exam.q: State the molecular formula of buckminsterfullerene.
exam.tip: Write the 60 as a subscript-style number after C: C60.

exam.q: Describe the structure of graphene.
model: A single layer of carbon atoms / one atom thick / single layer of graphite
Each carbon atom covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: thickness and bonding.

exam.q: Explain why graphene conducts electricity.
model: Graphene has delocalised electrons
which are free to move through the structure / carry charge
exam.tip: Do not mention ions.

exam.q: Explain why graphene is very strong.
model: Many strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms
Large amount of energy needed to break them
exam.tip: Use the word covalent.

exam.q: C60 is used as a lubricant. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why C60 is slippery.
model: C60 is made of separate (spherical) molecules
with weak intermolecular forces between them, so molecules can slide/roll past each other
exam.tip: Lubricant answers need molecules sliding plus weak intermolecular forces.

exam.q: Give one use of carbon nanotubes and the property that makes them suitable.
model: Use: reinforcing materials (e.g. tennis rackets) / electronics
Property: high tensile strength / conduct electricity (matched to use)
exam.tip: The property must match the use you chose.

exam.q: Explain why C60 has a much lower sublimation point than graphene.
model: C60 is simple molecular / graphene is giant covalent
In C60 only weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome
In graphene many strong covalent bonds must be broken
Less energy needed for C60 than for graphene
exam.tip: Balance the answer: two marks for each substance.

exam.q: Describe the structure of buckminsterfullerene.
model: Molecule of 60 carbon atoms / C60
Hollow sphere/cage shape
Made of hexagonal and pentagonal rings, each carbon bonded to three others
exam.tip: Hollow and pentagons are the marks students most often miss.

exam.q: Graphene and diamond are both made of carbon atoms. Explain why graphene conducts electricity but diamond does not.
model: In graphene each carbon atom bonds to three others
leaving one delocalised electron per atom which can move
In diamond each carbon atom bonds to four others
so there are no delocalised/free electrons
exam.tip: Count bonds per carbon atom and say what happens to the fourth outer electron.

exam.q: Graphene, C60 and carbon nanotubes are all forms of carbon. Compare their structures and explain how their structures lead to their properties and uses.
model: All are carbon with each atom covalently bonded to three others in hexagonal rings, with delocalised electrons
Graphene is a single layer one atom thick, giant covalent
Graphene: very strong and high melting point due to many strong covalent bonds; conducts as delocalised electrons move; used in electronics/composites
C60 is a hollow spherical simple molecule with weak intermolecular forces
C60: low melting point and slippery, used as lubricant/drug delivery; poor conductor as electrons cannot move between molecules
Nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with high length:diameter ratio; high tensile strength and conduct electricity; used to reinforce materials and in electronics
exam.tip: Structure each substance as: structure, then property with reason, then use. Cover all three for full marks.

worked.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of C60 and the mass of one mole of it. (Ar of C = 12)
steps: Mr = number of atoms x Ar = 60 x 12
Mass of 1 mole = Mr in grams
worked.ans: Mr = 720, so 1 mole of C60 has a mass of 720 g.

worked.q: A scientist adds carbon nanotubes to a plastic to make a bicycle frame. Explain why this is a good idea.
steps: Identify the needed property: a frame must be strong but light.
Nanotubes have high tensile strength because of strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms along the tube.
Nanotubes have a low density, so they add very little mass.
Link: the frame becomes stronger without becoming much heavier.
worked.ans: The nanotubes reinforce the plastic: strong covalent bonds give high tensile strength while their low density keeps the frame light.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why C60 has a low melting point but each C60 molecule is very stable.
steps: State the structure: C60 is a simple molecular substance.
Inside each molecule carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds, which need a lot of energy to break, so the molecule itself is stable.
Between molecules there are only weak intermolecular forces.
On melting only these weak intermolecular forces are overcome, which needs little energy.
worked.ans: Melting only overcomes weak intermolecular forces (low energy), while the strong covalent bonds within each ball stay intact, so the molecule is stable.

chem_edx.1.15.summary: A **polymer** is a very large molecule made when many small molecules called **monomers** join together in a long chain. Edexcel uses **poly(ethene)** as the example: thousands of **ethene** (C2H4) monomers join so that the polymer is a long chain of carbon atoms held together by **strong covalent bonds**, with hydrogen atoms attached. Because the molecules are so long, the **intermolecular forces between chains** are much stronger than between small molecules, so poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature, yet it still softens and melts when heated because the covalent bonds inside the chains do not need to break.

core.p: A **polymer** is a substance made of very **large molecules**, each containing a long **chain** of atoms. The chain is built from many small repeating molecules called **monomers**. The word comes from poly (many) and mer (part).
bullets: **Monomer**: a small molecule that can join to others to form a polymer.
**Polymer**: a very large molecule made of many monomers joined in a chain.
Simple polymers like poly(ethene) have a backbone that is a **chain of carbon atoms**.
A single polymer molecule may contain thousands (even tens of thousands) of carbon atoms.
Atoms along the chain are joined by **covalent bonds**.
Polymers are covalent, molecular substances, not giant lattices: each chain is one (very long) molecule.

callouts.p: A large molecule (long-chain molecule) made from many small molecules called monomers joined together.
A small molecule that can join with many other monomer molecules to form a polymer.

core.p: Ethene is the simplest **alkene**, with formula **C2H4**. Its two carbon atoms are joined by a **carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)**, and each carbon also bonds to two hydrogen atoms. The double bond is the key: it is what lets ethene molecules join together.
bullets: Molecular formula: C2H4.
Contains a C=C double bond, so it is **unsaturated**.
Each carbon forms four covalent bonds in total (two to H, two in the double bond).
Ethene is a gas at room temperature: small molecules, weak intermolecular forces.
Ethene is made by cracking hydrocarbons from crude oil.

callouts.p: One of the two bonds in C=C can open up, freeing each carbon to bond to a carbon atom in a neighbouring molecule. This is how a chain forms.

core.p: When ethene is heated under **high pressure** with a **catalyst**, the double bonds open and thousands of ethene molecules join end to end. This is called **addition polymerisation** because the monomers simply add together and **nothing else is produced**: the polymer is the only product.
bullets: Equation in words: many ethene molecules form poly(ethene).
Equation with n: n C2H4 gives (C2H4)n, where n is a very large number.
The C=C double bond in each monomer becomes a C-C single bond in the polymer.
Every carbon atom in the chain ends up bonded to 2 carbons and 2 hydrogens.
Poly(ethene) is **saturated**: it has no C=C double bonds.
Total mass is conserved: the mass of polymer equals the mass of monomer used.

callouts.p: In addition polymerisation the polymer is the only product, so the empirical formula of poly(ethene), CH2, is the same as that of ethene.

core.p: Because the chain is far too long to draw, chemists draw one **repeat unit** inside square brackets with a bond sticking out of each side and an **n** after the bracket. For poly(ethene) the repeat unit is -CH2-CH2-.
bullets: Repeat unit of poly(ethene): two carbons joined by a single bond, each with two H atoms.
The bonds that cross the brackets show the chain continues in both directions.
n means the repeat unit is repeated a very large number of times.
To get the repeat unit from a monomer: change C=C to C-C and add a bond out of each side.
To get the monomer from a repeat unit: remove the extension bonds and change C-C back to C=C.
The repeat unit has the same atoms as the monomer, C2H4.

callouts.t: Do not forget n and the extension bonds
callouts.p: A repeat unit drawn without the bonds through the brackets, or without n, usually loses the mark.

core.p: The spec point says simple polymers are **large molecules containing chains of carbon atoms**. In poly(ethene) the backbone is a single, unbroken chain of carbon atoms, each joined to the next by a **strong covalent bond**. Each carbon also has two hydrogens attached, so every carbon makes four bonds.
bullets: The carbon backbone is not straight: bond angles make it zig-zag, and chains can bend and coil.
Each carbon: 2 bonds to neighbouring carbons + 2 bonds to hydrogens = 4 covalent bonds.
Only the ends of the chain differ (other groups finish the chain off).
Chains in a sample have different lengths, so a polymer has an average relative formula mass, not one exact value.
Longer chains mean larger molecules and stronger overall attraction between chains.

core.p: Polymers have two kinds of attraction, and you must never mix them up. **Within** each chain, atoms are held by **strong covalent bonds**. **Between** separate chains there are **intermolecular forces**, which are much weaker than covalent bonds.
bullets: Covalent bonds: shared pairs of electrons between C-C and C-H; strong, need lots of energy to break.
Intermolecular forces: attractions between neighbouring chains; much weaker.
When poly(ethene) melts, the **intermolecular forces** are overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact.
Because chains are so long, there are many points of contact between them, so the total intermolecular force is much larger than in small molecules like ethene.
This is why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature while ethene is a gas.

callouts.p: The longer the molecules, the stronger the intermolecular forces between them, so the more energy is needed to separate them and the higher the melting point.

core.p: The structure of long chains with strong covalent bonds inside and weaker forces between them explains the properties that make poly(ethene) so useful.
bullets: **Solid at room temperature**: long chains give relatively strong intermolecular forces overall.
**Softens and melts on heating** (thermosoftening): only intermolecular forces need to be overcome, so it can be moulded and recycled by melting.
**Flexible**: chains can slide past one another and the zig-zag backbone can bend.
**Does not conduct electricity**: no ions and no delocalised electrons, so it is used as an electrical insulator.
**Insoluble in water** and **unreactive**: saturated chain with strong C-C and C-H bonds, so it is good for containers.
**Low density**: light, making it useful for bags and packaging.

head: Property
Reason
Use
rows: Only weak forces between chains overcome

core.p: Ethene and poly(ethene) contain the same elements in the same ratio, but their properties are very different because of the size of the molecules.
bullets: Both are hydrocarbons, both have empirical formula CH2.
Ethene: small molecules, weak intermolecular forces, gas at room temperature, boiling point about -104 degrees C.
Poly(ethene): huge molecules, much stronger intermolecular forces overall, solid at room temperature.
Ethene is reactive (C=C double bond, decolourises bromine water); poly(ethene) is unreactive (saturated, does not decolourise bromine water).
Same atoms, different arrangement and size: a great example of structure deciding properties.

callouts.p: Ethene turns orange bromine water colourless; poly(ethene) does not, because it has no C=C double bonds left.

core.p: Polymers are covalent and made of molecules, so they belong with simple molecular substances in the classification of structures (spec 1.32), but their huge size makes them behave differently from small molecules like water or methane.
bullets: Like small molecules: covalent bonds within, intermolecular forces between, do not conduct electricity.
Unlike small molecules: much higher melting points, solid at room temperature, because the molecules are so large.
Unlike giant covalent structures: melting does not break covalent bonds, so melting points are well below those of diamond or graphite.
Polymer melting points are often a range, not a sharp value, because chains have different lengths.

core.p: Other alkenes form polymers in exactly the same way: the C=C opens and the monomers join into a carbon chain. The name of the polymer is poly( ) with the monomer name inside the brackets.
bullets: Propene forms poly(propene): carbon chain with CH3 side groups; used for crates and ropes.
Chloroethene forms poly(chloroethene), PVC: carbon chain with Cl atoms; used for window frames and pipes.
Tetrafluoroethene forms poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE: used for non-stick pans.
In all of these the backbone is a chain of carbon atoms, just as in poly(ethene).
Only the two carbons that were in the C=C become part of the main chain; any other groups hang off the side.

callouts.p: For poly(propene) the CH3 group is a branch off the chain. Do not put the CH3 carbon into the backbone.

core.h: Polymer chain length and relative formula mass
core.p: Because n is huge, the relative formula mass of a polymer is enormous. You can estimate it by multiplying the Mr of the repeat unit by n, or work out n from a given Mr.
bullets: Mr of the repeat unit C2H4 = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) = 28.
Mr of polymer = 28 x n.
Number of carbon atoms in the chain = 2n.
Different chains in a sample have different n, so a quoted Mr is an average.

core.p: Questions on this point usually ask you to describe a polymer, draw a repeat unit, or explain a property such as why poly(ethene) is solid or softens on heating.
bullets: Use the words **large molecules**, **long chains of carbon atoms**, **monomers**, **covalent bonds**.
Distinguish **covalent bonds within chains** from **intermolecular forces between chains**.
When explaining melting or softening, say intermolecular forces are overcome, NOT that bonds break.
Always draw the repeat unit with brackets, extension bonds and n.
Link properties to uses with a reason.

callouts.p: Poly(ethene) consists of large molecules containing long chains of carbon atoms, made by joining many ethene monomers.

analogy.p: Think of each ethene monomer as a **paper clip** whose double bond is a closed loop that can be opened. Open the loop and hook it onto the next clip, again and again, and you get a long **paper-clip chain**: that is a polymer. The hooks between clips are the strong covalent bonds, so the chain itself is hard to break. Throw lots of chains into a box and they tangle and cling to each other a little (intermolecular forces); a box of long chains holds together far better than a box of loose clips, which is why poly(ethene) is solid while ethene is a gas. Where it breaks down: real monomers do not keep a separate clip shape, the double bond does not disappear but becomes a single bond, and real chains contain thousands of units, not dozens.

terms.d: A very large molecule made of many small monomer molecules joined together in a chain.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
The alkene C2H4, containing a C=C double bond; the monomer of poly(ethene).
The polymer made from ethene; long chains of carbon atoms each bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
A reaction in which many unsaturated monomers join together to form a polymer as the only product.
The smallest section of a polymer chain that repeats, drawn in brackets with extension bonds and n.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond, C=C.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
Weak forces of attraction between separate molecules, e.g. between polymer chains.
The continuous chain of carbon atoms that forms the main chain of a polymer molecule.
A large whole number showing how many repeat units are in the polymer chain.
A compound containing hydrogen and carbon only.
A polymer that softens and melts when heated because only intermolecular forces between chains are overcome.
A hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond, general formula CnH2n.

mistakes.w: Poly(ethene) melts because the covalent bonds break.
mistakes.r: On melting the intermolecular forces between chains are overcome; covalent bonds in the chains do not break.

mistakes.w: A polymer is made of many polymers joined together.
mistakes.r: A polymer is made of many monomers joined together.

mistakes.w: Poly(ethene) has a C=C double bond.
mistakes.r: The double bond opens during polymerisation; poly(ethene) has only C-C single bonds (saturated).

mistakes.w: Drawing the repeat unit with no bonds through the brackets or with no n.
mistakes.r: Draw -CH2-CH2- in brackets with a bond extending through each bracket and n outside.

mistakes.w: Poly(ethene) is a giant covalent structure.
mistakes.r: Poly(ethene) is made of very large separate molecules (chains) held together by intermolecular forces.

mistakes.w: Poly(ethene) is solid because it has strong ionic bonds.
mistakes.r: It is solid because its very long molecules give strong enough intermolecular forces between chains overall.

mistakes.w: The monomer of poly(ethene) is ethane.
mistakes.r: The monomer is ethene, C2H4, which has a C=C double bond; ethane is saturated and cannot polymerise.

mistakes.w: Polymers conduct electricity because they are long chains.
mistakes.r: Poly(ethene) does not conduct: it has no ions or delocalised electrons that are free to move.

exam.q: Name the monomer used to make poly(ethene).
model: Ethene / C2H4
exam.tip: Spell it ethene, not ethane.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by a polymer.
model: A large molecule / long chain molecule
made from many small molecules (monomers) joined together
exam.tip: Two ideas: large molecule, many monomers.

exam.q: Draw the repeat unit of poly(ethene).
model: Two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, each with two H atoms
Brackets with extension bonds through them and n
exam.tip: Check every carbon has four bonds.

exam.q: State the type of bond that holds the carbon atoms together in a poly(ethene) chain.
model: Covalent (bond)
exam.tip: Single covalent bond is also accepted.

exam.q: Describe the structure of poly(ethene).
model: Very large molecules / long chains of carbon atoms
each carbon covalently bonded to two other carbons and two hydrogen atoms
exam.tip: The spec wording is large molecules containing chains of carbon atoms.

exam.q: Ethene is a gas at room temperature but poly(ethene) is a solid. Explain why.
model: Poly(ethene) molecules are much larger/longer than ethene molecules
so intermolecular forces between poly(ethene) chains are stronger
more energy needed to overcome them (so higher melting point)
exam.tip: Say intermolecular forces, not bonds.

exam.q: Explain why poly(ethene) softens when heated.
model: Intermolecular forces between chains are weak / overcome by heating
chains can then move/slide past each other (covalent bonds not broken)
exam.tip: Mention chains moving past each other.

exam.q: Explain why poly(ethene) is used to insulate electrical cables.
model: It does not conduct electricity
because it has no free electrons or ions that can move
exam.tip: Link property to reason.

exam.q: Compare the structure and bonding of ethene and poly(ethene).
model: Ethene has a C=C double bond / is unsaturated
Poly(ethene) has only C-C single bonds / is saturated
Ethene is a small molecule; poly(ethene) is a very large molecule / long chain of carbon atoms
Both have covalent bonds within molecules and intermolecular forces between molecules
exam.tip: Compare means similarities and differences.

exam.q: Explain how the structure and bonding of poly(ethene) account for its properties and uses.
model: Poly(ethene) is made of long chains of carbon atoms from many ethene monomers
Atoms within chains held by strong covalent bonds
Weaker intermolecular forces between chains; but long chains mean these are strong enough for it to be solid at room temperature
Softens/melts on heating as only intermolecular forces are overcome, so it can be moulded and recycled
Chains slide past each other so it is flexible: used for bags and cling film
No ions or delocalised electrons so it is an insulator; saturated with strong bonds so unreactive: used for containers
exam.tip: Work through structure, bonding, then each property with a matched use.

worked.q: A sample of poly(ethene) has chains containing on average 4000 repeat units. Calculate the average relative formula mass and the number of carbon atoms in one chain. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
steps: Repeat unit is C2H4: Mr = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) = 28
Polymer Mr = 28 x 4000 = 112 000
Each repeat unit has 2 carbon atoms, so carbons = 2 x 4000 = 8000
worked.ans: Average Mr = 112 000; each chain has about 8000 carbon atoms.

worked.q: A poly(ethene) molecule has a relative formula mass of 70 000. How many ethene monomers joined to make it?
steps: Mr of one ethene unit C2H4 = 28
worked.ans: 2500 ethene monomers.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why poly(ethene) can be melted and remoulded but this does not change it into ethene.
steps: Heating supplies energy to overcome the intermolecular forces between chains.
The chains can then move past each other, so the polymer melts and can be reshaped.
The strong covalent bonds within each chain need far more energy and are not broken.
So the long carbon chains stay intact and no ethene monomer is formed.
worked.ans: Melting only overcomes intermolecular forces between chains; the covalent C-C bonds in the chains remain, so the polymer stays as poly(ethene).

chem_edx.1.16.summary: In a metal, the atoms lose their outer shell electrons to form a **giant lattice of positive metal ions** surrounded by a **sea of delocalised electrons**. **Metallic bonding** is the strong **electrostatic attraction** between these positive ions and the delocalised electrons, and it acts in all directions throughout the structure. This single model explains all the typical properties of metals: high melting points (strong attractions in a giant structure), **conduction of electricity** and heat (delocalised electrons free to move), and **malleability** (layers of ions can slide over each other while the electrons keep holding them together).

core.p: Metal atoms have only a few electrons in their outer shell, and these are lost easily. In a solid metal each atom releases its outer electrons into a shared pool, leaving behind **positive metal ions**. The ions are packed closely in a regular **giant lattice** (layers), and the freed electrons are **delocalised**: they are not attached to any one ion and are free to move through the whole structure.
bullets: Structure: **giant lattice of positive metal ions** arranged in regular layers.
The outer shell electrons become **delocalised**, forming a **sea of electrons**.
**Metallic bond**: the **electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons**.
The attraction acts in **all directions**, holding the whole lattice together.
The metal as a whole is neutral: total negative charge of electrons = total positive charge of ions.
It is a **giant** structure: there are no separate molecules.

callouts.p: The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
There are no negative ions in a metal. The negative charge is carried by delocalised electrons.

core.h: Where do the delocalised electrons come from?
core.p: The delocalised electrons are the **outer shell electrons** of the metal atoms. The number each atom gives up usually matches its group number, so the charge on the ions and the number of delocalised electrons depend on the metal.
bullets: Sodium (group 1): each atom gives 1 electron, forming Na+ ions.
Magnesium (group 2): each atom gives 2 electrons, forming Mg2+ ions.
Aluminium (group 3): each atom gives 3 electrons, forming Al3+ ions.
More delocalised electrons and higher ion charge give stronger electrostatic attraction.
Smaller ions are also attracted more strongly, as the electrons can get closer to the nucleus.

callouts.p: Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium because Mg2+ ions have a greater charge and there are twice as many delocalised electrons per atom, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger.

core.h: Property 1: high melting and boiling points
core.p: Most metals have **high melting and boiling points**. To melt a metal you must overcome the strong electrostatic attractions between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons throughout a giant structure, which requires a lot of energy.
bullets: Metallic bonds are **strong** and there are **many** of them in the giant lattice.
**Lots of energy** must be transferred to overcome the attractions.
So most metals are solids at room temperature with high melting points (iron about 1538 degrees C, tungsten about 3422 degrees C).
Exceptions: mercury is a liquid at room temperature; group 1 metals have relatively low melting points.
Low melting points in group 1: ions only have a 1+ charge and there is just one delocalised electron per atom, so the attraction is weaker.

callouts.p: Giant structure + strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons + lots of energy needed to overcome = high melting point.

core.p: Metals are **good conductors of electricity** in both the solid and the liquid state. An electric current is a flow of charged particles. In a metal, the **delocalised electrons** are free to **move through the structure**, so when a potential difference is applied they drift towards the positive terminal, carrying charge.
bullets: Charge carriers in metals: **delocalised electrons** (NOT ions).
The positive ions stay vibrating in fixed positions in the lattice.
Electrons enter one end of the metal from the negative terminal and leave the other end towards the positive terminal.
Metals conduct when solid and when molten.
Use: copper for electrical wiring because it is an excellent conductor and ductile.

callouts.p: Writing that metals conduct because of free ions. In metals it is delocalised electrons that move; ions only carry charge in molten or dissolved ionic compounds.

core.p: Metals are **good conductors of heat**. When one end of a metal is heated, the delocalised electrons there gain kinetic energy and move quickly through the lattice, transferring energy to other parts of the metal. The closely packed ions also pass on vibrations to their neighbours.
bullets: Delocalised electrons carry energy rapidly through the structure.
Vibrating ions pass energy to neighbouring ions.
Use: saucepans and radiators are made of metals such as aluminium, copper and steel.
Good electrical conductors are usually also good thermal conductors, because both depend on delocalised electrons.

core.p: Metals are **malleable**: they can be **hammered or bent into shape** without shattering. They are also **ductile**: they can be drawn into wires. This is because the positive ions are arranged in **layers**, and these layers can **slide over each other** when a force is applied. The delocalised electrons move with them, so the electrostatic attraction holding the structure together is **not broken**.
bullets: Ions are in regular **layers** of the same type of atom.
A force makes the **layers slide over each other**.
The **sea of delocalised electrons** still surrounds the ions in their new positions.
The metallic bonding is not disrupted, so the metal changes shape instead of breaking.
Compare ionic solids: when layers move, ions of the same charge line up and repel, so the crystal shatters (brittle).
Uses: aluminium sheets for drinks cans and car bodies, copper drawn into wires, gold beaten into gold leaf.

callouts.p: Can be hammered or pressed into different shapes without breaking.
Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the metallic bonding (attraction to delocalised electrons) is maintained.
