core.p: The same model explains several other properties you may be asked about.
bullets: **High density**: ions are closely packed in the lattice.
**Shiny (lustrous)** when freshly cut or polished: delocalised electrons reflect light.
**Insoluble in water**: water cannot overcome the strong metallic bonding (though some reactive metals react with water).
**Strong** (high tensile strength): strong attraction between ions and electrons throughout.
**Sonorous**: ring when struck.
These are general properties; there are exceptions (e.g. sodium is soft and less dense than water).

head: Property
Explanation from model
rows: Strong electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice needs lots of energy to overcome
Delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge
Delocalised electrons carry energy through the structure
Layers of ions slide over each other; bonding maintained

core.p: Comparing metals with other structures shows why the metallic model is so useful and is a favourite exam question.
bullets: Metallic: positive ions and delocalised electrons; conducts when solid and liquid; malleable.
Ionic (giant ionic lattice): positive and negative ions; conducts only when molten or dissolved (ions move); brittle.
Giant covalent (diamond): atoms joined by covalent bonds; usually does not conduct (graphite is an exception); very hard and brittle.
Simple molecular: weak intermolecular forces; low melting points; do not conduct.

callouts.p: A substance that conducts as a solid and as a liquid and has a high melting point is metallic.

core.p: An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. The added atoms are a different size from the main metal ions, so they **distort the regular layers**. This makes it **harder for the layers to slide** over each other, so alloys are **harder and stronger** than pure metals.
bullets: Pure metals are often too soft for many uses because layers slide easily.
Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers.
Layers cannot slide as easily, so the alloy is harder.
Examples: steel (iron and carbon), brass (copper and zinc), gold alloys for jewellery.
Alloys still contain delocalised electrons, so they still conduct electricity.

core.h: Using properties to choose a metal
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of data and ask you to choose the best metal for a job and explain why. Match each requirement to a property and give the structural reason.
bullets: Electrical wiring: excellent electrical conductor and ductile, e.g. copper.
Saucepans: good thermal conductor, high melting point, e.g. aluminium or stainless steel.
Aircraft bodies: low density and strong, e.g. aluminium alloys.
Drinks cans: malleable and low density, e.g. aluminium.
Always use data from the table in your answer when it is given.

core.h: Limitations of the metallic bonding model
core.p: Like all models in chemistry, the sea of electrons picture is a simplification. You should be ready to say what it shows well and what it misses.
bullets: It shows ions as fixed spheres, but really they vibrate.
2D diagrams cannot show the true 3D arrangement of ions.
It does not explain why some metals are magnetic or why metals have different colours.
It does not easily explain differences in conductivity between metals.
It is still excellent for explaining melting points, conductivity and malleability.

core.p: Most questions want a description of metallic bonding plus an explanation of one or two properties. Mark schemes reward precise phrases.
bullets: Describe: **positive (metal) ions** in a **lattice/layers** with **delocalised electrons**.
Bond: **electrostatic attraction** between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
Electricity: delocalised electrons **can move** through the structure and carry charge.
Malleable: **layers** of ions can **slide over each other**.
High melting point: **strong** attractions, **lots of energy** needed to overcome them.
Never say metal atoms share electrons in covalent bonds, and never say metals have negative ions.

callouts.p: 'Free electrons' is often accepted, but 'delocalised electrons' is the safest term and appears in Edexcel mark schemes.

analogy.t: Marbles in a pool of honey
analogy.p: Picture a tray of tightly packed **marbles** (positive metal ions) sitting in a layer of **sticky honey** (the sea of delocalised electrons). The honey sticks every marble to the rest, in every direction, so the whole tray holds together strongly. Push the top row and the marbles roll along to new positions, but the honey flows with them and keeps them stuck: the metal bends instead of breaking (malleable). Because the honey flows, it can carry things from one side of the tray to the other, just as electrons carry charge and heat. Where it breaks down: honey is not charged and is not attracted to marbles by electrostatic forces, real electrons move extremely fast rather than oozing slowly, and real ions vibrate in a 3D lattice rather than sitting still in a flat tray.

terms.d: The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Electrons that are not attached to any one atom or bond and are free to move through the whole structure.
A metal atom that has lost its outer shell electron(s), leaving a positive charge.
A very large, regular, repeating arrangement of particles extending in all directions, with no separate molecules.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles.
Able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.
Able to be drawn out (stretched) into a wire.
A material that allows charge to flow through it because it contains charged particles free to move.
A material that transfers energy by heating quickly through itself.
The description of delocalised electrons surrounding the lattice of positive metal ions.
Rows/planes of identical metal ions in the lattice that can slide over one another.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements; usually harder than the pure metal because the layers are distorted.
Breaks or shatters when hit, rather than bending (typical of ionic and covalent solids).
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid; high for most metals because strong metallic bonding must be overcome.

mistakes.w: Metals conduct electricity because they have free ions.
mistakes.r: Metals conduct because delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge.

mistakes.w: Metallic bonding is between positive and negative ions.
mistakes.r: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons; there are no negative ions.

mistakes.w: Metals are malleable because the bonds are weak.
mistakes.r: Metals are malleable because the layers of ions can slide over each other while the metallic bonding is maintained; the bonds are strong.

mistakes.w: Metal atoms share electrons in covalent bonds.
mistakes.r: Metal atoms lose outer electrons, which become delocalised; this is metallic bonding, not covalent.

mistakes.w: Metals have high melting points because of strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Metals have no molecules; high melting points are due to strong electrostatic attraction between ions and delocalised electrons in a giant lattice.

mistakes.w: The delocalised electrons come from the inner shells.
mistakes.r: The delocalised electrons are the outer shell electrons of the metal atoms.

mistakes.w: Metals only conduct electricity when molten.
mistakes.r: Metals conduct when solid and when liquid; it is ionic compounds that only conduct when molten or dissolved.

mistakes.w: When a metal is bent, the bonds break and reform.
mistakes.r: The layers slide but the delocalised electrons still hold the ions, so the metallic bonding is not broken.

exam.q: Name the type of bonding found in copper.
model: Metallic (bonding)
exam.tip: One word answer: metallic.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a metal.
model: Lattice / layers of positive (metal) ions
surrounded by (a sea of) delocalised electrons
exam.tip: Both ions and electrons are needed.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by metallic bonding.
model: Electrostatic attraction
between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
exam.tip: Say electrostatic attraction and name both particles.

exam.q: Explain why metals conduct electricity.
model: Metals have delocalised electrons
which can move through the structure (and carry charge)
exam.tip: Never mention ions moving.

exam.q: Explain why metals are malleable.
model: Layers of ions / atoms
can slide over each other (without breaking the metallic bonding)
exam.tip: The key word is layers.

exam.q: Explain why most metals have high melting points.
model: Giant structure / lattice
strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
lots of energy needed to overcome these attractions
exam.tip: Strong + lots of energy are both needed.

exam.q: Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium. Explain why.
model: Magnesium ions are Mg2+ / have a higher charge than Na+
magnesium has more delocalised electrons per atom (2 vs 1)
so stronger electrostatic attraction / more energy needed to overcome
exam.tip: Compare both charge and number of electrons.

exam.q: Explain why copper is used for electrical wiring.
model: Good conductor of electricity because delocalised electrons can move
Ductile / can be drawn into wires as layers slide
exam.tip: Two properties, each with a reason.

exam.q: Sodium chloride and sodium both have high melting points. Compare their ability to conduct electricity when solid and explain the difference.
model: Solid sodium conducts electricity
because delocalised electrons can move through the structure
Solid sodium chloride does not conduct
because its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move
exam.tip: Name the charge carrier for each and say whether it can move.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why metals have high melting points, conduct electricity and are malleable.
model: Metals consist of a giant lattice of positive ions in layers surrounded by delocalised electrons
Metallic bonding is strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
High melting point: many strong attractions, lots of energy needed to overcome them
Conduct electricity: delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge
Malleable: layers of ions can slide over each other when a force is applied
Bonding is maintained as delocalised electrons move with the ions, so the metal changes shape rather than breaking
exam.tip: Describe the model first, then give one paragraph per property, each with its reason.

worked.q: Use the data to identify which substance is a metal. A: melting point 801 degrees C, conducts only when molten. B: melting point 1085 degrees C, conducts when solid and molten. C: melting point -7 degrees C, never conducts.
steps: A conducts only when molten: ions free to move only in liquid, so A is ionic.
C has a low melting point and never conducts: simple molecular.
B has a high melting point and conducts as a solid: delocalised electrons move in a giant metallic lattice.
worked.ans: B is the metal (its data match copper).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why aluminium (Al3+ ions) is a better electrical conductor than sodium (Na+ ions), assuming conductivity depends on the number of delocalised electrons.
steps: Each aluminium atom loses 3 outer electrons to form Al3+.
Each sodium atom loses 1 outer electron to form Na+.
So aluminium has three times as many delocalised electrons per atom.
More delocalised electrons that can move means more charge can be carried.
worked.ans: Aluminium provides 3 delocalised electrons per atom compared with 1 for sodium, so more mobile charge carriers are available.

worked.q: A blacksmith hammers a piece of hot iron into a horseshoe. Explain why the iron changes shape but does not shatter.
steps: Iron has a giant metallic lattice of Fe ions in layers surrounded by delocalised electrons.
The hammer blow applies a force that makes the layers of ions slide over each other.
The delocalised electrons move with the ions, so the electrostatic attraction is maintained in the new position.
Because the bonding is not broken, the iron changes shape instead of shattering.
worked.ans: Layers of ions slide over each other while the sea of delocalised electrons keeps holding them together, so iron is malleable.

chem_edx.1.2.summary: Every atom of an element has the **same number of protons** in its nucleus, and this number (the **atomic number**) is unique to that element: it is what makes carbon carbon. The **mass number** is the total number of protons plus neutrons. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these are called **isotopes**. Using the atomic number and mass number you can work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom or ion.

core.h: Quick recap: the three subatomic particles
core.p: An atom has a tiny central **nucleus** containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus because protons and neutrons are each about 1836 times heavier than an electron. These numbers are the tools you need for this whole spec point.
bullets: Protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus; electrons are in shells around the nucleus.
A proton has relative charge **+1** and relative mass **1**.
A neutron has relative charge **0** and relative mass **1**.
An electron has relative charge **-1** and relative mass about **1/1836** (negligible).
Because electrons are so light, they are ignored when counting the mass of an atom.

callouts.p: Atomic number counts protons only. Mass number counts protons and neutrons. Electrons never appear in the mass number.

core.h: Atomic number: the identity card of an element
core.p: The **atomic number** (symbol Z, also called the proton number) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. All atoms of a particular element have the **same number of protons**, and no other element has that number. So the atomic number tells you which element an atom is. If you changed the number of protons, you would have a different element.
bullets: Hydrogen always has 1 proton, helium 2, carbon 6, oxygen 8, sodium 11, chlorine 17.
The number of protons is **unique to each element**.
Elements in the modern periodic table are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Changing the number of neutrons or electrons does NOT change the element; changing the number of protons does.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of a given element all have the same number of protons in the nucleus, and this number is unique to that element.

core.p: The **mass number** (symbol A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom. Protons and neutrons are together called **nucleons**. Since each has a relative mass of 1 and electrons are almost massless, the mass number is roughly the relative mass of that atom. The mass number is always a whole number because you cannot have part of a particle.
bullets: Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Mass number is always greater than or equal to the atomic number (hydrogen-1 has A = Z = 1).
The mass number is always a **whole number**; relative atomic mass (on the periodic table) need not be.
Mass number refers to ONE particular atom (one isotope), not the element as a whole.

callouts.p: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

callouts.t: Not the same as relative atomic mass
callouts.p: Chlorine has a relative atomic mass of 35.5 but no chlorine atom has a mass number of 35.5. Mass numbers are whole numbers (35 or 37).

core.p: Atoms are written with the mass number at the **top left** and the atomic number at the **bottom left** of the chemical symbol. The bigger number is always the mass number. From this one symbol you can find every particle in the atom.
bullets: Top number = mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
Bottom number = atomic number (Z) = protons.
Isotopes can also be written in words, e.g. sodium-23 or carbon-14, where the number is the mass number.
On the Edexcel periodic table each box shows relative atomic mass at the top and atomic (proton) number at the bottom.

callouts.p: If you forget which is which, the mass number is always the larger number because it includes the neutrons as well as the protons.

fig.cap: Nuclide notation for sodium-23. The mass number (23) is top left, the atomic number (11) is bottom left. Protons = 11, neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12, and in a neutral atom electrons = protons = 11.

core.h: Calculating protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms
core.p: Given the atomic number and mass number you can calculate the numbers of each subatomic particle. In a **neutral atom** the number of electrons equals the number of protons, because the positive and negative charges must cancel out.
bullets: Protons = atomic number.
Electrons (neutral atom) = atomic number.
Neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
Always state each answer separately and clearly label it (protons, neutrons, electrons).
Check: protons + neutrons should add back up to the mass number.

callouts.p: protons = Z; neutrons = A - Z; electrons = Z (for a neutral atom).

core.p: An atom has no overall charge. Each proton has a charge of +1 and each electron a charge of -1, so for the charges to cancel there must be equal numbers of protons and electrons. Neutrons have no charge, so the number of neutrons has no effect on the overall charge.
bullets: Total positive charge = number of protons x (+1).
Total negative charge = number of electrons x (-1).
Equal numbers means overall charge = 0.
Neutrons can vary without changing the charge, which is why isotopes are still neutral atoms.

callouts.t: Do not link neutrons to electrons
callouts.p: The number of neutrons is NOT equal to the number of electrons in general. Only protons and electrons are equal in a neutral atom.

core.h: Applying the same idea to ions
core.p: An **ion** is an atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, so it has an overall charge. Only the electrons change: the nucleus (protons and neutrons) stays exactly the same. A positive ion has **lost** electrons; a negative ion has **gained** electrons.
bullets: Protons and neutrons in an ion are worked out exactly as for the atom.
Electrons in a positive ion = Z - charge, e.g. Na+ has 11 - 1 = 10 electrons.
Electrons in a negative ion = Z + size of charge, e.g. Cl- has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons.
Mg2+ (Z = 12) has 10 electrons; O2- (Z = 8) has 10 electrons.
The element is unchanged because the number of protons is unchanged.

callouts.p: Overall charge of a particle = number of protons - number of electrons. Use this to check any ion answer.

fig.cap: Working out the particles in a chloride ion, 35Cl-. The nucleus is unchanged from the chlorine atom (17 protons, 18 neutrons); the ion has gained one electron, so it has 18 electrons and an overall charge of -1.

core.p: Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but they can have **different numbers of neutrons**. These different forms are called **isotopes**. Because they have the same number of protons they are the same element, but because the number of neutrons differs they have **different mass numbers**.
bullets: Isotopes have the **same atomic number** but a **different mass number**.
Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 all have 6 protons and 6 electrons, but 6, 7 and 8 neutrons.
Chlorine-35 (18 neutrons) and chlorine-37 (20 neutrons) are both chlorine: 17 protons each.
Most elements exist naturally as a mixture of isotopes.
Isotopes are named using the mass number, e.g. uranium-235, carbon-14.

callouts.p: Different atoms of the same element containing the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei.

core.p: Hydrogen is a favourite exam example because it is so simple. All hydrogen atoms have 1 proton and 1 electron. Hydrogen-1 has no neutrons, hydrogen-2 (deuterium) has 1 neutron, and hydrogen-3 (tritium) has 2 neutrons.
bullets: Hydrogen-1: 1 proton, 0 neutrons, 1 electron (the only atom with no neutrons).
Hydrogen-2 (deuterium): 1 proton, 1 neutron, 1 electron.
Hydrogen-3 (tritium): 1 proton, 2 neutrons, 1 electron.
All three react in the same way, e.g. all burn in oxygen to form water.

callouts.p: If asked which atom has no neutrons, the answer is hydrogen-1. Every other atom has at least one neutron.

core.h: Why isotopes react in the same way
core.p: Chemical reactions involve **electrons**, not the nucleus. Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and so the same number of electrons, arranged in the same electronic configuration. This means isotopes have the **same chemical properties**. The extra neutrons only change the mass of the atom.
bullets: Same number of electrons means the same number of outer-shell electrons, so the same reactions.
Isotopes differ in mass, so properties that depend on mass (such as density) can be slightly different.
Some isotopes have unstable nuclei and are radioactive, e.g. carbon-14, while carbon-12 is stable.
Neutrons have no charge, so they do not affect how strongly electrons are attracted in a way that changes reactions at GCSE level.

callouts.p: Isotopes have the same electronic configuration, so they have the same chemical properties.

core.h: Atomic number versus mass number versus relative atomic mass
core.p: Students often muddle three different numbers. The atomic number and mass number are always whole numbers and describe a single atom. Relative atomic mass is an average over all the isotopes of an element (covered in spec 1.11-1.12) and can be a decimal.
bullets: Atomic number: protons only; whole number; same for every atom of the element.
Mass number: protons + neutrons; whole number; differs between isotopes.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): weighted mean mass of the isotopes; can be a decimal (e.g. Cl = 35.5).
When a question gives you a periodic table, the atomic number is the smaller (bottom) number in the box.

callouts.p: If a question asks for the neutrons in 'an atom of chlorine-37', use 37 - 17 = 20, not the 35.5 from the periodic table.

core.p: These are quick marks if you are precise. Examiners want the correct number for each particle and correct use of the words proton, neutron, electron and nucleus.
bullets: Always identify Z and A first and write them down.
Use 'nucleus' when describing where protons and neutrons are; never say 'neutrons orbit'.
For isotopes definitions, you must say **same number of protons** AND **different numbers of neutrons**; 'same element' alone is not enough for both marks.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of electrons or different atomic numbers.
For ions, change only the electrons.

callouts.p: Same number of protons (1) but different number of neutrons (1).

analogy.p: Think of an element as a football club and the atomic number as the club badge: every player (atom) wearing that badge belongs to that club, and no other club uses that badge. Neutrons are like the kit bag each player carries: some carry heavier bags than others (isotopes have different masses), but they still play for the same club and play the same way (same chemistry). The mass number is the total weight of badge plus bag. Where it breaks down: a player can change clubs by swapping a badge, but you cannot change an atom's protons by any chemical reaction, and real neutrons do affect nuclear stability (some isotopes are radioactive), which a kit bag does not.

terms.d: The smallest particle of an element, with a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons; it has no overall charge.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, containing the protons and neutrons.
Particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.
Particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge 0.
Particle in shells around the nucleus with relative mass 1/1836 and relative charge -1.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; unique to each element.
Another name for atomic number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
A particle found in the nucleus: a proton or a neutron.
Different atoms of the same element containing the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei.
A substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons.
An atom or group of atoms with an overall charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
Having no overall charge; in an atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Writing an atom as its symbol with the mass number at top left and the atomic number at bottom left.
The weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (see 1.11-1.12).

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different numbers of protons.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the SAME number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different numbers of electrons.
mistakes.r: Atoms of isotopes have the same number of electrons (equal to the number of protons).

mistakes.w: Mass number is the number of protons and electrons.
mistakes.r: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Number of neutrons = mass number (or = atomic number).
mistakes.r: Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number.

mistakes.w: Using 35.5 to work out neutrons in a chlorine atom, giving 18.5 neutrons.
mistakes.r: Use the mass number of the specific isotope (35 or 37); particles come in whole numbers.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different chemical properties because they have different masses.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same chemical properties because they have the same number and arrangement of electrons.

mistakes.w: A Na+ ion has 12 electrons (gained one).
mistakes.r: A positive ion has LOST electrons: Na+ has 11 - 1 = 10 electrons.

mistakes.w: The atomic number is the number of electrons.
mistakes.r: The atomic number is the number of protons; it equals the electrons only in a neutral atom.

mistakes.w: When an atom forms an ion its number of protons changes.
mistakes.r: Only electrons are gained or lost; protons and neutrons stay the same, so it is still the same element.

exam.q: State the meaning of the term atomic number.
model: The number of protons in the nucleus (of an atom).
exam.tip: Say protons, not 'particles'.

exam.q: State the meaning of the term mass number.
model: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus (of an atom).
exam.tip: Do not include electrons.

exam.q: An atom of fluorine has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. Give the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
model: Protons 9 and electrons 9 (1).
Neutrons 10 (1).
exam.tip: Neutrons = 19 - 9.

exam.q: Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Explain, in terms of subatomic particles, why these are isotopes of the same element.
model: Both have the same number of protons (17) (1).
They have different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20) (1).
exam.tip: Same protons is what makes them the same element.

exam.q: Which statement about the atoms carbon-12 and carbon-14 is correct? A: different numbers of protons; B: same mass number; C: different numbers of neutrons; D: different numbers of electrons.
model: C
exam.tip: Isotopes differ only in neutrons.

exam.q: Explain why atoms have no overall charge.
model: Atoms contain equal numbers of protons and electrons (1).
The positive charge of the protons (+1 each) cancels the negative charge of the electrons (-1 each); neutrons have no charge (1).
exam.tip: Refer to charges of both particles.

exam.q: An ion of magnesium is written 24Mg2+ (atomic number 12). Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion.
model: 12 protons (1).
12 neutrons (1).
10 electrons (1).
exam.tip: 2+ means two electrons lost.

exam.q: Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties.
model: They have the same number of electrons / same electronic configuration (1).
Chemical reactions depend on the electrons, (and neutrons do not affect reactions) (1).
exam.tip: Link to electrons, not mass.

exam.q: Potassium-39 and potassium-41 are isotopes of potassium (atomic number 19). Compare the atoms of these two isotopes in terms of their subatomic particles and their properties.
model: Both have 19 protons (1).
Both have 19 electrons (1).
Potassium-39 has 20 neutrons and potassium-41 has 22 neutrons (1).
Same chemical properties as same electronic configuration but potassium-41 atoms are heavier (1).
exam.tip: Compare means state similarities AND differences.

exam.q: Describe the structure of the atoms of two isotopes of hydrogen, hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-3, and explain how scientists can tell that both are hydrogen. Use ideas about atomic number and mass number in your answer.
model: Both atoms have a nucleus at the centre with an electron in a shell around it.
Hydrogen-1 has 1 proton and no neutrons in its nucleus.
Hydrogen-3 has 1 proton and 2 neutrons in its nucleus.
Both have 1 electron so both atoms are neutral.
Atomic number (number of protons) is 1 for both, and this number is unique to hydrogen, so both are hydrogen.
Mass numbers differ (1 and 3) because the number of neutrons differs, so they are isotopes with the same chemical properties.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need structure, particle numbers and the link to atomic number being unique.

worked.q: An atom of iron has atomic number 26 and mass number 56. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
steps: Identify Z = 26 and A = 56.
Protons = Z = 26.
Neutrons = A - Z = 56 - 26 = 30.
Electrons = Z = 26 because the atom is neutral.
Check: 26 + 30 = 56 = mass number.
worked.ans: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons.

worked.q: A particle has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons. Identify the element, give its mass number and state the charge on the particle.
steps: 16 protons means atomic number 16, which is sulfur.
Mass number = protons + neutrons = 16 + 16 = 32.
Charge = protons - electrons = 16 - 18 = -2.
So it is a sulfide ion with mass number 32.
worked.ans: Sulfur, mass number 32, charge 2- (a 32S2- ion).

worked.q: Element X has two isotopes: one with 10 neutrons and mass number 20, and one with 12 neutrons. Find the atomic number of X and the mass number of the second isotope.
steps: Atomic number = mass number - neutrons = 20 - 10 = 10.
Isotopes have the same number of protons, so the second isotope also has 10 protons.
Mass number of second isotope = 10 + 12 = 22.
Z = 10 is neon.
worked.ans: Atomic number 10 (neon); second isotope has mass number 22.

chem_edx.1.3.summary: Most elements exist as a mixture of **isotopes**, atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons and so different masses. The **relative atomic mass (Ar)** of an element is the **weighted mean** mass of its atoms, taking into account how common (abundant) each isotope is. Because it is an average of different whole-number masses, Ar is often not a whole number, for example chlorine is 35.5. You must be able to calculate Ar from the masses and abundances of the isotopes.

core.p: A single atom has a mass of around 10^-23 g, which is far too small to work with. Instead, chemists compare the masses of atoms with each other on a **relative** scale. Relative masses have **no units** because they are a comparison, not an actual mass.
bullets: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1; electrons are negligible.
So the relative mass of one isotope is roughly equal to its mass number.
The scale is fixed using the carbon-12 atom, which is given a mass of exactly 12.
Relative atomic mass has the symbol **Ar** and no units.

callouts.p: Ar is a ratio, so never write g or any unit after it.

core.p: The relative atomic mass of an element is an average that takes into account every isotope of the element and how much of each there is. It is measured against the carbon-12 standard.
bullets: 'Weighted' means more common isotopes count for more in the average.
'Mean' means it is an average of the masses of the atoms.
It applies to the element as found naturally, not to a single atom.
The value on the Edexcel periodic table (top number in each box) is the relative atomic mass.

callouts.p: The weighted mean (average) mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
If asked to define Ar, 'the average mass of the atoms of an element, taking into account the abundance of each isotope' gains credit; adding 'relative to carbon-12' makes it complete.

core.p: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different masses. In a natural sample the isotopes are not present in equal amounts. The **abundance** of an isotope tells you how much of it there is, usually as a percentage of all the atoms of that element.
bullets: Percentage abundances of all the isotopes add up to 100%.
Abundance may also be given as a ratio (e.g. 3 : 1) or as relative abundance from a bar chart.
Chlorine: chlorine-35 is 75% and chlorine-37 is 25% of natural chlorine atoms.
Isotopes have the same chemical properties, so the mix behaves as one element in reactions.

callouts.p: The proportion of the atoms of an element that are a particular isotope, often given as a percentage.

core.h: Why some relative atomic masses are not whole numbers
core.p: Each isotope has a whole-number mass number. But an element is usually a mixture of isotopes, so its relative atomic mass is an **average** of different masses. An average of different whole numbers is usually not a whole number. That is why chlorine has Ar = 35.5 even though no chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5.
bullets: If an element had only one isotope (e.g. fluorine-19), its Ar would be (almost exactly) a whole number.
The more evenly mixed the isotopes, the further Ar is from a whole number.
No individual atom has the mass shown by Ar; it is a property of the whole sample.
This is the explanation the spec asks for: existence of isotopes leads to non-whole-number Ar.

callouts.p: Elements exist as a mixture of isotopes with different masses; Ar is the weighted mean of these masses, so it is often not a whole number.

fig.cap: A model sample of chlorine atoms. For every four atoms, three are chlorine-35 and one is chlorine-37. The average mass is (35 + 35 + 35 + 37) / 4 = 35.5, so Ar is not a whole number.

core.h: Weighted mean, not a simple mean
core.p: A simple mean of 35 and 37 would be 36, but that is wrong for chlorine because there are three times as many chlorine-35 atoms as chlorine-37 atoms. A **weighted mean** multiplies each mass by how common it is, so the answer is pulled towards the most abundant isotope.
bullets: Simple mean: add the masses and divide by the number of isotopes (ignores abundance) - WRONG for Ar.
Weighted mean: multiply each mass by its abundance, add, then divide by the total abundance - CORRECT.
Ar always lies between the lightest and heaviest isotope masses.
Ar is always closest to the mass of the most abundant isotope.

callouts.p: Never just average the mass numbers. You must use the abundances.

core.h: The formula for relative atomic mass
core.p: To calculate Ar, multiply the mass of each isotope by its abundance, add all these together, then divide by the total abundance. When abundances are percentages the total is 100.
bullets: Ar = sum of (isotope mass x abundance) / total abundance.
With percentages: Ar = [(mass 1 x % 1) + (mass 2 x % 2) + ...] / 100.
With a ratio a : b: Ar = [(mass 1 x a) + (mass 2 x b)] / (a + b).
Use the relative isotopic mass given; at GCSE this is usually the mass number.
Give the answer to the number of decimal places asked (often 1 d.p.).

callouts.p: Ar = total of (mass x abundance) / total abundance

core.p: This is the most common exam calculation. Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Imagine 100 atoms: 75 have mass 35 and 25 have mass 37. Find the total mass of the 100 atoms and divide by 100.
bullets: Check: 35.5 lies between 35 and 37 and is closer to 35, the more abundant isotope.

callouts.p: Percentages are just 'number of atoms out of 100', so the total mass of 100 atoms divided by 100 gives the mean.

core.h: Abundances given as a ratio or relative abundance
core.p: Sometimes the abundances do not add to 100. They may be given as a ratio or as relative abundances read from a bar chart. In this case, divide by the **sum of the abundances**, not by 100.
bullets: Boron: B-10 and B-11 in the ratio 1 : 4.
Total abundance = 1 + 4 = 5.
Dividing by 100 here would give a nonsense answer (0.54), which fails the 'between the isotope masses' check.

callouts.p: Only divide by 100 when the abundances are percentages that add to 100.

core.h: Elements with three or more isotopes
core.p: The method is exactly the same however many isotopes there are: one 'mass x abundance' term for each isotope.
bullets: Magnesium: Mg-24 79%, Mg-25 10%, Mg-26 11%.
Check the abundances add to 100% before you start; if one is missing, it is 100 minus the others.

callouts.p: Setting out a table like this makes it easy to show working and earn method marks even if you slip on the final answer.

core.h: Reading abundances from a bar chart
core.p: Questions often show the isotopes of an element as a bar chart (a simplified mass spectrum). The x-axis shows the mass of each isotope and the bar height shows its abundance. Read each bar carefully, then use the usual method.
bullets: Each bar = one isotope; x-value = its mass; height = its (relative) abundance.
If the heights are percentages that total 100, divide by 100.
If they are relative abundances (e.g. 3 and 1), divide by their sum.
The tallest bar is the most abundant isotope, so Ar will be closest to its mass.

callouts.p: If only one percentage is given for a two-isotope element, the other is 100 minus that value.

core.p: A harder question gives you Ar and the isotope masses and asks for the abundances. Let the percentage of one isotope be x; the other is then (100 - x). Substitute into the formula and solve.
bullets: Boron has Ar = 10.8 and isotopes B-10 and B-11.
Let % of B-10 = x, so % of B-11 = 100 - x.

callouts.p: Ar = 10.8 is much closer to 11 than to 10, so B-11 must be the more abundant isotope, which matches 80%.

core.p: Examiners award a final mark for a correctly rounded answer. Quick checks catch most slips before they cost marks.
bullets: The answer must lie between the smallest and largest isotope masses.
It should be closest to the most abundant isotope.
Give the answer to the stated number of decimal places or significant figures; if none is stated, 1 d.p. matches the periodic table.
Do not round intermediate values; only round the final answer.
No units.

callouts.p: If your Ar is bigger than the heaviest isotope or smaller than the lightest, you have divided by the wrong number or misread the data.

analogy.p: Imagine your final grade is worked out from homework worth 25% and an exam worth 75%. Scoring 37 on homework and 35 on the exam does not give you 36; the exam counts three times as much, so your weighted average is 35.5. Isotopes work the same way: the abundance is the 'weighting' of each isotope's mass. Where it breaks down: test weightings are chosen by a teacher, but isotope abundances are fixed by nature, and in a real sample there are billions of atoms each with an actual whole-number mass rather than one score.

terms.d: The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
How much of a particular isotope is present in a natural sample of the element, usually as a percentage of the atoms.
The percentage of all atoms of an element that are a particular isotope; all values add up to 100%.
The amount of each isotope compared with the others, e.g. as a ratio or bar height, not necessarily adding to 100.
An average in which each value is multiplied by how often it occurs before adding and dividing by the total.
An average that adds values and divides by how many there are, ignoring how common each is; not used for Ar.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom; a whole number.
The mass of one isotope compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; at GCSE taken as the mass number.
The isotope of carbon used as the standard for relative masses, given a mass of exactly 12.
A mass compared with a standard, so it has no units.
A chart showing the mass of each isotope on the x-axis and its abundance as the bar height.
The number of protons in the nucleus; the same for all isotopes of an element.

mistakes.w: Ar of chlorine = (35 + 37) / 2 = 36.
mistakes.r: Use a weighted mean: (35 x 75 + 37 x 25) / 100 = 35.5.

mistakes.w: Ar is not a whole number because the mass of electrons is included.
mistakes.r: Ar is not a whole number because it is the weighted mean of the masses of different isotopes.

mistakes.w: Dividing by 100 when the abundances are a ratio (e.g. 1 : 4).
mistakes.r: Divide by the total abundance, e.g. 1 + 4 = 5.

mistakes.w: Writing the answer as 35.5 g.
mistakes.r: Relative atomic mass has no units.

mistakes.w: Some chlorine atoms have a mass of 35.5.
mistakes.r: No atom has a mass of 35.5; atoms are either 35 or 37; 35.5 is an average.

mistakes.w: Rounding each product before adding, giving an inaccurate final answer.
mistakes.r: Keep full values in the working and round only the final answer.

mistakes.w: Ar is the mass number of the most common isotope.
mistakes.r: Ar is the weighted mean of all the isotopes, not just the most common one.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different numbers of protons, so different masses.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

exam.q: State what is meant by the relative atomic mass of an element.
model: The (weighted) mean/average mass of the atoms of the element (1).
Taking into account the abundance of the isotopes / compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (1).
exam.tip: Mention average and isotopes or carbon-12.

exam.q: The relative atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5. Explain why it is not a whole number.
model: Chlorine exists as (a mixture of) isotopes / chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 (1).
Ar is the (weighted) average mass of these isotopes (1).
exam.tip: Use the word isotopes.

exam.q: Bromine consists of 50% bromine-79 and 50% bromine-81. Calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine.
exam.tip: Equal abundance gives the simple mean, but still show the method.

exam.q: Gallium has two isotopes, Ga-69 (60%) and Ga-71 (40%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium to one decimal place.
exam.tip: Check it is closer to 69.

exam.q: Which is the relative atomic mass of an element with isotopes of mass 6 (abundance 7.5%) and 7 (abundance 92.5%)? A 6.1  B 6.5  C 6.9  D 7.5
model: C
exam.tip: Answer must be close to 7, the more abundant isotope.

exam.q: Boron contains the isotopes boron-10 and boron-11 in the ratio 1 : 4. Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.
exam.tip: Divide by the sum of the ratio.

exam.q: Silicon has three isotopes: Si-28 (92%), Si-29 (5%) and Si-30 (3%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon. Give your answer to one decimal place.
exam.tip: One term per isotope.

exam.q: An element X has two isotopes, X-63 and X-65. The relative atomic mass of X is 63.5. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
exam.tip: Let one abundance be x and the other 100 - x.

exam.q: A sample of an element contains isotopes with mass numbers 20 and 22 only. The relative atomic mass of the element is 20.2. Explain, without calculation, which isotope is more abundant, and then calculate its percentage abundance.
model: The isotope of mass 20 is more abundant (1).
Because Ar is closer to 20 than to 22 (1).
x = 90, so mass-20 isotope is 90% (1).
exam.tip: Give a reason before calculating.

exam.q: Describe how the existence of isotopes affects the relative atomic masses of elements, and explain how the relative atomic mass of an element with two isotopes is calculated from its isotope masses and abundances. Use chlorine (Cl-35 75%, Cl-37 25%) as an example.
model: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so different masses.
Most elements exist as a mixture of isotopes in fixed proportions (abundances).
Ar is the weighted mean mass of the atoms compared with carbon-12, so it is often not a whole number.
Multiply each isotope mass by its abundance: 35 x 75 = 2625 and 37 x 25 = 925.
Add and divide by the total abundance: 3550 / 100 = 35.5.
Ar is closer to 35 because chlorine-35 is more abundant; no single atom has mass 35.5.
exam.tip: Link the explanation to a full calculation.

worked.q: Copper is often given in data questions as 70% Cu-63 and 30% Cu-65. Calculate the relative atomic mass from these data to one decimal place.
steps: Multiply each mass by its abundance: 63 x 70 = 4410 and 65 x 30 = 1950.
Add the products: 4410 + 1950 = 6360.
Divide by the total abundance (100): 6360 / 100 = 63.6.
Check: 63.6 lies between 63 and 65 and is closer to 63, the more abundant isotope.

worked.q: The bar chart for an element shows isotopes of mass 24, 25 and 26 with relative abundances 8, 1 and 1. Calculate the relative atomic mass.
steps: These are relative abundances, so total abundance = 8 + 1 + 1 = 10.
Mass x abundance: 24 x 8 = 192, 25 x 1 = 25, 26 x 1 = 26.
This matches magnesium on the periodic table.
worked.ans: Ar = 24.3 (magnesium)

worked.q: Rubidium has isotopes Rb-85 and Rb-87 and a relative atomic mass of 85.5. Calculate the percentage abundance of Rb-85.
steps: Let % of Rb-85 = x, so % of Rb-87 = 100 - x.

chem_edx.1.4.summary: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements known at the time in order of **increasing relative atomic mass**, but he also put elements with **similar properties (and similar compounds)** into the same groups. To make this work he **left gaps** for undiscovered elements and **swapped the order** of some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine. He used the gaps to **predict the properties** of missing elements like germanium, and when these were discovered with properties that matched, his table was accepted. We now know the pair swaps were needed because the true order is by atomic number, and relative atomic mass is affected by the **relative abundance of isotopes**.

core.h: The problem chemists faced in the 1800s
core.p: By the 1860s about 60 elements were known. Chemists had measured their **atomic weights** (what we now call relative atomic masses) and knew that some elements, such as lithium, sodium and potassium, behaved in very similar ways. They wanted a way of organising the elements that showed these patterns. Protons, neutrons and electrons had not yet been discovered, so atomic number could not be used.
bullets: Only relative atomic masses and chemical properties were available to sort elements.
Earlier attempts (for example Newlands' law of octaves) ordered elements by atomic weight but forced elements into groups where they did not fit.
Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869.
His key ideas were to group by properties, leave gaps and make predictions.

callouts.p: Mendeleev could not order by atomic number because subatomic particles had not been discovered; he used relative atomic mass.

core.p: Mendeleev arranged the elements known at the time in order of **increasing relative atomic mass**. He then placed them in rows and columns so that elements with **similar properties** lined up in the same vertical column (group). Crucially, he did not let mass order alone decide where an element went: if an element's properties did not fit, he changed its position.
bullets: Elements were placed in order of increasing relative atomic mass.
Elements with similar chemical properties were placed in the same group.
He used the properties of the elements **and their compounds** to decide the groups.
He left gaps where no known element fitted.
He swapped some pairs of elements so that they sat with elements of similar properties.

callouts.p: Mendeleev arranged the elements known at that time in a periodic table by using the properties of these elements and their compounds.

core.h: Using the properties of elements and their compounds
core.p: Mendeleev looked closely at how each element reacted and at the **formulae of its compounds**, especially oxides and chlorides. Elements that formed compounds with the same type of formula, and had similar properties, went into the same group. This is why the groups in his table genuinely contained 'families' of elements.
bullets: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water and form oxides with formula M2O, so they go together.
Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are reactive non-metals that form similar compounds, so they form a group.
Carbon and silicon both form oxides with formula XO2 and chlorides XCl4.
Similar compound formulae show a similar combining power, which we now link to the number of outer electrons.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'properties of the elements and their compounds', not just 'properties'.

core.p: If the next element by mass did not have properties that matched the group it would fall into, Mendeleev concluded that an element was **missing** and left a **gap**. This was a bold step: instead of forcing elements into the wrong place, he assumed some elements had simply not yet been discovered.
bullets: For example, after zinc the next known element was arsenic, but arsenic behaves like phosphorus, not like aluminium or silicon.
So he left two gaps between zinc and arsenic, below aluminium and below silicon.
He called these missing elements eka-aluminium and eka-silicon ('eka' means 'one beyond').
These were later discovered as gallium and germanium.

callouts.p: By leaving gaps, Mendeleev made sure that elements in each group had similar properties.

core.h: Predicting the properties of missing elements
core.p: Because each gap sat in a group, Mendeleev could **predict the properties** of the missing element from the properties of the elements above and below it and on either side. He predicted its relative atomic mass, density, appearance and the formulae of its compounds. His most famous prediction was eka-silicon, the element below silicon.
bullets: Properties in a group change gradually (show trends), so a missing element should have values between its neighbours.
He predicted eka-silicon would have a relative atomic mass of about 72 and a density of about 5.5 g/cm3.
He predicted it would form an oxide with formula XO2 and a chloride with formula XCl4, like silicon.
Germanium was discovered in 1886 and its properties matched his predictions very closely.

callouts.p: Mendeleev used his table to predict the existence and properties of some elements not then discovered.

core.h: Predictions confirmed: gallium, scandium and germanium
core.p: Within about 17 years of his table, three of Mendeleev's missing elements were found, and each had properties close to his predictions. This turned his table from an interesting idea into a widely accepted scientific model.
bullets: Gallium (eka-aluminium) was discovered in 1875.
Scandium (eka-boron) was discovered in 1879.
Germanium (eka-silicon) was discovered in 1886.
Each discovery fitted into a gap in the right group with the predicted properties.
Later, the noble gases were discovered (argon in 1894) and fitted neatly as a whole new group.

callouts.p: Mendeleev's predictions were tested and found to be correct when the missing elements were discovered, so scientists accepted his periodic table.

core.h: Why making predictions was so important
core.p: A good scientific theory does more than explain what is already known: it makes **predictions that can be tested**. Mendeleev's table predicted elements nobody had seen. When those predictions came true, it gave strong evidence that the table reflected a real pattern in nature.
bullets: Earlier tables only described known elements, so they could not be tested in the same way.
Mendeleev's correct predictions persuaded other scientists to accept his table.
This is an example of how scientific ideas gain acceptance: predictions, testing and evidence.
His table was also flexible enough to absorb a whole new group (the noble gases) when they were discovered.

callouts.p: If asked why Mendeleev's table was accepted, the best answer refers to his predictions being confirmed by the discovery of elements such as germanium.

core.p: Strict order of relative atomic mass would put iodine (126.9) before tellurium (127.6). That would place iodine in the same group as oxygen, sulfur and selenium, and tellurium with the halogens, which is wrong because iodine clearly behaves like chlorine and bromine. Mendeleev therefore **swapped** them so that each was in the group with similar properties.
bullets: Tellurium Ar = 127.6; iodine Ar = 126.9.
By mass alone, iodine would come first and fall in the oxygen group.
Iodine's properties match the halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine), so Mendeleev put it there.
Tellurium's properties match sulfur and selenium, so it went in that group.
He trusted chemical properties over the measured masses.

callouts.t: Do not say he got it wrong
callouts.p: Swapping tellurium and iodine was correct. It is ordering by mass that would have been wrong.

core.h: Why ordering by mass does not always work: isotopes
core.p: Mendeleev **thought** he had arranged the elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass, and he believed the few exceptions were due to errors in measuring atomic weights. In fact the masses were measured correctly. The real reason is **isotopes**: relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of the masses of an element's isotopes, so it depends on their **relative abundance**, not just on the number of protons.
bullets: The correct order of the elements is by atomic number (number of protons).
Relative atomic mass depends on protons AND neutrons, and on how common each isotope is.
Tellurium has 52 protons; iodine has 53, so tellurium really does come first.
But a large proportion of tellurium atoms are heavy isotopes (with many neutrons), such as tellurium-128 and tellurium-130.
Iodine exists naturally as just one isotope, iodine-127.
So tellurium's weighted mean mass (127.6) ends up greater than iodine's (126.9), even though tellurium has fewer protons.

callouts.p: Mendeleev thought he had arranged elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass, but this was not always true because of the relative abundance of isotopes of some pairs of elements.

core.h: Other pairs out of mass order
core.p: Tellurium and iodine is the classic example, but there are other pairs in the modern periodic table where the element with the higher atomic number has the lower relative atomic mass. The cause is always the same: the relative abundance of their isotopes.
bullets: Argon (Z = 18, Ar = 39.9) comes before potassium (Z = 19, Ar = 39.1).
Most argon atoms are argon-40, while most potassium atoms are potassium-39.
Argon was not known in 1869; when noble gases were found they had to be placed before the alkali metals, again out of mass order.
Cobalt (Z = 27) comes before nickel (Z = 28) even though cobalt's Ar (58.9) is slightly higher than nickel's (58.7).
These pairs are only correctly ordered when atomic number is used.

callouts.p: On the data sheet, compare the top numbers (relative atomic mass) of argon and potassium: the order looks 'wrong' by mass but is correct by atomic number.

core.h: Mendeleev's table compared with the modern periodic table
core.p: The modern periodic table keeps Mendeleev's key idea of groups of similar elements, but it is ordered by **atomic number**. When this is done, the pair swaps happen automatically and no special exceptions are needed. This confirms that Mendeleev's decisions based on properties were correct.
bullets: Mendeleev: ordered by relative atomic mass, with gaps and swaps.
Modern: ordered by atomic number, no gaps, no swaps needed.
Both: groups of elements with similar properties in vertical columns.
Modern table includes the noble gases (group 0), which Mendeleev's original table did not.

core.p: These questions are often 2 to 6 marks and reward specific key words. Learn the three big ideas: arranged by atomic mass and properties, gaps with predictions, swaps explained by isotopes.
bullets: Always use 'relative atomic mass' (or 'atomic weight'), not 'atomic number', for Mendeleev's ordering.
Say he grouped elements with **similar properties** using properties of **elements and their compounds**.
Say he **left gaps** for **undiscovered elements** and **predicted their properties**.
Name an example: eka-silicon / germanium.
For the problem with mass order: name the pair (Te and I) and explain using **relative abundance of isotopes**.
In 6-mark answers, link each action to a reason.

callouts.p: Mendeleev did NOT order by atomic number. Protons had not been discovered.

analogy.p: Imagine arranging students for a photo in order of height, but also making sure friends from the same club stand in the same column. Usually height order works, but sometimes a slightly shorter student has to stand after a taller one so they are in their club's column, and you leave empty spaces for club members who are absent, predicting roughly how tall they will be. Mendeleev did the same: height is relative atomic mass, clubs are groups of similar elements, and the spaces are gaps for undiscovered elements. Where it breaks down: in a photo, height is the 'real' order; for elements, mass is not the true basis at all, atomic number is, and the mismatches come from isotope abundance rather than people simply being out of line.

terms.d: An arrangement of the elements in which elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical groups.
Russian chemist who published a periodic table in 1869, ordering elements by relative atomic mass and grouping by properties.
The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; called atomic weight in Mendeleev's time.
The historical name for relative atomic mass, used by Mendeleev.
A vertical column of elements with similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table.
A space Mendeleev left in his table for an element he believed existed but had not yet been discovered.
A statement about the properties of something not yet observed, which can be tested; Mendeleev predicted properties of missing elements.
Mendeleev's name for the missing element below silicon, later discovered as germanium (1886).
Mendeleev's name for the missing element below aluminium, later discovered as gallium (1875).
Placing two elements out of mass order, such as tellurium before iodine, so they fit groups with similar properties.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The proportion of the atoms of an element that are each isotope; it affects the element's relative atomic mass.
The number of protons in the nucleus; the basis for ordering the modern periodic table.
Group 7 elements such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine, which have similar properties.

mistakes.w: Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic number.
mistakes.r: He arranged them in order of increasing relative atomic mass; atomic number was not known then.

mistakes.w: Mendeleev put the elements in order of mass and nothing else.
mistakes.r: He also grouped elements by similar properties of the elements and their compounds, left gaps and swapped pairs.

mistakes.w: Mendeleev left gaps because he could not fit elements in.
mistakes.r: He left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and predicted their properties.

mistakes.w: Tellurium and iodine are out of order because their masses were measured wrongly.
mistakes.r: The masses are correct; the order differs because of the relative abundance of their isotopes.

mistakes.w: Iodine has more neutrons so it is heavier.
mistakes.r: Tellurium has the higher Ar because a large proportion of its atoms are heavy isotopes; iodine has one isotope, iodine-127.

mistakes.w: His table was accepted because it included all the elements.
mistakes.r: It was accepted because his predictions of undiscovered elements (e.g. germanium) were later shown to be correct.

mistakes.w: Mendeleev included the noble gases in a group.
mistakes.r: The noble gases had not been discovered in 1869; they were added later.

mistakes.w: Swapping tellurium and iodine was a mistake in his table.
mistakes.r: The swap was correct and is confirmed by ordering by atomic number in the modern table.

exam.q: State how Mendeleev ordered the elements in his periodic table.
model: In order of (increasing) relative atomic mass / atomic weight.
exam.tip: Not atomic number.

exam.q: Give two reasons why Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table.
model: For elements that had not yet been discovered (1).
So that elements with similar properties were in the same group (1).
exam.tip: Both the 'undiscovered' and the 'similar properties' ideas.

exam.q: Explain how Mendeleev used his table to predict the properties of undiscovered elements.
model: He used the gaps in the table / the position of the gap in a group (1).
He used the properties of the neighbouring elements (in the same group) to predict the properties of the missing element (1).
exam.tip: Mention neighbouring elements.

exam.q: Which element was predicted by Mendeleev as eka-silicon? A gallium  B germanium  C scandium  D tin
model: B
exam.tip: Eka-silicon is below silicon in group 4.

exam.q: Mendeleev predicted that eka-silicon would form an oxide with the formula XO2. Explain why he made this prediction.
model: Eka-silicon was in the same group as carbon and silicon (1).
Carbon and silicon form oxides with formula CO2 / SiO2, and elements in the same group form compounds with similar formulae (1).
exam.tip: Link the group to compound formulae.

exam.q: Explain why the discovery of germanium helped scientists to accept Mendeleev's periodic table.
model: Germanium's properties matched Mendeleev's predictions (for eka-silicon) (1).
This showed his table (and its predictions) was correct / gave evidence for it (1).
exam.tip: Predictions confirmed = evidence.

exam.q: Tellurium has a relative atomic mass of 127.6 and iodine has a relative atomic mass of 126.9. Explain why Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine in his table.
model: Iodine has similar properties to the elements in group 7 / the halogens (e.g. chlorine and bromine) (1).
Tellurium has similar properties to the elements in group 6 (e.g. sulfur and selenium), so they were swapped (1).
exam.tip: Properties beat mass order.

exam.q: Explain why tellurium has a higher relative atomic mass than iodine, even though iodine has a higher atomic number.
model: Relative atomic mass depends on the masses and relative abundances of an element's isotopes (1).
A high proportion of tellurium atoms are heavy isotopes / have many neutrons (1).
Iodine has only one isotope (iodine-127), so its mean mass is lower (1).
exam.tip: Use the phrase relative abundance of isotopes.

exam.q: Argon (Ar 39.9) is placed before potassium (Ar 39.1) in the modern periodic table. Explain why this is correct even though it is not in order of relative atomic mass.
model: The modern table is ordered by atomic number; argon has 18 protons and potassium 19 (1).
Argon's properties match the noble gases and potassium's match the alkali metals (1).
Argon has a higher Ar because most argon atoms are the heavier isotope argon-40 (relative abundance of isotopes) (1).
exam.tip: Atomic number, properties, isotopes.

exam.q: Describe how Mendeleev arranged the elements in his periodic table and explain how he dealt with the problems he found. Refer to gaps, predictions and the order of some pairs of elements.
model: He arranged the known elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass.
He put elements with similar properties (of the elements and their compounds) in the same groups.
Where no known element fitted, he left gaps for elements not yet discovered.
He predicted the properties of the missing elements from neighbouring elements, e.g. eka-silicon, later discovered as germanium with matching properties.
He swapped some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, so they were in groups with similar properties.
He thought he had ordered by relative atomic mass, but these pairs are out of mass order because of the relative abundance of isotopes; the modern table uses atomic number.
exam.tip: Cover all three ideas: arrangement, gaps and predictions, pair swaps with isotope explanation.

worked.q: Model answer: A student says 'Mendeleev just listed the elements by mass.' Use the example of iodine to explain why this is not true.
steps: State the actual method: Mendeleev ordered elements by increasing relative atomic mass but grouped elements with similar properties together.
Give the data: iodine Ar = 126.9 is less than tellurium Ar = 127.6.
Apply: by mass alone iodine would come before tellurium and sit in the group with oxygen, sulfur and selenium.
Explain: iodine's properties are like chlorine and bromine, so Mendeleev placed it after tellurium with the halogens.
Conclude: he let properties override strict mass order.
worked.ans: Mendeleev did not just list by mass: he swapped tellurium and iodine so iodine was in the halogen group with elements of similar properties.

worked.q: Applied example: Silicon has Ar 28 and density 2.3 g/cm3; tin has Ar 119 and density 7.3 g/cm3. Eka-silicon lies between them in the group. Show how Mendeleev could estimate the Ar and density of eka-silicon, and compare with germanium (Ar 72.6, density 5.35 g/cm3).
steps: Properties change gradually down a group, so the missing element should lie roughly halfway between its neighbours above and below.
Estimate Ar: (28 + 119) / 2 = 73.5, close to Mendeleev's prediction of about 72.
Estimate density: (2.3 + 7.3) / 2 = 4.8 g/cm3, which is in the right range (Mendeleev predicted about 5.5).
Compare: germanium has Ar 72.6 and density 5.35 g/cm3, close to these estimates.
Conclusion: the trend-based prediction was confirmed, supporting the table.
worked.ans: Estimates of Ar about 73 and density about 5 g/cm3 agree well with germanium (72.6 and 5.35 g/cm3), showing how gaps allowed accurate predictions.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why argon and potassium appear out of order of relative atomic mass in the modern periodic table.
steps: Give the data: argon Z = 18, Ar = 39.9; potassium Z = 19, Ar = 39.1.
The modern table is ordered by atomic number, so argon comes first.
Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of the isotopes and depends on their relative abundance.
Almost all argon atoms are argon-40, while most potassium atoms are potassium-39.
So argon's mean mass is higher even though it has fewer protons.
worked.ans: Because of the relative abundance of their isotopes, argon (fewer protons) has a higher Ar than potassium; ordering by atomic number puts them correctly.

chem_edx.1.5.summary: The modern periodic table arranges every element in order of **increasing atomic number** (the number of protons in the nucleus), so each element has a unique position. Horizontal rows are **periods** and vertical columns are **groups**; elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer electrons. A stepped (staircase) line splits the table into **metals** on the left and centre and **non-metals** on the right, a division that is explained by atomic structure: metal atoms tend to lose electrons to form positive ions, while non-metal atoms tend to gain or share electrons.

core.p: Every element is defined by its **atomic number (Z)**, which is the **number of protons in the nucleus** of one of its atoms. No two elements share an atomic number, so it acts like a unique ID. The atomic number is also the element's **position** in the periodic table: hydrogen is 1st, helium 2nd, lithium 3rd and so on.
bullets: Atomic number = number of protons in the nucleus.
In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons = atomic number.
Changing the number of protons changes the element; changing neutrons only gives an isotope of the same element.
The atomic number is the smaller of the two numbers on a periodic table tile; the larger is the relative atomic mass.
Moving one place to the right along a period adds **one proton** (and one electron).

callouts.p: The atomic number of an element is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of that element. It is equal to the position of the element in the periodic table.
Every atom of a particular element has the same number of protons; atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.

core.h: Arranged in order of increasing atomic number
core.p: In the modern periodic table the elements are placed in order of **increasing atomic number**, reading left to right along each row, then continuing on the next row. This is different from Mendeleev, who used relative atomic mass. Ordering by atomic number puts pairs such as argon (Z = 18) and potassium (Z = 19) the right way round, even though argon has the larger relative atomic mass.
bullets: Order = increasing atomic number (proton number), not increasing mass.
Ordering by atomic number means every element falls into the group that matches its properties, with no swaps needed.
Example: Ar (Z = 18, Ar = 40) comes before K (Z = 19, Ar = 39); argon is a noble gas and potassium is a reactive alkali metal.
Example: Te (Z = 52) comes before I (Z = 53), so iodine sits with the other halogens in group 7.
Atomic number explains why there are no gaps left for undiscovered elements between known ones: every whole number from 1 upwards is one element.

callouts.p: Chemical properties depend on electrons, and the number of electrons in an atom equals its atomic number. So ordering by atomic number automatically lines up elements with similar electron arrangements.
Do not write that the modern table is arranged by atomic mass or by mass number. That was Mendeleev's starting point.

core.p: A **period** is a horizontal row of the periodic table. Along a period, the atomic number goes up by one each step. All elements in the same period have the **same number of occupied electron shells**, and the period number equals that number of shells.
bullets: Period 1: only H and He (one shell).
Period 2: Li to Ne (two shells). Period 3: Na to Ar (three shells).
Each period starts with a reactive metal in group 1 and ends with an unreactive noble gas in group 0.
Properties change gradually across a period, from metallic on the left to non-metallic on the right.
Period number = number of occupied shells (detail of electron configurations is in 1.19-1.20).

callouts.p: A horizontal row of elements in the periodic table.

core.p: A **group** is a vertical column. Elements with **similar chemical properties** are placed in the same group. This is because they have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**, and it is the outer electrons that take part in reactions.
bullets: Main groups are numbered 1 to 7, then group 0 (the noble gases).
Group 1 = alkali metals (Li, Na, K...), react vigorously with water.
Group 7 = halogens (F, Cl, Br, I), reactive non-metals.
Group 0 = noble gases (He, Ne, Ar...), very unreactive.
The transition metals form a central block between groups 2 and 3.
For groups 1 to 7, group number = number of outer-shell electrons; group 0 elements have a full outer shell.

callouts.p: A vertical column of elements in the periodic table; elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
In explanations always link: same group, so same number of outer electrons, so similar chemical properties.

core.h: Reading the layout of the table
core.p: The diagram shows the main-group part of the table for periods 1 to 4. Group numbers run along the top and period numbers down the side. The thick stepped line separates metals (blue) from non-metals (yellow).
bullets: Hydrogen sits at the top but is a non-metal and does not truly belong to group 1.
Helium is placed in group 0 because it is unreactive, even though it has only 2 outer electrons.
The staircase line starts between boron and aluminium and steps down to the right.
Transition metals (not shown) would sit between groups 2 and 3 from period 4 onwards.

core.h: Metals and non-metals: where they are
core.p: About three quarters of the elements are **metals**. They are found on the **left** and in the **centre** of the periodic table (groups 1 and 2, the transition metals and the lower parts of groups 3 to 6). **Non-metals** are found on the **right** of the table, above and to the right of the stepped line, plus hydrogen.
bullets: Metals: left of the staircase line, e.g. Na, Mg, Al, Fe, Cu.
Non-metals: right of the staircase line, e.g. C, N, O, S, Cl, Ar.
Hydrogen is a non-metal despite sitting at the top left.
Metallic character increases going down a group (e.g. group 4: carbon non-metal at top, tin and lead metals at bottom).
Metallic character decreases going across a period from left to right.

callouts.p: Left of the stepped line = metal. Right of the line = non-metal. If asked to identify an element from its position, use this rule.

core.h: Why the division? Atomic structure explained
core.p: The metal / non-metal split is explained by the **number of electrons in the outer shell** and how easily the atom can reach a stable, full outer shell. **Metal atoms** have only a **few outer electrons** (usually 1, 2 or 3), so it takes less energy for them to **lose** these electrons and form **positive ions**. **Non-metal atoms** have **more outer electrons** (usually 4 to 7) and are closer to a full shell, so they tend to **gain** electrons to form **negative ions**, or **share** electrons in covalent bonds.
bullets: Metals: few outer electrons, lose electrons, form positive ions (cations), e.g. Na to Na+.
Non-metals: many outer electrons, gain electrons to form negative ions (anions), e.g. Cl to Cl-, or share electrons.
On the left of a period the outer electrons are few and held relatively weakly, so they are easily lost.
On the right of a period there are more protons pulling on the outer shell, and it is nearly full, so electrons are gained rather than lost.
Going down a group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily; this is why elements become more metallic down a group.
Noble gases (group 0) already have a full outer shell, so they neither lose nor gain electrons easily.

callouts.p: Metals form positive ions because their atoms lose electrons; non-metals form negative ions because their atoms gain electrons (or they share electrons).
Mention both the number of outer electrons AND what happens to them (lost or gained) to get both marks.
