core.h: Typical physical properties linked to position
core.p: Because metals and non-metals bond differently, they have different typical properties. You only need to use these here to back up a classification; the full property list is in 1.42.
bullets: Metals: shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, usually high melting points, solids at room temperature (except mercury).
Non-metals: dull, poor conductors (graphite is an exception), brittle when solid, usually low melting and boiling points, many are gases.
Oxides of metals are basic; oxides of non-metals are often acidic.
Elements near the staircase (such as silicon) can show some properties of each.

core.p: Once you know where an element sits you can predict a lot about it without memorising everything. The group tells you the outer electrons and so the type of ion and reactivity pattern; the side of the staircase tells you metal or non-metal.
bullets: Element in group 2, period 3 (magnesium): metal, 2 outer electrons, forms Mg2+.
Element in group 6, period 2 (oxygen): non-metal, 6 outer electrons, forms O2-.
An unknown element in group 1 will be a reactive metal forming a 1+ ion.
An unknown element in group 7 will be a non-metal that forms a 1- ion and behaves like chlorine.
Elements in the same group form compounds with similar formulae, e.g. NaCl and KCl.

callouts.p: Exams often give an unfamiliar element and its position. Use group and side of the line to predict its properties, and say WHY using outer electrons.

core.p: Mendeleev's table (1.13-1.15) was ordered mainly by relative atomic mass, and he had to swap some pairs to keep elements in groups with similar properties. The discovery of protons and isotopes showed that atomic number, not mass, is the true basis for the order.
bullets: Mendeleev: ordered by atomic mass, left gaps, swapped pairs such as Te and I.
Modern: ordered by atomic number, so the 'swaps' are no longer needed.
Mass order fails because of isotopes: an element with more heavy isotopes can have a larger relative atomic mass than the next element.
Both tables group elements with similar properties in columns.

callouts.p: If the question asks how the modern table is arranged, answer with atomic number, periods and groups. Only bring in Mendeleev if asked to compare.

core.p: For full marks on this point you should be able to do each of these quickly and use the right words.
bullets: Define atomic number as the number of protons in the nucleus.
State that elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
State that rows are called periods and columns are called groups.
State that elements in the same group have similar properties because they have the same number of outer electrons.
Identify any element as a metal or non-metal from its position relative to the stepped line.
Explain the division: metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain or share electrons.

analogy.p: Think of the periodic table as a cinema where every seat number is an atomic number: each element has its own ticket number and they sit in strict numerical order. Each row is a period, and people in the same column (group) are wearing the same team shirt, so they behave alike. The metal fans all sit on the left side of the aisle (the staircase line) and the non-metal fans on the right. Where it breaks down: in a cinema the row lengths are equal and your seat does not change how you behave, whereas periods have different lengths and an element's position is a direct result of its atomic structure, not an arbitrary choice.

terms.d: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; equal to the element's position in the periodic table.
Another name for atomic number.
A table of all elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number, in periods and groups.
A horizontal row of the periodic table; elements in a period have the same number of occupied electron shells.
A vertical column of the periodic table; elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
The highest occupied electron shell of an atom; its electrons take part in reactions.
An element found left of the stepped line whose atoms tend to lose electrons to form positive ions.
An element found right of the stepped line whose atoms tend to gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.
The group 1 elements; reactive metals with one outer electron.
The group 7 elements; reactive non-metals with seven outer electrons.
The group 0 elements; unreactive non-metals with a full outer shell.
The block of metals between groups 2 and 3.

mistakes.w: The periodic table is arranged in order of atomic mass.
mistakes.r: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

mistakes.w: Atomic number is the number of protons and neutrons.
mistakes.r: Atomic number is the number of protons only; protons plus neutrons is the mass number.

mistakes.w: Groups are the rows and periods are the columns.
mistakes.r: Periods are horizontal rows; groups are vertical columns.

mistakes.w: Elements in a group have the same properties.
mistakes.r: They have similar chemical properties, because they have the same number of outer electrons.

mistakes.w: Elements in the same period have similar properties.
mistakes.r: Properties change across a period; it is groups that contain similar elements.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is a metal because it is in group 1.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a non-metal; it is placed at the top but is not an alkali metal.

mistakes.w: Metals gain electrons to become positive.
mistakes.r: Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions; gaining electrons makes negative ions.

mistakes.w: Non-metals are on the left of the table.
mistakes.r: Metals are on the left and centre; non-metals are on the right of the stepped line.

exam.q: State what is meant by the atomic number of an element.
model: The number of protons in the nucleus (of an atom of the element).
exam.tip: Say protons, and say nucleus. Do not mention neutrons.

exam.q: Describe how the elements are arranged in the modern periodic table.
model: In order of increasing atomic number.
In horizontal rows called periods.
Elements with similar properties in vertical columns called groups.
exam.tip: Three separate ideas for three marks: order, periods, groups.

exam.q: Element X has atomic number 16. State the position of X in the periodic table.
model: It is the 16th element (period 3, group 6) - sulfur.
exam.tip: Atomic number gives the position directly.

exam.q: Using the periodic table, state whether calcium is a metal or a non-metal. Give a reason.
model: Metal.
It is on the left of the periodic table / in group 2 / left of the stepped line.
exam.tip: The reason must refer to position.

exam.q: Explain why lithium, sodium and potassium are in the same group.
model: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (one).
So they have similar chemical properties / react in similar ways.
exam.tip: Link outer electrons to similar properties.

exam.q: Argon has a greater relative atomic mass than potassium, but argon is placed before potassium. Explain why.
model: The table is arranged in order of atomic number.
Argon has a lower atomic number (18) than potassium (19) / fewer protons.
exam.tip: Atomic number, not mass, decides the order.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why sodium is classed as a metal and sulfur as a non-metal.
model: Sodium has 1 electron in its outer shell.
Sodium atoms lose this electron to form a positive ion (Na+).
Sulfur has 6 electrons in its outer shell.
Sulfur atoms gain (2) electrons to form a negative ion (S2-) / share electrons.
exam.tip: Give the outer electron number AND what happens to the electrons for each element.

exam.q: State the name given to a horizontal row in the periodic table.
model: Period.
exam.tip: Do not confuse with group.

exam.q: An element is in group 7 and period 4. Predict two properties of this element.
model: Non-metal.
Forms a 1- ion / gains one electron / has 7 outer electrons / similar reactions to chlorine.
exam.tip: Use the group to predict chemistry.

exam.q: Explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is linked to its atomic structure. Refer to atomic number, groups, periods and the division into metals and non-metals.
model: Position is set by atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus.
Elements are arranged in increasing atomic number.
Rows are periods; elements in the same period have the same number of occupied shells.
Columns are groups; elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons.
So elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
Metals (left) have few outer electrons and lose them to form positive ions.
Non-metals (right) have more outer electrons and gain or share electrons / form negative ions.
exam.tip: Six-markers reward a logical chain. Cover all four named ideas and link each one to electrons or protons.

worked.q: An element has 20 protons. Identify it, state its period and group, and say whether it is a metal or non-metal.
steps: Atomic number = number of protons = 20, so it is the 20th element: calcium.
Count along: period 1 has 2 elements, period 2 has 8, period 3 has 8, so element 19 starts period 4; element 20 is the second element of period 4.
Second column is group 2.
Group 2 is on the left of the stepped line, so it is a metal; it has 2 outer electrons which it loses to form Ca2+.
worked.ans: Calcium, period 4, group 2, a metal.

worked.q: Tellurium (Te, Ar = 127.6) has atomic number 52 and iodine (I, Ar = 126.9) has atomic number 53. Explain which comes first in the modern periodic table and why this places iodine correctly.
steps: The modern table is ordered by increasing atomic number.
Te has 52 protons, I has 53, so Te comes first even though its relative atomic mass is greater.
This puts iodine in group 7 with fluorine, chlorine and bromine.
Iodine has 7 outer electrons and reacts like the other halogens, so this is the correct group.
worked.ans: Tellurium comes first because it has the lower atomic number; this places iodine in group 7 where its properties match.

chem_edx.1.6.summary: The **electronic configuration** of an atom shows how its electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus, written as numbers separated by dots, for example sodium is **2.8.1**. For the first 20 elements the first shell holds up to **2** electrons and the next two shells hold up to **8** each, with any further electrons (in potassium and calcium) going into the fourth shell. The configuration tells you the element's position: the **number of occupied shells = period number** and the **number of outer-shell electrons = group number** (with full outer shells in group 0).

core.p: Electrons in an atom occupy **energy levels** called **shells**. An electronic configuration lists how many electrons are in each shell, starting with the shell closest to the nucleus. It can be shown as a **diagram** (circles with dots or crosses) or in **written form** such as 2.8.1.
bullets: Number of electrons in a neutral atom = atomic number (number of protons).
Electrons fill the **lowest energy shell first**, which is the shell closest to the nucleus.
Numbers are separated by dots (or commas): 2.8.1 means 2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, 1 in shell 3.
The last number is the number of **outer-shell electrons**.
The numbers must add up to the atomic number.

callouts.p: The arrangement of electrons in the shells (energy levels) of an atom.
Always add your numbers up. If they do not equal the atomic number, your configuration is wrong.

core.h: Shell capacities for the first 20 elements
core.p: For GCSE you use a simple rule. The **first shell holds up to 2** electrons. The **second shell holds up to 8**. The **third shell** takes up to 8 before the fourth shell starts to fill (this is true for the first 20 elements). Potassium (19) and calcium (20) therefore put their last electrons into the **fourth shell**.
bullets: Shell 1: maximum 2 electrons.
Shell 2: maximum 8 electrons.
Shell 3: 8 electrons before shell 4 is used (for elements 1 to 20).
Shell 4: begins with potassium (2.8.8.1) and calcium (2.8.8.2).
A shell must be filled (to its GCSE limit) before the next shell is used.

callouts.p: After argon (2.8.8) the next electron goes into the fourth shell. Potassium is 2.8.8.1 and calcium is 2.8.8.2.

core.p: You must be able to predict the configuration of any of the first 20 elements. Learn the pattern rather than the list: fill 2, then 8, then 8, then the remainder.
bullets: Period 1: H 1, He 2.
Period 4 (start): K 2.8.8.1, Ca 2.8.8.2.

core.p: In a shell diagram, the nucleus is drawn in the centre (often with its symbol or proton number) and each shell is a circle around it. Electrons are drawn as dots or crosses on the circles. Spread the electrons out, and often in pairs on the outer shell, so they are easy to count.
bullets: Draw one circle per occupied shell, innermost first.
Put the correct number of electrons on each circle (2, then up to 8, then up to 8...).
Label the nucleus with the symbol or number of protons if asked.
You do not need to show neutrons or exact positions; examiners count electrons per shell.
Make sure the total number of electrons equals the atomic number.

callouts.p: Place the 8 electrons of a full shell in four pairs (top, bottom, left, right) so the examiner can count them easily.

fig.cap: Shell diagram of a magnesium atom (atomic number 12). There are 12 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 2 in the third, so the configuration is 2.8.2.

core.h: Period number = number of occupied shells
core.p: Each new period starts when a new shell begins to fill. So the **number of shells containing electrons** in an atom equals the **period number** of the element.
bullets: H and He: 1 shell, period 1.
Li (2.1) to Ne (2.8): 2 shells, period 2.
Na (2.8.1) to Ar (2.8.8): 3 shells, period 3.
K (2.8.8.1) and Ca (2.8.8.2): 4 shells, period 4.
Count the numbers in the written configuration: 2.8.3 has three numbers, so period 3.

callouts.p: Number of occupied shells = period number.

core.h: Group number = number of outer electrons
core.p: Elements in the same group have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**. For groups 1 to 7, the **group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons**. This is the reason elements in a group have **similar chemical properties**: reactions involve the outer electrons.
bullets: Group 1: Li 2.1, Na 2.8.1, K 2.8.8.1, all end in 1.
Group 2: Be 2.2, Mg 2.8.2, Ca 2.8.8.2, all end in 2.
Group 7: F 2.7, Cl 2.8.7, all end in 7.
The last number of the configuration gives the group (for groups 1 to 7).
Group 0: outer shell is full (Ne 2.8, Ar 2.8.8, He 2).

callouts.p: Number of electrons in the outer shell = group number (groups 1 to 7).
Helium (2) has only 2 outer electrons but is in group 0, not group 2, because its outer shell is full.

core.h: The pattern on the periodic table
core.p: Putting both rules together, the periodic table is really a map of electronic configurations. Moving one step right adds one outer electron; moving one step down adds one extra shell.
bullets: Across a period: same number of shells, outer electrons increase by one each step.
Down a group: same number of outer electrons, one more shell each step.
At the end of each period (group 0) the outer shell is full, and the next element starts a new shell.
This is why the table has 2 elements in period 1 and 8 in periods 2 and 3.

core.h: Working backwards: from position to configuration
core.p: Exams often give the position and ask for the configuration, or the reverse. Use the two rules together.
bullets: Period 3, group 5: three shells, 5 outer electrons, so 2.8.5 (phosphorus).
Period 2, group 7: two shells, 7 outer, so 2.7 (fluorine).
Period 4, group 2: four shells, 2 outer, so 2.8.8.2 (calcium).
Configuration 2.8.6: three numbers so period 3, ends in 6 so group 6 (sulfur).
Configuration 2.8: full outer shell, so group 0, period 2 (neon).

callouts.p: Once you know the number of shells and outer electrons, the inner shells must all be full: 2, then 8, then 8.

core.p: Atoms react to reach a more stable arrangement, usually a **full outer shell** like a noble gas. The number of outer electrons decides how this happens, which is why elements in the same group behave alike.
bullets: Group 1 (1 outer electron): lose 1 electron to form 1+ ions, e.g. Na 2.8.1 to Na+ 2.8.
Group 2 (2 outer): lose 2 electrons to form 2+ ions.
Group 6 (6 outer): gain 2 electrons to form 2- ions.
Group 7 (7 outer): gain 1 electron to form 1- ions, e.g. Cl 2.8.7 to Cl- 2.8.8.
Group 0 (full outer shell): very unreactive, rarely lose or gain electrons.
Ion formation itself is covered in 1.21-1.24; here you just link outer electrons to properties.

callouts.p: Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways and form ions with the same charge.

core.p: Potassium is the first element in the list that needs a fourth shell. It is a common exam example because students often wrongly put 9 electrons in the third shell.
bullets: Potassium: atomic number 19, so 19 electrons.
2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, 8 in shell 3 = 18; the 19th goes in shell 4.
Configuration 2.8.8.1: four shells so period 4; 1 outer electron so group 1.
This matches its position directly below sodium (2.8.1) in group 1.

fig.cap: Shell diagram of potassium (19 electrons): 2.8.8.1. Four occupied shells place it in period 4 and its single outer electron places it in group 1, below sodium.

core.p: Make sure you can do all of the following.
bullets: Write the configuration of any element 1 to 20 in the form 2.8.1.
Draw a correct shell diagram with the right number of electrons in each shell.
State that the number of occupied shells equals the period number.
State that the number of outer electrons equals the group number (groups 1 to 7).
Recognise that group 0 elements have a full outer shell.
Deduce position from configuration and configuration from position.
Explain that elements in the same group have similar properties because they have the same number of outer electrons.

analogy.t: A block of flats with lifts
analogy.p: Imagine electrons as residents filling a block of flats from the ground floor up. The ground floor (shell 1) has only 2 rooms, floors 2 and 3 have 8 rooms each, and nobody moves upstairs until the floor below is full. The number of floors in use is the period, and how many people live on the top occupied floor is the group. Neighbours on the same top-floor count behave similarly. Where it breaks down: electrons are not fixed in rooms at exact places; shells are energy levels, and real atoms beyond calcium do not follow the simple 2, 8, 8 rule.

terms.d: The arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom, e.g. 2.8.1.
A region around the nucleus where electrons are found, each at a different energy.
The highest occupied (outermost) shell of an atom.
Electrons in the outer shell; they are involved in chemical reactions.
The number of protons in the nucleus, equal to the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
A horizontal row of the periodic table; its number equals the number of occupied shells.
A vertical column of the periodic table; for groups 1 to 7 its number equals the number of outer electrons.
An outer shell holding its maximum number of electrons (2 for shell 1, 8 for shells 2 and 3), as in noble gases.
The noble gases, whose atoms have full outer shells and are very unreactive.
A diagram showing electrons as dots or crosses on circles around the nucleus.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A tiny negatively charged particle (relative charge -1) found in shells around the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Potassium is 2.8.9.
mistakes.r: Potassium is 2.8.8.1; the third shell holds 8 before the fourth shell starts (for the first 20 elements).

mistakes.w: The first shell holds 8 electrons.
mistakes.r: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

mistakes.w: Group number is the number of shells.
mistakes.r: Group number = number of outer electrons; period number = number of shells.

mistakes.w: Helium is in group 2 because it has 2 outer electrons.
mistakes.r: Helium is in group 0 because its outer shell is full.

mistakes.w: Configuration uses the mass number to count electrons.
mistakes.r: The number of electrons in a neutral atom equals the atomic number, not the mass number.

mistakes.w: Elements in a group have the same number of shells.
mistakes.r: Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons; the number of shells increases down a group.

mistakes.w: Chlorine is 2.7.8.
mistakes.r: Shells fill from the inside out: chlorine is 2.8.7.

mistakes.w: Drawing shell diagrams with the wrong total number of electrons.
mistakes.r: The total electrons drawn must equal the atomic number.

exam.q: Give the electronic configuration of an aluminium atom (atomic number 13).
exam.tip: Check the numbers add up to 13.

exam.q: Draw a diagram to show the electronic configuration of an oxygen atom (atomic number 8).
model: Two shells drawn with 2 electrons in the first shell.
6 electrons in the second shell.
exam.tip: Draw neat circles and count your electrons.

exam.q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2.8.6. State the group and period of this element.
model: Group 6.
Period 3.
exam.tip: Last number gives group; how many numbers gives period.

exam.q: Give the electronic configuration of calcium (atomic number 20).
exam.tip: Remember the fourth shell after 2.8.8.

exam.q: Explain how the electronic configuration of an element is related to its position in the periodic table.
model: The number of (occupied) shells is equal to the period number.
The number of electrons in the outer shell is equal to the group number.
exam.tip: State both rules for both marks.

exam.q: Explain why sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties. Use their electronic configurations in your answer.
model: Sodium is 2.8.1 and potassium is 2.8.8.1.
Both have one electron in their outer shell.
Reactions involve outer electrons, so they react similarly / both lose one electron to form 1+ ions.
exam.tip: Write the configurations, then the shared feature, then link to properties.

exam.q: Element Q is in period 2 and group 5. Give its electronic configuration and name it.
model: Nitrogen.
exam.tip: Two shells, five outer electrons.

exam.q: Explain why argon is placed in group 0 rather than group 8.
model: Argon (2.8.8) has a full outer shell.
Elements with full outer shells are the noble gases, group 0 / it is unreactive.
exam.tip: Group 0 means full outer shell.

exam.q: Element X has 17 electrons. Predict, with reasons, its position in the periodic table and one chemical property.
model: Configuration 2.8.7.
Three shells, so period 3.
Seven outer electrons, so group 7.
Gains one electron to form a 1- ion / reacts like other halogens / is a non-metal.
exam.tip: Always show the configuration first; examiners award a mark for it.

exam.q: Using electronic configurations, explain the arrangement of the first 20 elements in the periodic table into periods and groups.
model: Electrons fill shells in order: first shell holds 2, second 8, third 8 (for first 20).
Hydrogen and helium fill the first shell, forming period 1 (two elements).
A new period begins each time a new shell starts to fill (Li, Na, K).
So the number of occupied shells equals the period number.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, which equals the group number.
Group 0 elements (He, Ne, Ar) have full outer shells.
Same outer electrons means similar chemical properties, which is why they are grouped together.
exam.tip: Explain why periods 2 and 3 have 8 elements: the shell holds 8.

worked.q: Write the electronic configuration of sulfur (atomic number 16) and use it to find its group and period.
steps: Number of electrons = atomic number = 16.
Shell 1 takes 2 (14 left).
Shell 2 takes 8 (6 left).
Shell 3 takes the remaining 6: configuration 2.8.6.
Three numbers, so three shells: period 3.
Last number 6, so 6 outer electrons: group 6.
worked.ans: 2.8.6; period 3, group 6.

worked.q: An element is in period 4 and group 1. Give its electronic configuration and identify it.
steps: Period 4 means 4 occupied shells.
Group 1 means 1 electron in the outer (fourth) shell.
Inner shells must be full: 2, 8, 8.
Configuration 2.8.8.1, total 19 electrons.
Atomic number 19 is potassium.
worked.ans: 2.8.8.1, potassium.

chem_edx.1.7.summary: An **ionic bond** forms when electrons are **transferred** from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other strongly. Metal atoms in **groups 1 and 2** lose 1 or 2 outer electrons to form **cations** (1+ and 2+), while non-metal atoms in **groups 6 and 7** gain 2 or 1 electrons to form **anions** (2- and 1-), so that each ion has a full outer shell like a noble gas. You must be able to show this with **dot and cross diagrams**, recall what an ion is, and work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in simple ions.

core.p: An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons (+) and electrons (-). If it loses or gains electrons, the charges no longer balance and it becomes an **ion**. The number of protons never changes when an ion forms; only the number of electrons changes.
bullets: Lose electrons: more protons than electrons, so a **positive ion (cation)**.
Gain electrons: more electrons than protons, so a **negative ion (anion)**.
The size of the charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained.
Ions can be single atoms (Na+, Cl-) or groups of atoms (e.g. sulfate SO4 2-, hydroxide OH-, ammonium NH4+).
Charge is written as a superscript after the symbol, number first then sign: Mg2+, O2-.

callouts.p: An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.
A cation is a positively charged ion; an anion is a negatively charged ion.

core.p: Atoms are more stable when they have a **full outer shell**, the same electronic configuration as a noble gas. Metals with only 1 or 2 outer electrons reach this most easily by **losing** them, exposing the full shell underneath. Non-metals with 6 or 7 outer electrons reach it most easily by **gaining** 2 or 1 electrons.
bullets: Na 2.8.1 loses 1 electron to become Na+ 2.8 (same as neon).
Cl 2.8.7 gains 1 electron to become Cl- 2.8.8 (same as argon).
Losing 7 electrons or gaining 7 would need far too much energy, so it does not happen.
The ions formed have a **noble gas electronic configuration** (a stable full outer shell).
An ion and a noble gas atom can have the same configuration but are different particles because they have different numbers of protons.

callouts.p: In ionic bonding both atoms end up with a full outer shell: the metal ion by losing electrons, the non-metal ion by gaining them.

core.p: The charge on an ion can be predicted from the group number. This is limited at GCSE to groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 for simple monatomic ions.
bullets: Group 1 (alkali metals): lose 1 electron, form 1+ ions: Li+, Na+, K+.
Group 2: lose 2 electrons, form 2+ ions: Mg2+, Ca2+.
Group 6: gain 2 electrons, form 2- ions: O2-, S2-.
Group 7 (halogens): gain 1 electron, form 1- ions: F-, Cl-, Br-, I-.
Metals always form positive ions; non-metals form negative ions.
Groups 4 and 0 do not normally form simple ions (carbon shares electrons; noble gases already have full shells).

callouts.p: Metal: charge = + group number. Non-metal: charge = -(8 - group number).

core.h: Forming an ionic bond: electron transfer
core.p: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons are **transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom**. This creates a cation and an anion. The **ionic bond** is the **strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions**.
bullets: Electrons move from metal to non-metal, never the other way.
Total electrons lost by the metal = total electrons gained by the non-metal.
Overall the compound is neutral: total positive charge = total negative charge.
The ions are held together by electrostatic attraction acting in all directions, forming a giant ionic lattice (structure details in 1.27).
Ionic bonding happens between a metal and a non-metal; two non-metals share electrons instead (covalent).

callouts.p: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
Never say electrons are shared in an ionic bond. Shared electrons means covalent bonding.

fig.cap: Sodium (2.8.1, crosses) transfers its single outer electron to chlorine (2.8.7, dots). The red arrow shows the electron being transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.

core.p: A **dot and cross diagram** shows where the electrons in the ions came from. Electrons from one atom are drawn as **dots** and from the other as **crosses**. After transfer, the ions are drawn in **square brackets** with the **charge at the top right**.
bullets: Use crosses for the metal's electrons and dots for the non-metal's (or the other way round, but be consistent).
The transferred electron appears in the anion as a different symbol from its other electrons.
Show full shells of the ions; for Na+ the outer shell shown is the full second shell.
Square brackets go around each ion, with the charge outside, top right.
You may be allowed to show only the outer shells, but the brackets and charges are always needed.
If there are two ions of one type, draw both or write a 2 in front, e.g. 2[Na]+.

callouts.p: Correct electrons in each ion, the transferred electron shown as the other symbol, brackets, and the correct charge on each ion.

fig.cap: Dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride. Na+ has 2.8 (all crosses) and Cl- has 2.8.8, with one cross in its outer shell showing the electron that came from sodium. Each ion is in square brackets with its charge.

core.p: Magnesium (2.8.2) has 2 outer electrons and oxygen (2.6) needs 2 more to fill its outer shell. So **two electrons** transfer from one Mg atom to one O atom, giving Mg2+ and O2- in a 1 : 1 ratio. Because the charges are larger (2+ and 2-), the attraction between the ions is stronger than in sodium chloride.
bullets: Mg 2.8.2 loses 2 electrons: Mg2+ 2.8.
O 2.6 gains 2 electrons: O2- 2.8.
Formula MgO (charges +2 and -2 balance).
Word equation: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide.
Balanced equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.

fig.cap: Dot and cross diagram of magnesium oxide. Mg2+ has 2.8 (crosses). O2- has 2.8 with two crosses in its outer shell, the two electrons transferred from magnesium.

core.h: Compounds with unequal numbers of ions
core.p: When the charges are different sizes, more than one of an ion is needed so that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained.
bullets: Magnesium chloride: Mg loses 2 electrons, each Cl gains only 1, so 2 Cl atoms are needed: MgCl2 (Mg2+ and 2Cl-).
Sodium oxide: O gains 2 electrons, each Na loses only 1, so 2 Na atoms are needed: Na2O (2Na+ and O2-).
Calcium fluoride: CaF2. Potassium sulfide: K2S. Calcium oxide: CaO.
In the dot and cross diagram, draw every ion or use a number in front of the bracket.
Check: total positive charge = total negative charge.

callouts.p: Electrons are not created or destroyed. Electrons lost by metal atoms must equal electrons gained by non-metal atoms.

core.h: Protons, neutrons and electrons in ions
core.p: You can calculate the numbers of subatomic particles in an ion from its atomic number, mass number and charge. **Protons and neutrons do not change** when an ion forms; only electrons do.
bullets: Protons = atomic number.
Neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
Electrons in a positive ion = atomic number - charge (e.g. Mg2+: 12 - 2 = 10).
Electrons in a negative ion = atomic number + size of charge (e.g. O2-: 8 + 2 = 10).
Na+, Mg2+, O2-, F- and Ne all have 10 electrons, the same configuration 2.8 (isoelectronic), but different numbers of protons.

callouts.p: A plus charge means electrons have been lost, so subtract. A minus charge means electrons gained, so add.

core.h: Oxidation and reduction in ion formation (Higher link)
core.p: When ions form, the metal atom loses electrons and the non-metal atom gains them. Losing electrons is **oxidation** and gaining electrons is **reduction**. You can write **half equations** to show each change.
bullets: Na -> Na+ + e- (sodium is oxidised, loses an electron).
Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl- (chlorine is reduced, gains electrons).
Memory aid OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Half equations must balance both atoms and charge.

callouts.p: Electrons appear on the right when they are lost (metal) and on the left when they are gained (non-metal).

core.p: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is strong and acts in **all directions**, so each ion is attracted to many neighbours. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces. The attraction is stronger when the charges on the ions are larger.
bullets: MgO (2+ and 2-) has stronger attractions than NaCl (1+ and 1-), so MgO has a much higher melting point.
The force is between ions, not between molecules: there are no molecules in an ionic compound.
This strength links to properties covered in 1.33 (high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved).

core.p: Make sure you can do each of these without notes.
bullets: Recall that an ion is an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.
Explain ionic bonding as the transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal atoms forming cations and anions.
Explain that the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Predict ion charges for groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 and explain them using outer electrons.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for compounds such as NaCl, MgO, MgCl2, Na2O, with brackets and charges.
Calculate protons, neutrons and electrons in simple ions.

analogy.t: Passing a hot potato to complete a set
analogy.p: Imagine two players each collecting sets of 8 cards. The metal player has a full set of 8 plus one spare card, and the non-metal player has 7 cards, one short of a set. Handing the spare card over leaves both with complete sets, which is the stable result. Now the giver is owed a card (positive) and the receiver owes one (negative), and that debt pulls them together like the electrostatic attraction. Where it breaks down: the attraction in a real ionic compound is between millions of ions in a 3D lattice in all directions, not just between one pair, and the 'debt' is a real electric charge, not a feeling.

terms.d: An atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.
A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
The movement of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom during ionic bonding.
The force of attraction between opposite electric charges.
A diagram using dots and crosses to show which atom each electron came from.
A full outer shell of electrons, as in group 0 elements; ions formed in ionic bonding have this.
A compound made of positive and negative ions held by ionic bonds, usually a metal with a non-metal.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it does not change when an ion forms.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Loss of electrons (as when a metal atom forms a positive ion).
Gain of electrons (as when a non-metal atom forms a negative ion).
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, e.g. Na -> Na+ + e-.

mistakes.w: In ionic bonding, electrons are shared between the atoms.
mistakes.r: Electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.

mistakes.w: Sodium gains a proton to become Na+.
mistakes.r: Sodium loses an electron; the number of protons does not change.

mistakes.w: Chlorine forms a Cl+ ion.
mistakes.r: Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl-, a negative ion.

mistakes.w: Electrons move from the chlorine to the sodium.
mistakes.r: Electrons move from the metal (sodium) to the non-metal (chlorine).

mistakes.w: Mg2+ has 14 electrons.
mistakes.r: Mg2+ has 12 - 2 = 10 electrons; a positive charge means electrons were lost.

mistakes.w: Dot and cross diagram with no brackets or charges.
mistakes.r: Each ion must be in square brackets with its charge shown at the top right.

mistakes.w: The ionic bond is the transfer of electrons.
mistakes.r: The transfer forms the ions; the bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

mistakes.w: Ions become noble gas atoms, e.g. Na+ turns into neon.
mistakes.r: Na+ has the same electronic configuration as neon but still has 11 protons, so it is still sodium.

mistakes.w: Oxygen forms O- by gaining 1 electron.
mistakes.r: Oxygen is in group 6 and gains 2 electrons to form O2-.

exam.q: State what is meant by an ion.
model: An atom or group of atoms with a (positive or negative) charge.
exam.tip: Include 'or group of atoms' to cover ions like sulfate.

exam.q: Give the charge on an ion of a group 2 element.
exam.tip: Metals lose electrons, so the charge is positive.

exam.q: An ion of sulfur has the formula S2-. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this ion. Sulfur has atomic number 16 and mass number 32.
model: Protons = 16.
Neutrons = 32 - 16 = 16.
Electrons = 16 + 2 = 18.
exam.tip: Negative charge means extra electrons.

exam.q: Describe how a sodium atom becomes a sodium ion.
model: The sodium atom loses one electron (from its outer shell).
Forming a positive ion / Na+ (with configuration 2.8).
exam.tip: Say 'loses one electron' and 'positive'.

exam.q: Draw a dot and cross diagram to show the ions in magnesium oxide. Show outer electrons only.
model: Mg2+ with no outer electrons shown / with a full outer shell of 8 crosses (from inner shell).
O2- with 8 outer electrons, 6 dots and 2 crosses.
Square brackets and correct charges 2+ and 2- on both ions.
exam.tip: Show the 2 transferred electrons as a different symbol.

exam.q: Explain why the formula of calcium chloride is CaCl2.
model: Calcium forms Ca2+ (loses 2 electrons); chlorine forms Cl- (gains 1 electron).
Two chloride ions are needed to balance the charge / accept the 2 electrons.
exam.tip: Link charges to the ratio.

exam.q: Write a half equation for the formation of a potassium ion from a potassium atom.
exam.tip: Electron on the right because it is lost.

exam.q: Explain why fluorine forms an ion with a 1- charge but magnesium forms an ion with a 2+ charge.
model: Fluorine has 7 outer electrons (2.7).
It gains 1 electron to get a full outer shell, so 1- charge.
Magnesium has 2 outer electrons (2.8.2).
It loses 2 electrons to get a full outer shell, so 2+ charge.
exam.tip: Give configuration, gain or loss, and the full shell for each atom.

exam.q: Sodium reacts with oxygen to form sodium oxide, Na2O. Explain, in terms of electrons, how the ionic bonds form.
model: Each sodium atom transfers/loses 1 electron.
The oxygen atom gains 2 electrons, so 2 sodium atoms are needed.
Forming Na+ and O2- ions, each with a full outer shell / 2.8.
Oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic attraction (ionic bond).
exam.tip: End with the electrostatic attraction; that is the bond.

exam.q: Explain how ionic bonding occurs in magnesium chloride. In your answer refer to the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions, the movement of electrons and the forces holding the compound together.
model: Magnesium is 2.8.2 and is in group 2; chlorine is 2.8.7 and is in group 7.
Electrons are transferred from magnesium to chlorine.
Magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons forming Mg2+ (2.8).
Each chlorine atom gains 1 electron forming Cl- (2.8.8).
So two chlorine atoms are needed for each magnesium: MgCl2.
The ions have full outer shells / noble gas configurations.
Oppositely charged ions are held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction (ionic bonds) in all directions.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence: atoms, transfer, ions, ratio, attraction.

worked.q: Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion 27Al3+ (aluminium, atomic number 13, mass number 27).
steps: Protons = atomic number = 13.
Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 27 - 13 = 14.
A 3+ charge means 3 electrons have been lost.
Electrons = 13 - 3 = 10.
worked.ans: 13 protons, 14 neutrons, 10 electrons.

worked.q: Describe, with a dot and cross description, the formation of potassium sulfide, K2S.
steps: Potassium (group 1) is 2.8.8.1; sulfur (group 6) is 2.8.6.
Each potassium atom loses 1 electron to form K+ (2.8.8).
The sulfur atom needs 2 electrons for a full outer shell, so it gains 1 electron from each of two potassium atoms.
It becomes S2- (2.8.8): in the diagram its outer shell has 6 dots and 2 crosses.
Draw 2 [K]+ and [S]2- each in square brackets with charges.
Charges balance: 2 x (+1) + (-2) = 0, so the formula is K2S.
worked.ans: Two K atoms each transfer one electron to one S atom, giving 2K+ and S2- held by electrostatic attraction: K2S.

worked.q: Identify which of these has the same number of electrons as an argon atom: Na+, Cl-, Mg2+, O2-.
steps: Argon has 18 electrons (2.8.8).
Na+: 11 - 1 = 10 electrons.
Cl-: 17 + 1 = 18 electrons.
Mg2+: 12 - 2 = 10 electrons.
O2-: 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.
worked.ans: Cl- (18 electrons, 2.8.8).

chem_edx.1.8.summary: The name of an ionic compound tells you exactly which ions it contains: the metal (positive ion) comes first and keeps its name, and the non-metal part comes second. An ending of **-ide** means the negative ion is a single element (usually), while **-ate** means the negative ion contains that element joined to **oxygen**. To deduce a formula you balance the charges so the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, because every ionic compound is **electrically neutral** overall.

core.p: An ionic compound is made of positive ions (cations, usually from metals) and negative ions (anions, from non-metals or groups of atoms). The name and the formula are two ways of saying the same thing: which ions are present and in what ratio.
bullets: The **positive ion is always named first**, e.g. sodium chloride, calcium carbonate.
The positive metal ion keeps the name of the metal: sodium atom forms the sodium ion Na+.
The negative ion is named second and its ending changes: chlorine becomes **chloride**.
The formula shows the **simplest whole-number ratio** of ions, not a molecule.
Edexcel 1.25 asks you to explain the endings -ide and -ate; 1.26 asks you to deduce formulae from the formulae of the ions.

callouts.p: Name: metal first, non-metal second. Formula: total positive charge = total negative charge.

core.p: When a non-metal element gains electrons to form a simple negative ion, its name changes to end in **-ide**. The -ide ending tells you the compound contains **only two elements** (with the important exception of hydroxide).
bullets: chlorine to **chloride** Cl-; bromine to **bromide** Br-; iodine to **iodide** I-; fluorine to **fluoride** F-.
oxygen to **oxide** O2-; sulfur to **sulfide** S2-.
nitrogen to **nitride** N3-.
Examples: sodium chloride NaCl, magnesium oxide MgO, potassium iodide KI, calcium sulfide CaS.
A compound ending in -ide is usually a **binary compound** - made of just two elements.
**Exception: hydroxide OH-** ends in -ide but contains two elements (O and H) in the one ion.

callouts.p: The ending -ide shows that the compound contains a negative ion made from a single non-metal element (except hydroxide, OH-).

core.p: An ending of **-ate** means the negative ion is a **compound ion** containing a non-metal joined to **oxygen**. These are groups of covalently bonded atoms that carry an overall charge and stay together in reactions.
bullets: **sulfate** SO4 2- contains sulfur and oxygen.
**nitrate** NO3- contains nitrogen and oxygen.
**carbonate** CO3 2- contains carbon and oxygen.
Other -ate ions you may meet: phosphate PO4 3-.
So copper sulfide CuS has only Cu and S, but copper sulfate CuSO4 has Cu, S and O.
A compound ending in -ate contains **three or more elements**, one of which is oxygen.

callouts.p: The ending -ate shows that the compound contains a negative ion which includes oxygen as well as another element.
Sulfide S2- has no oxygen. Sulfate SO4 2- has four oxygen atoms. Mixing these up is a classic lost mark.

core.p: Most positive ions are metal ions and simply take the metal's name. The charge comes from the group number for groups 1, 2 and 3.
bullets: Group 1 metals form **1+** ions: Li+, Na+, K+.
Group 2 metals form **2+** ions: Mg2+, Ca2+, Ba2+.
Group 3: aluminium forms **Al3+**.
Transition metals can form ions with different charges, shown with Roman numerals: iron(II) Fe2+, iron(III) Fe3+, copper(II) Cu2+.
Some common ions: silver Ag+, zinc Zn2+.
The **ammonium ion NH4+** is a positive compound ion made only of non-metals - ammonium chloride is NH4Cl.

callouts.p: In iron(III) oxide, the (III) is the charge on the iron ion, 3+. It is not the number of iron atoms in the formula.

core.h: Table of ions you must know
core.p: The exam usually gives the ion formulae, but knowing the common ones makes you faster and safer. Learn these charges.
bullets: Charges on simple ions come from the number of electrons lost or gained to reach a full outer shell.
Group 6 non-metals gain 2 electrons: **2-**. Group 7 gain 1 electron: **1-**.
Compound ion charges must be learned (or read from the question).
Brackets are only used in formulae around compound ions when more than one is needed.

core.p: An ionic compound has **no overall charge**, so the ions must combine in a ratio where the positive charges cancel the negative charges exactly. This is why the formula is fixed for each compound.
bullets: Step 1: write the two ions with their charges.
Step 2: find the lowest common multiple of the charge sizes.
Step 3: work out how many of each ion are needed to reach that total.
Step 4: write the formula with the numbers as **subscripts**; leave out the charges.
Example: Na+ and Cl-: 1+ and 1- already cancel, so **NaCl**.
Example: Mg2+ and Cl-: need two Cl- for one Mg2+, so **MgCl2**.
Example: Al3+ and O2-: LCM is 6, so 2 Al3+ (6+) and 3 O2- (6-), giving **Al2O3**.

callouts.p: Electrons lost by the metal atoms equal the electrons gained by the non-metal atoms, so total positive charge equals total negative charge.

fig.cap: Balancing charges in aluminium oxide: two Al3+ ions give 6+ and three O2- ions give 6-, so the formula is Al2O3.

core.p: A quick method is to **swap** the charge numbers over and **drop** them down as subscripts, then simplify. It works because it automatically makes both totals equal.
bullets: Al3+ and O2-: swap to give Al2 O3, so Al2O3.
Ca2+ and O2-: swap gives Ca2O2, which **must be simplified** to CaO.
Mg2+ and N3-: swap gives Mg3N2.
Always **cancel to the simplest ratio** - ionic formulae are ratios, not molecules.
Check your answer: multiply each charge by its number; the totals must match.

callouts.p: Swap and drop gives Mg2O2 for magnesium oxide. The correct formula is MgO.

core.p: When you need **more than one** compound ion, put the whole ion in **brackets** and write the number outside. The subscript inside the bracket belongs to the ion itself and must never be changed.
bullets: Calcium hydroxide: Ca2+ and two OH-, so **Ca(OH)2**.
Magnesium nitrate: Mg2+ and two NO3-, so **Mg(NO3)2**.
Ammonium sulfate: two NH4+ and one SO4 2-, so **(NH4)2SO4**.
Aluminium sulfate: two Al3+ (6+) and three SO4 2- (6-), so **Al2(SO4)3**.
If only one compound ion is needed, no brackets: NaOH, CaCO3, KNO3, CuSO4.
Writing CaOH2 would mean one O and two H - wrong, because the 2 must apply to the whole OH group.

callouts.p: In Al2(SO4)3 there are 2 Al, 3 S and 12 O atoms. The 3 multiplies everything inside the bracket.

fig.cap: Calcium hydroxide needs two hydroxide ions to balance one Ca2+ ion, so OH is placed in brackets: Ca(OH)2.

core.p: Edexcel names these families specifically. Practise each type with metals from groups 1, 2 and 3.
bullets: **Oxides** contain O2-: Na2O, MgO, Al2O3, Fe2O3 (iron(III) oxide), CuO.
**Hydroxides** contain OH-: NaOH, KOH, Mg(OH)2, Ca(OH)2, Fe(OH)3.
**Halides** contain a group 7 ion (F-, Cl-, Br-, I-): KBr, CaCl2, AlCl3, MgI2.
Group 1 oxide: two 1+ ions balance one 2- ion, so M2O.
Group 2 halide: one 2+ ion needs two 1- ions, so MX2.

core.p: These are the -ate compounds named in the spec. The ion keeps its own formula and is bracketed when more than one is needed.
bullets: **Nitrates** contain NO3-: NaNO3, Ca(NO3)2, Al(NO3)3, AgNO3.
**Carbonates** contain CO3 2-: Na2CO3, CaCO3, CuCO3, Al2(CO3)3.
**Sulfates** contain SO4 2-: K2SO4, MgSO4, CuSO4, Fe2(SO4)3.
Sodium carbonate needs **two** Na+ to balance one CO3 2-, so Na2CO3 (no brackets needed for Na).
Never write CO3 as C3O or change NO3 to NO2 - that would be a different ion.

core.h: Going from formula back to name
core.p: Exams also ask you to name a compound from its formula. Identify the positive ion first, then decide whether the negative part is a single element (-ide) or contains oxygen (-ate).
bullets: KBr: potassium + bromide = **potassium bromide**.
Na2SO4: sodium + SO4 = **sodium sulfate**.
CaCO3: calcium + CO3 = **calcium carbonate**.
FeCl3: iron must be 3+ to balance three Cl-, so **iron(III) chloride**.
LiOH: **lithium hydroxide** (the -ide exception).
NH4NO3: **ammonium nitrate** - both ions are compound ions.

callouts.t: Working out a transition metal charge
callouts.p: Use the known anion charge to work back: in CuO, O is 2-, so copper must be 2+, giving copper(II) oxide.

core.p: The ratio in a formula is not arbitrary - it reflects how many electrons each atom loses or gains (from 1.21-1.24). This is the grade 9 explanation of why formulae are fixed.
bullets: Magnesium (group 2) loses **2 electrons**; each chlorine (group 7) gains **1 electron**.
So one magnesium atom must give electrons to **two** chlorine atoms: MgCl2.
Aluminium loses 3 electrons; oxygen gains 2. The smallest numbers that match are 2 Al (6 lost) and 3 O (6 gained): Al2O3.
Electrons lost = electrons gained, which is why total charges balance.
This lets you **predict** formulae for unfamiliar compounds, e.g. rubidium sulfide Rb2S, strontium bromide SrBr2.

callouts.p: Group number gives the charge for groups 1, 2, 3 (positive) and 6, 7 (2- and 1-). Elements in the same group form compounds with the same type of formula.

analogy.p: Think of positive ions sitting on one side of a see-saw and negative ions on the other. The compound only exists when the see-saw is perfectly level, so you add ions to each side until the charge weights match: one Mg2+ on one side needs two Cl- on the other. Compound ions like SO4 2- are like a single sealed suitcase - you can add more suitcases (brackets), but you can never open one and change what is inside. Where it breaks down: a real ionic solid is a giant 3D lattice with millions of ions, not one balanced pair, and the formula only gives the ratio.

terms.d: An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge because electrons have been lost or gained.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons; usually a metal ion.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons or from a group of atoms.
A compound made of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
Name ending showing the negative ion is made from a single non-metal element, e.g. chloride, oxide (exception: hydroxide).
Name ending showing the negative ion contains oxygen as well as another element, e.g. sulfate, nitrate, carbonate.
A charged group of two or more covalently bonded atoms that stays together, e.g. SO4 2-, NO3-, OH-, NH4+.
OH-, a compound ion containing oxygen and hydrogen with a 1- charge.
SO4 2-, one sulfur and four oxygen atoms with a 2- charge.
NO3-, one nitrogen and three oxygen atoms with a 1- charge.
CO3 2-, one carbon and three oxygen atoms with a 2- charge.
NH4+, a positive compound ion of nitrogen and hydrogen.
A compound containing a group 7 ion: fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide.
Having no overall charge: total positive charge equals total negative charge.
The small number after a symbol or bracket in a formula, giving how many of that atom or ion are present.
Number in brackets after a metal name, e.g. iron(III), giving the charge on the metal ion.

mistakes.w: Sodium chlorine
mistakes.r: Sodium chloride - the non-metal ion takes the -ide ending.

mistakes.w: Sulfide and sulfate mean the same thing
mistakes.r: Sulfide S2- contains only sulfur; sulfate SO4 2- contains sulfur and oxygen.

mistakes.w: CaOH2 for calcium hydroxide
mistakes.r: Ca(OH)2 - brackets are needed so the 2 multiplies the whole OH- ion.

mistakes.w: Ca2O2 for calcium oxide
mistakes.r: CaO - formulae must be in the simplest whole-number ratio.

mistakes.w: MgCl for magnesium chloride
mistakes.r: MgCl2 - one Mg2+ needs two Cl- to balance the charges.

mistakes.w: Writing charges in the final formula, e.g. Mg2+Cl2-
mistakes.r: Charges are used to work out the ratio and are then left out: MgCl2.

mistakes.w: Na(SO4)2 or NaSO4 for sodium sulfate
mistakes.r: Na2SO4 - two Na+ (2+) balance one SO4 2- (2-).

mistakes.w: Iron(III) means three iron atoms
mistakes.r: (III) is the charge on the ion, Fe3+; iron(III) oxide is Fe2O3.

mistakes.w: Hydroxide contains one element because it ends in -ide
mistakes.r: Hydroxide OH- contains oxygen and hydrogen; it is the exception to the -ide rule.

exam.q: Give the name of the compound with formula KI.
model: potassium iodide
exam.tip: Iodine becomes iodide, not iodine or iodate.

exam.q: Explain the difference between the compounds magnesium sulfide and magnesium sulfate.
model: magnesium sulfide contains only magnesium and sulfur / the -ide ending shows two elements
magnesium sulfate also contains oxygen / the -ate ending shows oxygen is present
exam.tip: Always say what -ate tells you: oxygen is present.

exam.q: The formula of the sulfate ion is SO4 2-. The formula of the aluminium ion is Al3+. Write the formula of aluminium sulfate.
model: Al2(SO4)3
exam.tip: LCM of 3 and 2 is 6. Brackets are essential.

exam.q: Write the formula of calcium nitrate. The nitrate ion is NO3-.
model: Ca(NO3)2
exam.tip: Ca2+ needs two 1- ions.

exam.q: Explain why the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO but the formula of sodium oxide is Na2O.
model: magnesium ion is Mg2+ and sodium ion is Na+ while oxide ion is O2-
one Mg2+ balances one O2- but two Na+ are needed to balance one O2- (compound has no overall charge)
exam.tip: Mention the charges and the idea of neutrality.

exam.q: Name the compound with formula Fe2O3.
model: iron(III) oxide
exam.tip: Work back: 3 O2- = 6-, so each of two Fe is 3+.

exam.q: Lithium forms Li+ ions and nitrogen forms N3- ions. Deduce the formula of lithium nitride and explain your answer.
model: Li3N
three Li+ give 3+ to balance one N3- (3-)
exam.tip: The -ide ending confirms only Li and N are present.

exam.q: Write the formula of ammonium carbonate. Ammonium ion NH4+, carbonate ion CO3 2-.
model: (NH4)2CO3
exam.tip: Two ammonium ions need brackets.

exam.q: State the number of oxygen atoms in one formula unit of Al(NO3)3.
exam.tip: 3 x 3 = 9; the outside number multiplies everything in the bracket.

exam.q: A student writes the formula of potassium sulfate as KSO4. Explain the error and give the correct formula.
model: K+ has a 1+ charge and SO4 2- has a 2- charge, so the charges do not balance
correct formula K2SO4
exam.tip: Show the charge totals in your answer.

exam.q: Using ideas about electron transfer and ion charges, explain how the names and formulae of calcium chloride, calcium carbonate and aluminium oxide are deduced.
model: calcium is in group 2 so loses 2 electrons to form Ca2+
chlorine (group 7) gains 1 electron to form Cl-; name ends in -ide as only chlorine in the anion
two Cl- balance one Ca2+ so CaCl2
carbonate ion CO3 2- contains carbon and oxygen so name ends in -ate
one Ca2+ balances one CO3 2- so CaCO3
Al loses 3 electrons (Al3+), O gains 2 (O2-); LCM 6 so 2 Al3+ and 3 O2- gives Al2O3; compound neutral overall
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a linked chain: group, electrons, ion charge, naming rule, balancing, final formula.

worked.q: Deduce the formula of iron(III) sulfate.
steps: Iron(III) means Fe3+.
Sulfate is SO4 2-.
LCM of 3 and 2 is 6.
Need 2 Fe3+ (6+) and 3 SO4 2- (6-).
Sulfate is a compound ion needed more than once, so use brackets.
worked.ans: Fe2(SO4)3

worked.q: Name the compound Mg(OH)2 and state how many atoms of each element it contains.
steps: Mg is magnesium, forming Mg2+.
OH is the hydroxide ion, OH-.
Name: magnesium hydroxide.
The 2 outside the bracket multiplies O and H.
Atoms: Mg = 1, O = 2, H = 2.
worked.ans: Magnesium hydroxide; 1 Mg, 2 O, 2 H (5 atoms in total).

worked.q: Barium is in group 2 and bromine in group 7. Predict the name and formula of the compound formed.
steps: Group 2: barium loses 2 electrons to form Ba2+.
Group 7: bromine gains 1 electron to form Br-.
Anion is a single element, so ending is -ide: bromide.
One Ba2+ needs two Br- to be neutral.
worked.ans: Barium bromide, BaBr2

chem_edx.1.9.summary: An ionic compound such as sodium chloride is not made of separate molecules. It is a **giant ionic lattice**: a **regular arrangement of ions** repeating in three dimensions, held together by **strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions** (ionic bonds). These forces act in all directions, so every ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it, which explains why ionic compounds are hard, crystalline and have high melting points.

core.p: Edexcel 1.27 asks you to explain the structure of an ionic compound as a lattice structure consisting of a **regular arrangement of ions**, held together by **strong electrostatic forces (ionic bonds) between oppositely charged ions**. Both parts are needed for full marks.
bullets: Key word 1: **lattice** - a giant, repeating 3D arrangement.
Key word 2: **regular arrangement** of positive and negative ions.
Key word 3: **strong electrostatic forces of attraction**.
Key word 4: between **oppositely charged ions**.
The forces are called **ionic bonds**.
Sodium chloride (NaCl) is the standard example.

callouts.p: A giant three-dimensional structure consisting of a regular arrangement of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

core.p: Ions form when metal atoms transfer electrons to non-metal atoms (1.21-1.24). Once the ions exist, they do not pair off - they pack together into a giant lattice.
bullets: Sodium atom loses 1 electron: Na to Na+ (2.8).
Chlorine atom gains 1 electron: Cl to Cl- (2.8.8).
Huge numbers of Na+ and Cl- ions form at once.
Opposite charges attract, so the ions pull together into the lowest-energy arrangement.
The result is a crystal containing billions of ions in a fixed ratio.

core.p: In the lattice the ions are arranged in a **regular, repeating pattern**. Each positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and each negative ion is surrounded by positive ions, so like charges are kept apart.
bullets: Ions **alternate**: + next to -, never + next to + in the nearest positions.
The pattern repeats in **all three dimensions**.
This order is why ionic compounds form **crystals** with flat faces and sharp edges.
Salt grains under a microscope look like tiny cubes because the NaCl lattice is cubic.
The ions vibrate about fixed positions in the solid but do not move from place to place.

callouts.p: Every ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge. This maximises attractions and minimises repulsions.

fig.cap: A 2D slice through a sodium chloride lattice: Na+ and Cl- ions alternate in a regular pattern, and each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.

fill='#1b2540'>pattern</text></svg>

core.p: The ions are held in place by **electrostatic forces of attraction** between oppositely charged ions. These forces are the **ionic bonds**, and they are very **strong**.
bullets: Electrostatic force = the attraction between opposite charges (like the pull between opposite poles of magnets).
Each Na+ attracts the Cl- ions around it, and each Cl- attracts the Na+ ions around it.
The forces act **in all directions** (they are non-directional), not just between one pair.
Breaking the lattice means overcoming **many** strong forces, which needs a lot of energy.
The ionic bond is **not** a pair of atoms sharing electrons - that is covalent bonding.

callouts.p: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Never say 'NaCl molecules' or 'intermolecular forces' for an ionic compound. It is a giant lattice of ions with ionic bonds.

core.p: A crucial grade 9 idea: in NaCl each Na+ is surrounded by **6** Cl- ions, and each Cl- by **6** Na+ ions. Each ion is attracted to all of its neighbours at once.
bullets: The 6 neighbours sit above, below, left, right, in front and behind.
So there is no single 'bond partner' - attractions spread out through the lattice.
This is why it is meaningless to pick out one 'NaCl unit'.
There are also weaker repulsions between like ions further apart, but attractions are greater overall.
This all-round attraction holds the ions very firmly in fixed positions.

callouts.p: In sodium chloride each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge.

core.p: An ionic lattice is called a **giant** structure because it continues in all directions until the edge of the crystal. A bigger crystal simply has more ions in the same pattern.
bullets: There is no fixed number of ions in a lattice.
A tiny salt grain contains around 10^18 ions.
The formula (NaCl) gives the **ratio** of ions (1:1), not the number in a molecule.
In MgCl2 the lattice contains twice as many Cl- ions as Mg2+ ions.
This ratio keeps the whole lattice **electrically neutral**.

callouts.p: For an ionic compound, say the formula shows the ratio of ions in the lattice. This avoids the 'molecule' trap.

core.p: Exams show ionic lattices in several ways. You need to recognise each and know its strengths and weaknesses.
bullets: **Ball-and-stick model**: shows the 3D arrangement clearly, but the sticks wrongly suggest bonds between specific pairs and the gaps are exaggerated.
**Space-filling (close-packed) model**: shows ions touching and the relative sizes, but hides inner ions.
**2D diagram**: easy to draw but shows only one layer.
**Dot-and-cross diagram**: shows electron transfer for one pair of ions but not the lattice arrangement.
No single model shows everything - links to 1.41 limitations of models.

head: Model
Shows well
Limitation
rows: Sticks are not real bonds; ions not touching
Hard to see inner ions and pattern

fig.cap: Ball-and-stick model of a cube of the NaCl lattice: small blue Na+ ions and larger green Cl- ions alternate at the corners. The sticks only show positions; ions are really packed closely together.

core.h: Why Cl- is drawn bigger than Na+
core.p: In diagrams the chloride ion is usually drawn larger than the sodium ion. This reflects real ion sizes and is a nice extension point.
bullets: Na+ (2.8) has lost its outer shell, so it has only **2 shells** of electrons.
Cl- (2.8.8) has **3 shells**, so it is larger.
In general positive metal ions are smaller than their atoms; negative ions are larger than their atoms.
Ion sizes affect how ions pack, which is why different compounds have different lattice shapes.
At GCSE you only need the NaCl cubic arrangement.

core.p: The lattice structure explains the properties covered in 1.33. Use the structure as the starting point of every property explanation.
bullets: **High melting and boiling points**: lots of energy needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
**Hard but brittle**: a force can shift a layer so like charges line up and repel, splitting the crystal.
**Do not conduct when solid**: ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move.
**Conduct when molten or dissolved**: the lattice breaks down so ions are free to move and carry charge.
Many ionic compounds **dissolve in water**, as water molecules can separate the ions from the lattice.

head: Property
Explained by
rows: Many strong ionic bonds to break

callouts.p: Molten ionic compounds conduct because ions move. Never say electrons move through an ionic lattice.

core.h: Strength of the forces: charge matters
core.p: Not all ionic lattices are equally strong. Ions with **larger charges** attract each other more strongly, so their lattices need more energy to break.
bullets: NaCl contains Na+ and Cl- (charges 1+ and 1-): melting point about 801 C.
MgO contains Mg2+ and O2- (charges 2+ and 2-): melting point about 2852 C.
Bigger charges give **stronger electrostatic attraction**.
So MgO has a much higher melting point - used as a heat-resistant lining in furnaces.
Smaller ions can also get closer together, which strengthens attraction.

callouts.p: When comparing two ionic compounds, refer to the size of the ion charges and the strength of the electrostatic forces.

core.p: Being able to contrast the ionic lattice with other structures helps in classification questions (1.32).
bullets: **Ionic lattice**: positive and negative ions; electrostatic attraction between opposite ions.
**Giant covalent** (e.g. diamond): atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout.
**Simple molecular** (e.g. water): small molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them.
**Metallic**: positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
Only ionic lattices contain both positive and negative ions arranged alternately.

core.p: Most marks for this point come from a short description of the structure. Learn a model sentence and practise adapting it to any ionic compound.
bullets: Name the structure: **giant ionic lattice**.
Describe it: **regular arrangement** of positive and negative ions, repeating in 3D.
Name the ions: e.g. Mg2+ and O2- for magnesium oxide.
Explain the bonding: **strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions**.
Add: forces act **in all directions**; each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions.

callouts.p: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice: a regular arrangement of Na+ and Cl- ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.

analogy.p: Imagine a giant 3D chessboard where every black square holds a magnet with its north pole up and every white square holds one with its south pole up. Each magnet is pulled by all its neighbours at once, so the whole block locks together firmly and the pattern repeats as far as the board goes. That maps onto the regular, alternating arrangement and the all-round electrostatic attraction. Where it breaks down: magnets are pulled by magnetic forces, but ions are held by electric charge; real ions vibrate, are different sizes, and there is no board holding them - the attractions alone hold the lattice together.

terms.d: A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
A positive ion, e.g. Na+.
A negative ion, e.g. Cl-.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of particles.
A giant 3D structure of a regular arrangement of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
The force of attraction (or repulsion) between electric charges; opposite charges attract.
Ions placed in a fixed, repeating pattern, with each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge.
A structure containing a very large, non-fixed number of particles continuing in all directions.
A solid with a regular shape and flat faces, resulting from a regular arrangement of particles.
Acting equally in all directions; ionic attractions are not between one specific pair of ions.
The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, e.g. NaCl is 1 Na+ : 1 Cl-.
Having no overall charge; total positive charge equals total negative charge in the lattice.
A model showing ions as balls and their positions joined by sticks; good for 3D shape but sticks are not real bonds.

mistakes.w: Sodium chloride is made of NaCl molecules
mistakes.r: It is a giant ionic lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions; there are no molecules.

mistakes.w: Ionic compounds have weak intermolecular forces
mistakes.r: There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

mistakes.w: The ions are held by sharing electrons
mistakes.r: Electrons are transferred; ions are held by electrostatic attraction (ionic bonds).

mistakes.w: Strong forces between atoms
mistakes.r: Strong forces between oppositely charged ions - the word ions is required.

mistakes.w: Each Na+ is bonded to one Cl-
mistakes.r: Each Na+ is surrounded by and attracted to six Cl- ions; forces act in all directions.

mistakes.w: The ions are randomly arranged
mistakes.r: The ions are in a regular, repeating arrangement.

mistakes.w: Solid ionic compounds conduct because electrons move
mistakes.r: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct; ions are fixed. They conduct when molten or dissolved because ions move.

mistakes.w: The sticks in the model are the ionic bonds
mistakes.r: The sticks only show positions; the attraction is all-round electrostatic, not a stick-like bond between pairs.

exam.q: Name the type of structure in solid sodium chloride.
model: giant ionic lattice
exam.tip: 'Giant' and 'ionic' both help; 'lattice' is the key word.

exam.q: Describe the structure of sodium chloride.
model: regular arrangement / lattice of (sodium and chloride) ions
held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
exam.tip: Two marks, two parts: arrangement and forces.

exam.q: State what is meant by an ionic bond.
model: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
exam.tip: Must mention oppositely charged ions.

exam.q: How many chloride ions surround each sodium ion in the sodium chloride lattice?
exam.tip: And six Na+ around each Cl-.

exam.q: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride.
model: Mg2+ and O2- ions have larger charges than Na+ and Cl-
so stronger electrostatic forces / more energy needed to overcome them
exam.tip: Compare charges, then link to force strength and energy.

exam.q: A ball-and-stick model of sodium chloride is shown. Give one limitation of this model.
model: sticks suggest bonds between pairs / ions not shown touching / ions not drawn to scale / only shows a small part of the lattice
exam.tip: Any one valid limitation.

exam.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
model: giant lattice with many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
a lot of (heat) energy needed to overcome these forces
exam.tip: Say 'overcome', not 'break the molecules'.

exam.q: The formula of calcium chloride is CaCl2. Explain what this formula tells you about the lattice.
model: ratio of Ca2+ ions to Cl- ions is 1:2
so the lattice is electrically neutral / not a molecule of 3 atoms
exam.tip: Ratio of ions is the key idea.

exam.q: Explain why solid potassium bromide does not conduct electricity but molten potassium bromide does.
model: in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice / cannot move
when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge
exam.tip: Mention ions, never electrons.

exam.q: Describe and explain the structure and bonding in magnesium oxide. In your answer, refer to how the ions are formed and how they are arranged.
model: magnesium atom loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+
oxygen atom gains 2 electrons to form O2-
electrons are transferred from magnesium to oxygen
ions form a giant lattice with a regular arrangement
each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions / alternating pattern in 3D
held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions acting in all directions
exam.tip: Structure the answer: ion formation, then arrangement, then forces.

worked.q: Describe the structure of potassium chloride and explain why it is a solid at room temperature.
steps: Identify ions: K+ and Cl-.
Structure: giant ionic lattice with a regular arrangement of K+ and Cl- ions.
Bonding: strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions.
Room temperature does not give enough energy to overcome these many strong forces.
So the ions stay in fixed positions and it is solid.
worked.ans: KCl is a giant ionic lattice of K+ and Cl- held by many strong electrostatic forces, which need much more energy to overcome than is available at room temperature, so it is a solid.

worked.q: In a lattice of magnesium chloride there are 3.0 x 10^20 magnesium ions. How many chloride ions are there, and what is the total number of ions?
steps: Formula MgCl2 means ratio Mg2+ : Cl- = 1 : 2.
Chloride ions = 2 x 3.0 x 10^20 = 6.0 x 10^20.
Check neutrality: 3.0 x 10^20 x 2+ = 6.0 x 10^20 x 1-.
worked.ans: 6.0 x 10^20 chloride ions; 9.0 x 10^20 ions in total.

worked.q: Melting points: NaF 993 C, MgO 2852 C. Use ideas about the lattice to explain the difference.
steps: Both are giant ionic lattices held by electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
NaF contains Na+ and F- (charges 1+ and 1-).
MgO contains Mg2+ and O2- (charges 2+ and 2-).
Higher charges mean stronger electrostatic attraction between ions.
So more energy is needed to overcome the forces in MgO.
worked.ans: MgO has higher-charged ions, so stronger electrostatic forces in its lattice need more energy to overcome, giving a much higher melting point.
